There are chances enough out there to double, treble and quadruple the present output of the country, and with that wonderful heritage at our hand I see no difficulty whatever in getting more immigration.

I went over the Transcontinental last year, and I saw people taking up the forest land in the province of Quebec and hewing out homes for themselves in the wilderness! I found the same thing in the northern part of New Brunswick. When I was in British Columbia I visited the copper mines, and found them to be simply marvellous. When we consider the resources of our country, a man would be out of his mind to insinuate for a moment that we cannot pay our debt, and at the same time carry on the public services. But we have to adopt cautious business methods in order to tide ourselves over the	next four	or five years.
We have to consider all our expenditures. This year we are expending money, which, we admit, is borrowed money -borrowed, it is true, from the people of Canada, but borrowed just the same- money which must be repaid, principal and interest. But the expenditure has to be made; therefore I am not halting a moment in proposing the expenditure which we are asking Parliament to vote us for the present year. But I am asking the House to look carefully into the condition of affairs before the coming financial year is over, with a view to seeing what we are going to do in the future, and to look carefully and from a business standpoint into the question where we are going to get the extra $100,000,000 of revenue which we shall require after this fiscal year.
I believe that Canada will go through the reconstruction period in better condition than any other of the warring nations except the United States, and possibly we shall be in as good a position as that country. We have some unemployment, but, I am happy to say, not very much. When all the works which the Government of Canada is proposing and will propose in the Estimates to be brought down in a few days, as well as the works which are foreshadowed in the speech from the Throne, are carried out; when the provinces and the municipalities do their share, and when the manufacturers and employers of labour do their duty, we shall make some progress. I think that here I ought to say what I have said in public on two or three occasions. Hundreds of firms in Canada have grown rich through carrying on war business, and it is their duty to employ every man they possibly can employ during the reconstruction period, whether they make profits or not. I do not say that they should do that to the extent of losing their capital, but if they do no more than break even, it is their duty to keep on employing men, to assist

in avoiding unemployment throughout the country. The watchword of the governments, federal and provincial, and municipal; of business men, farmers, and all who can employ labour during the next year or two, ought to be, keep unemployment out of the country if you possibly can. If we keep every man employed who ought to be employed or who wants to be employed, it is a very small question to us what our debt may be or what our method of taxation may be. If we keep our people employed for the next year or two we shall have no Bolshevism or anarchism and many of our difficulties will be solved; we shall have no trouble in getting back to ordinary conditions of civil life, and there is no reason why Canada should not go on and prosper.
Having said this, I have said all that I wish to say; I simply wanted to throw out this warning. I have faith in the ability of our country to overcome all obstacles.
I am confident that the people will do their share, and if this Parliament does its duty during the next year or two I have no fear for the outcome; Canada will be back to a peace basis, a richer, prouder and happier nation than ever.

The minister has invited a question, and before he concludes I want to put it to him. He asked three or four times how we were going to get this $100,000,000. Perhaps the minister, having some inside information, will tell us what he himself thinks about it.

I think I stated that I was not making a budget speech; that I was simply asking the House and the country to do some thinking. By the time the Budget is brought down, my hon. friend, as well as members on this side of the House, will have had time to give thought to the matter and the question can then, perhaps, be answered.

So far, the minister
does not know.
Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and . Guysborough): Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my old room-mate and intimate friend (Mr. McKenzie) on being appointed temporarily to the position of leader of the Liberal party. Knowing him as I do, I feel sure that he will fill the position with great credit to himself as well as to the men who have honoured him with their confidence.
I wish also to be permitted to thank the leader of the House (Sir Thomas White)
for the very generous and eloquent tribute he paid yesterday to my departed leader. The speeches yesterday were of a very high order indeed and quite worthy of the traditions of this House. I wish to add a few words on behalf of the old Liberal guard of Nova Scotia. The leader of the Opposition spoke for the Liberals of all Canada, but I want; to speak for a moment specially for the Liberals of Nova Scotia as to the loss that we have sustained in the death of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I believe that in no province of Canada, unless it be the province of Quebec, did the departed leader have a more loyal and devoted following than he had in Nova Scotia. Throughout his long career he has been admired and trusted by the Liberal party of that province. Since the days of Joseph Howe no public man has secured the confidence and devotion of the Liberals of Nova Scotia to the same extent as Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He was to the Liberals of that province what the trusted and revered Highland chieftain was in the old days to the clansmen in the Scottish glens.

I do not want to miss any of the speech of the hon. member.
I would like to hear what is said. We cannot hear very plainly, and I would, therefore, ask my hon. friend most respectfully if he would speak a little louder.

I shall endeavour to meet the wishes of my hon. friend. I am not now referring to the leaders of the party in the province of Nova Scotia; I am referring chiefly to the rank and file. In that province, in the farm houses on the hillsides and in the valleys, in the homes of the fishermen in the harbours and coves along our rock-bound coast, in the huts of the lumbermen in the forests, as well as in our more populous towns and cities, there are tens of thousands of men and women who are feeling a deep sense of personal loss in the death of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. If, Sir, you will permit me a personal reference, I have known Sir Wilfrid for a quarter of a century. I had the honour of his friendship, and it was one of my most precious possessions. I have seen him scores of times when he was dealing with questions of more or less difficulty in his own room with his friends around him, or in the secret caucus of the party, where a man is bound to show his hand, and I have never known a single occasion, whether I agreed with him or not, on which I did not believe him to be actuated by the highest and best motives.

He had in marked degree two qualities that every great statesman must possess, namely initiative and courage. In 1911, with two years of his Parliamentary term yet to run, he staked all on a great issue and lost. To be satisfied that he was right was more to him than to be successful, and time has amply vindicated his course in regard to that great question. His followers, when that contest was over, all greatly admired the cheerful way in which he accepted his defeat, and at the age of seventy again hoisted the flag on a new battlefield. He was a good loser. He was great in victory, but he was even greater in defeat. He was a true democrat; was always willing to accept the verdict of the people. His lifelong ambition was to stamp out racial and religious strife from the public life of this country, and to help build up on the northern half of this continent a great, prosperous and united Canada, a land where there would be justice for all, free scope for all, a fair reward for labour and a new home for freedom. He always stood firmly for British connection, but he used to say that loyalty is the child of freedom, and that if British connection is to be built on an enduring foundation, the Canadian people must maintain the right to manage their own affairs.
Many things have been said about Sir Wilfrid Laurier in his time, but no Canadian worthy of the name ever doubted his honour or his patriotism. He was a great Canadian, but he was more than that. His reputation was wide as the Empire itself, and his memory will be cherished by men everywhere * who love liberty and admire courage and devotion to duty. He died in harness, with his heart still young and his intellect unimpaired. The manner of his taking off is, I am sure, what he would himself have chosen. Our grief is not for him; it is for his sorrowing, stricken and lonely widow', and for ourselves. He was a diligent student all his lifetime and his mind was well stored with the classics of both languages. His English models were Shakespeare and the Bible. Amongst his heroes in the affairs of State were such men as Bright, Gladstone and Lincoln. He also had great admiration for those doughty reformers of his ov'n mother land, Mon-talembert and Lacordaire. He had a firm grasp of current literature and current events. I have frequently heard him talk in his own delightful way about books and men and events, and on such occasions I have often thought, what a pity that death will some day come and make an end at one stroke of all this accumulated store of 
knowledge and experience. The stroke came and left us only the memory of his life and the inspiration of his example; but those are precious things to possess, and we are glad, even in the midst of our sorrow, that we knew him when he was here. We can say of Sir Wilfrid what was said by an English poet of the late Lord Roberts:
Clean, simple, valiant, well-beloved.
Flawless in faith in fame.
Whom neither ease nor honours moved A hair-breadth from his aim.
And yet from life a new life springs Through all the years to come,
And glory is the least of things That follow this man home.
Mr. Speaker, I wish, in referring briefly to the Address, to associate myself with the sentiment expressed in the Speech from the Throne regarding the successful ending of.the war. After four years of what looked at one time almost like a hopeless struggle, victory at last came. Our troubles, as the Hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Car-vell) has said, are not yet over; but it is a splendid thing amidst all our anxieties that the casualty list is closed and the guns are silent. This country has reason to be proud of its record, and it has a special reason to be proud of its soldiers. When their achievements in this war are recorded there will be no more splendid story in the history of this or any other country. Kipling says that this is the first time since creation when the whole world has united to fight the devil, and we have every reason to rejoice that the world has been successful. Prussianism has been beaten into the dust by its own weapons, and its brute force has been overcome by the valour of free men inspired by the knowledge that they were fighting for right against wrong. To my mind, the most hopeful feature of the situation is the destruction of autocracy in Central Europe. War lords never flourish in a democratic country. England was very loath to go to war; so was France,; so was the United States. The establishment of responsible Government in Central Europe is the best guarantee that we can have for the future peace of the world. As I have said, we have every reason to be proud of and to rejoice in our victory; but it is not a time to tighten our purse-strings or to relax our efforts, especially in so far as our soldiers and their dependents are concerned. More than ever, now that the war is over, we must make our soldiers feel that we are not indifferent to or ungrateful for the splendid work that they have done for us during the past four year?

I would like to be permitted to quote this plank from the platform of the Liberal party in Great Britain, adopted at a conference held in Manchester in Novembei last:-
This committee pledges itself to secure that our sailors and soldiers shall have the first claim upon the consideration of Parliament as they already have upon the gratitude of the nation; that none of those who have served in the national forces shall be allowed to fall into distress either from lack of employment or from any other defect in our social organization ; that those who have been incapacitated from following their old occupations shall be freely assisted to train themselves for new employments, and shall be further assisted by the State in every practicable way to establish themselves in business or as wage earners; that the pensions from the State to disabled men and to widows and children shall be sufficient in amount to secure a satisfactory standard of comfort, and that the Pension Fund shall be generously and sympathetically administered.
This language expresses the needs of the hour so clearly that in my judgment the Liberal party of Canada could not do better than adopt it, and bend their energies to enforce it. I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) in which he informed us that large grants were to be made for certain local improvements, including highways in the provinces, and housing. He told us that the Government intends to control the expenditure of this money, that conditions are to be attached to the expenditure, and an agreement is to be made between the local and federal government before the money can be expended. I wish to enter my protest against that proposal. I do not think there should be any dictation on the part of the federal government as to how the money is to be spent by the local governments. The local governments already have their machinery; they have highway organizations, and highways by the constitution have been placed absolutely under their jurisdiction. If this Government can afford to advance the provinces' money for that purpose, well and good; but I consider it a mistake to attempt to control the local governments in any way in the expenditure of the money that is placed in their hands. To my mind it is' an insiduous way of securing control over local affairs. I have noticed in recent years when grants have been made by this Government there has been a tendency to encroach on the rights of the legislatures in the various provinces. There is no reason why this Government should direct the expenditure of highway money any more than the expenditure of money for education. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) has in his way been a sort of champion of provincial rights. He has been claiming for the Western provinces their natural resources.
But has not got them yet.
But that is his policy.
Hear, hear.

Now he is a member of this Government. Why, then does he not stand up for the rights of the provinces. Why is he asking for the natural resources to be given to the West? I assume it is in order that the Western provinces may be put in a position to manage their own local affairs. Then why not allow rll the provinces to control without Federal supervision the money that is to be expended on their highways? I submit that this policy oi attempting to control the expenditure is wrong, and while I do not wish to be understood as opposing at the present time the grant for highways, I say it should be a free grant without any strings to it. If we have money to give to the provinces, I submit, the proper way to give it would be to increase the provincial subsidies and allow the provinces to manage their own affairs. The provinces are not mendicants. They are not asking for money that does not belong to them. The money comes from the provinces in the first place, and the Provincial Governments can be trusted to expend this money just as wisely as the Federal Government possibly could.
Does my hon. friend advocate the expenditure of mis money?	.

Yes, but I am opposed to any conditions being imposed by the Federal Government in connection with its expenditure. The Minister of Public Works also referred to the construction of ships. He told us the Government had embarked on a policy of building ships, and that a very large sum of money was to be expended. He admitted he could go into the market at the present time and buy ships cheaper than he could possibly build them. If that be true, why pay more than they are worth? As far as my information goes, I believe that he is paying under these contracts about four times the normal value for the ships he is proposing to build. In normal times ships could be built for about $50 per ton dead weight; but in the contracts I have seen the Government is paying something like $200 per ton. The Government will never see

their money again; I fear it is an improvident proposal. It took the Government four years finally to make up its mind to purchase ships. The time to purchase ships if they were to be of service in the war was in 1914 when the war broke out, but the Government waited until the war was about over, and then embarked on a very expensive programme of building ships for which they propose to pay four times the normal price. Such a policy is not at all likely to promote the building of ships in Canada. If the Government could devise a way of promoting and assisting ship-building in Canada, that .would be a very wise and proper move to make, but to buy ships at four times the normal price is certainly not likely to stimulate the building of ships by private enterprise. I am not in favour of Government ownership of tramp vessels; I do not think the policy a wise one, and I do not think it will do much to solve the problem of providing employment which I understood the Minister to say was the main reason for its adoption. If that is the Government's object, I can say that I know of no other industry that gives so little employment of labour for the amount of money expended as the building of steel ships. The production of the plates and other material call for a large amount of labour, but the material in the case of the present contracts is to come chiefly from the United States. The Government could easily have found some other industry where they could have employed a larger number of people with a smaller expenditure of money. Is there not something we can do in this country that would bring us in some return? Would it not be better, for instance, to buy tractors and plough np the western prairies and produce wheat?
We would need the ships to carry the wheat.

I am afraid if we make the rates of freight correspond with the outlay on the ships the wheat would be too expensive. Would it not be a saner policy to expend part of this money in building branch lines of railway in Nova Scotia? I can show my hon. friend places in my own constituency where by the construction of a branch line, he would open up the country and encourage production and help at the same time to make the Intercolonial profitable. Building branch lines of railway where they are needed would be doing something for the country, and would be a far better policy than buying expensive ships for which there does not seem to be any future to justify the expenditure involved. 
So much for the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. The return of peace creates a new situation in this country, so far as the two old political parties are concerned. The Union Government was formed ostensibly to carry on the war. Thousands of patriotic people voted for it because they believed that to be the real reason back of it. My humble opinion is that these people were deceived. What are the results? Our brave soldiers did their full share toward winning the war, but I am not so sure about the record of the Union Government. What they have done to win the war remains to be shown. If you say they won it by means of the Military Service Act, that statement will require to be substantiated; we have yet to learn that any substantial number of the soldiers conscripted under that Act ever reached the firing line. We on this side were not deceived. We were well aware that the Union Government was formed, not to win the war, but to defeat the Liberal party and win the election. There was a zig-zag streak in it from its inception. It is obvious that if it was a war move it should have come three years earlier. But it came on the eve of the election when it was clear to the Prime Minister and to everybody else that the old Conservative-Nationalist party could not win the election. But even if, for the sake of argument, we say it was formed to win the war, the war has been won and the reason for its formation no longer exists. What is wanted now in this country is a strong and efficient government, with a united party behind it. I do not think any one will pretend that this Government has a united party behind it. The supporters of this Government, like old Gaul, are divided into three parts. There are, first, the Unionist Liberals, a distinct class by themselves. Then there are the Unionist Conservatives, who, I am told, have no great love for some of the Unionist Liberals In the third place, there are the real Conservatives, who, I am also told do not waste any affection on either of the other two. Now on all sides the question is asked, will the Prime Minister, now that the war is over, attempt to keep this ramshackle party together. It is not for me to answer that question. If it is contended that Union Government should be kept together for the purpose of reconstruction I beg to take issue squarely with that proposition. To put forward such a contention would be to take refuge in an indefensible line of trenches. Will

any one seriously contend that a Cabinet dominated by the big interests and led by a dispenser of titles is likely to give an efficient lead to the work of reconstruction on democratic lines? Besides this, Union Government is regarded, even by its chief supporters, as a temporary makeshift. My hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) at Toronto, on January 12th, informed his audience that the Union Liberals proposed to remain until the soldiers got home. I understand this to mean that when the last transport ship touches the wharf at Halifax or St. John the whole combination will fall to pieces like a house of cards, and after that it will be every man for himself-and let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that the fate that is said to overtake the hindmost will not overtake any of them. But, speaking seriously, is it reasonable to expect any progressive or constructive legislation from a government with a death sentence like that hanging over it? You know, Mr. Speaker, that a man who is in prison awaiting his execution is most likely to spend most of his time preparing for death. Apart from this, the reconstruction party may well last for four or five years, and I submit it should not be left for a moment in the hands of a government that is not now, and never was, representative of the Canadian people. The Parliament that deals with reconstruction should be a parliament fresh from the people, elected without any switching of ballots, without any aid from the War Franchise Act, and without resort to the rusty tools of the bigot or the fanatic, and without any manipulation on the part of the press or the big interests. The Military Service Act, which was made a pretext for smashing the Liberal party, is no longer a live issue. Its usefulness, if it was useful, practically ended with the firing of the last gun. This gives rise to a new situation. The question arises, what will be the ultimate fate of the Liberals who strayed away from the fold? The question was raised yesterday, will these wanderers come back or will they end up by taking refuge in the bosom of the Prime Minister? These Liberal Unionists will have to decide that question for themselves. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) in his speech yesterday left the latch string out, and a light in the kitchen window. I want to warn these old friends of mine, however, not to make the mistake that the prodigal made, for he stayed so long in the far country that his new master put him to work at a very undignified and menial task. It
would be a positive grief to me, Sir, to think that any of these old friends of mine, who sat with me for so many years around the fireside of the Liberal party, should ever be set to work to fatten pork barons or other animals of that class. Permit me to suggest to these gentlemen that if they are coming back, the sooner the better. Besides, there is a limit to the time that the fatted calf may be kept waiting. The Union theory of government has had its day. It has been tried, and I submit that it has been found wanting. In 1917 certain wily politicians, assisted by the newspapers and a few energetic millionaires, spread the doctrine that in politics there should be no party, and that we should all be of one mind and do just what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance told us to do. The result of their proposals was to establish in Canada an autocratic government somewhat similar to the government that existed in Germany before the war. With the help of the War Franchise Act they succeeded. The result is that we have had an Administration that has thrown Parliament overboard and assumed more absolute control over the life and liberties of the people of this Dominion than was ever claimed by the Kaiser of Germany over his people. We must not lose sight of the fact that this country belongs to the people and not to the Union Government. The fact is that to-day in Canada we do not enjoy the blessings of responsible government. We are living under a government of party bosses, who, in secret conclave and behind closed doors, decide among themselves what we shall have and what we shall not have. The members of this Parliament are not masters of anybody. They are the servants of the Canadian people. What would you think, Mr. Speaker, of a servant who would not tell his master what he was doing? They have governed this country by orders in council, a system which has been aptly desciibed as law-making in the dark. Thousands of these orders have been passed, all in secret and behind closed doors. So arrogant did they become that some of these orders in council, of vital concern to the people of this country, were passed while Parliament was in session, without consulting the people's representatives. One of these secret regulations affected the liberty of every workingman in Canada, but it was passed without notice and without any opportunity for discussion. The theory of this Government evidently is that all the people have to do with the laws is

' to obey them and leave the making of them to their betters. So much for the methods of the Union Government. The old party system may be denounced by superfine philosophers but it is the best guarantee we have for good, clean, honest and progressive government. It has produced the soundest constiution in the world and worked that constitution in the Mother of Parliaments without a serious hitch for over two hundred years. The result of all this is the splendid fabric of British liberty, no part of which can be placed to the credit of the Mugwumps. An alert Opposition is always useful and desirable and is just as necessary in wartime as in times of peace. There is such a thing as checking graft and stopping extravagant and wasteful expenditure by prompt and courageous action on the part of the Opposition. We on this side frankly confess that we regarded it as a fitting thing that while the war was on, and the State was fighting for its life, no pains should be spared to promote a calm and friendly atmosphere and thereby focus attention upon the war and the issues arising out of the war. But even this can be carried too far. Everybody knows now that the easy-going method adopted by the Opposition during the early months of the war produced evil results. Graft became rampant. Millions of money were stolen and millions more wasted and the patronage system had spread so that the efficiency of the army was threatened. Then came the investigations and exposures. These exposures were of immense value to the country. No man can estimate their value. For example, after the investigations before the Public Accounts Committee, and the Kyte charges, and the exposures that followed, the operations of such grafters as Benjamin Franklyn Yoakum and Col. John Wesley Allison became impossible.
These recent experiences warrant the conclusion that an alert Opposition is the only safety and the first requisite of a decent democracy. The man who repudiates the party system, denies the doctrine of the sovereignty o* the people.
Reference has been made to the success of the Victory Loan, and it is certainly a matter for congratulation that the response was so cordial. The last two domestic loans aggregated over a billion dollars. The annual interest charge on these loans alone will exceed $50,000,000. This very large sum has been made absolutely free from taxation and in my judgment, improperly so. The large interest rate was ample without this concession, and if the Finance Minister had

trusted the people, if he had appealed to the patriotism of the people instead of their greed, he would not have been disappointed. Taxation or no taxation makes no difference to the small investor. It is in the case of the super-tax where the pinch comes. The small investor pays no super-tax. Why then were the bonds made free? There can only be the one answer. It was done to accommodate the plutocrats, or as Disraeli would say, " The paladins of High Finance."
Referring back to the election contest of 1917, what shall we say of a political party that was pledged to the hilt to the conscription of wealth, and when they secured power not only failed to conscript wealth but went so far in the opposite direction as to make wealth free from taxation? The result will be that while the returned soldier will have to pay, the millionaire and the profiteer will be free from the burden of the war. The hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has good points about him but he started wrong. If	he will	excuse me for	saying so. He entered public life, not as the representative of the people, but as the representative of	the	big interests. Underhis	management	the	manufacturers	havebeen treated tenderly; so have the banks, the	millionaires	and	the profiteers.	Myhon.	friend has been at the head
of our financial system for the past eight years, but so far as I know he never yet showed any disposition to drive any of the money changers out of the temple. This last act of freeing the war bonds from taxation is quite consistent with his past record and is what the people of Canada had every reason to expect. There appears to be no end to my hon. friend's borrowing. He has become a sort of political Oliver Twist. No sooner does he finish one plate of soup than he begins to clamour for another.
A few months ago he announced that in order to tide him over the year 1919 he would require about $300,000,000. A little later he hinted that he could make use of $500,000,000. By offering an extravagant rate of interest and freedom from taxation, he secured from the Canadian people about $687,000,000. But he was not satisfied. No sooner had he secured this enormous sum of money than he wants more. Without stopping to take breath he organizes a new borrowing scheme by means of thrift stamps. If this abnormal appetite for "more" continues, T suppose we shall have to resort to the old remedy of brimstone

and molasses. I am not saying that I object to thrift stamps, but the thrift will be very one-sided if there is no thrift on the part of the Government. Why should we ask the little children and old women in the country to save up their cents and invest their savings in war stamps in order to give money to a Government that will not take care of the money or use it properly when they get it?
Just a word on the food question. People everywhere are asking why the Food Board, which has been in operation for years, has failed to control prices, while the Food Boards in Great Britain and the United States have succeeded. It would be interesting to know the reason. The prices of food have gone sky-high, but only a very small part of the increase has gone to the farmer or the fisherman. The big millers and the pork barons and the middlemen have grown fat and flourished under the very noses of the hoard. While our soldiers were fighting the Hun in Europe, the Government gave the Hun profiteer at home a free hand to fleece the Canadian people. What does the hungry labourer with a large family to feed, and flour at $14 per barrel and bread at 14 cents for a 2-pound loaf, think when he reads in the papers that the Ogilvie Flour Mill Company has distributed to its millionaire shareholders 12 per cent dividend and 15 per cent bonus last year? When the labourer remembers how tenderly the celebrated pork baron of Toronto was treated after the O'Connor exposure, and when he sees these flour barons pocketing 27 per cent on their investment, while his family is feeling the pinch of these outrageous prices, is he not driven to the conclusion that in some way or other these big interests are under the protection of this Government?	_
There has been enormous expenditure of money in connection with the work of this Food Board, there Jiave been investigations and cartloads of advice, but I am not aware that any poor man in Canada, or any soldier's wife or widow, has been able to buy a pound of beef, or a loaf of bread, any cheaper by reason of the expenditure of all this money and all this energy. The question is naturally asked, What is the'fi to show for it all. I read a story recentlj in an English paper that a conservation orator over there was deploring the fact that Great Britain is compelled to import so much timber. " It is my belief," said the speaker, " that there is hot a man in this vast- audience who ever did a single thing to prevent the destruction of our forests." Thereupon a man arose in the
rear of the hall and said: "I beg your pardon, Sir, I have shot woodpeckers."
I will not say that the Food Board has accomplished nothing, but considering the money expended, the results have certainly been meagre. The control of prices was the most important task committed to them, and in this they have signally failed. If you want proof of this, I can furnish it from themselves. We have their own admission. On page 5 of the Canadian Food Bulletin of November, 1918, I find the following:
Plainly, the fixing of prices cannot he done by a centralized control at Ottawa, and it is worth noting that all food orders must, under our Constitution, be made for the whole of the Dominion; the only way to limit their application to one area is to make exceptions of all other areas. That is, the order must be chipped and whittled down negatively to the rer quired size if it is to be localized. If prices are to be fixed in a way which shall not cut off supplies, it must be done by local power. What other power better represents the people than a properly elected municipal council?
There you have it. During the past four years we have this highly paid organization fooling and fiddling over the prices of food, and at the end of it all we have the helpless admission that they cannot do anything at all, and that the only institution that is capable of doing anything is the municipal councils. Now, that may be true, but why, let me ask, go through all this solemn hocus-pocus covering a period of four years, to reach this conclusion? Mr. Speaker, >vhat do you think of this Food Board, and what do you think of a Government that during the whole four years of the war has tolerated this muddling and tinkering with a question so vital to the Canadian people?
Reference has been made in this debate to the prevalence of industrial unrest. I want to make the statement that the chief cause of industrial unrest is the high cost of living, and the general belief in the existence of profiteering. Wages have increased, but wages have not kept pace with the high cost of living. Under these circumstances what should the Government have done? They should have taken these profiteers and middlemen by the throat and compelled them to reduce their demands. What did the Government do? They took a short cut, they went behind closed doors and passed an Order in Council making it a criminal offence for a working man to strike, while at the same time the chief offenders were allowed to go scot free. They did more, they appointed a Director of Public Safety, and organized a

force of Dominion Police, so that if the hungry man clamoured too loudly for more wages they could furnish him with a pair of handcuffs. I want to say to my hon. friend the leader of the Government that we will never build the New Jerusalem in this free land of ours by resorting to these Hun methods.
This Administration has claimed a great
deal of credit for abolishing patronage and reforming the Civil Service. It would appear that some good people actually believe that they did these things. I have seen a report of a meeting of clergymen where they passed a resolution thanking the Lord that the Union Government had the grace and strength given them to effect these reforms. My own idea is that the Lord had nothing to do with it, and judging from the amount of deception practised in connection with the matter I am inclined to view that it came from the opposite quarter. The trouble with some well-meaning clergymen . is that their bump of credulity is abnormally large. The western farmers evidently do not think patronage iias been abolished. At their meeting in Winnipeg in November last, they placed the abolition of patronage as one of the chief planks of their platform for the next election. The trouble with the Civil Service is that it was debauched after 1911, and reform is impossible without first cleaning out the stable. It has not been forgotten that within two years after the Administration came into power, they crowded the Civil Service with 25,000 new appointments. There were only about half that number of vacancies made by deaths and dismissals. This new army was not needed, and they demoralized the whole service,
4	p.m. and this condition still prevails and cannot be remedied by organizing a board to make new appointments.
If the Government cannot muster the courage to send their unwelcome friends back to productive employment, the only thing to do is to wait for ten thousand funerals before any remedy is possible. Prof. W. L. Grant, who has been studying the situation, suggests as a partial remedy that no new appointments be made for the next five years. In this connection permit me to quote from The Civilian. The Civilian is the only paper in Canada that is wholly devoted to the Civil Service, and should be the best authority on that question. The item I refer to is a report of an interview between the executive of the Civil Service Association and Sir George Poster, relating to the distribution of a proposed war bonus. 
When the question arose as to what the total expenditure would amount to if this bonus were paid, we find the following statement:
This, of course was a mere matter of multiplication-so many civil servants at $350 apiece, total so much. But the difficulty Is in the first factor in the calculation, for, as was pointed out by Mr. Burling and others, nobody knows how many civil servants there are. The Civil Service Commission is carrying on at this moment a most elaborate inquiry partly with the object of ascertaining exactly what persons are to be counted-as belonging to the Service.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, from this item that the chief trouble is that the Government has crowded the departments with employees to such an extent that nobody can say how many civil servants there are, and they frankly confess their inability to count one another. I am informed that the Government actually employed a firm of experts in the United States to count and classify them. We must also remember that this is the condition of affairs in the year, of our Lord, 1918, after four years of war; and during that whole period the Government had been crying out about the scarcity of labour and imploring old and young, women and children, to volunteer to work in the fields and factories so as to save the nation and win the war; and all the time they had battalions of chairwarmers in their own offices paid at the public expense to do' nothing; and in the very months that the war ended, these employees were still so numerous that they themselves recognized the difficulty of counting one another. All I have to say is that the clergymen who thanked God for what the Union Government accomplished in connection with the Civil Service were satisfied with very small mercies.
Curious things have happened in this country the past year. A certain Rip Van Winkle by the name of Parsons, who, I am told, was recently the official head of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, has been attempting to raise the old, discredited cry of "No truck or trade with the Yankees. That cry, as hon. gentlemen will remember, did good service for him and his associates in 1911. The only explanation of his reverting to that cry now is that he must have been asleep during the last four years. In the face of all our recent experiences to the contrary he again quotes the worn-out remark of ex-President Taft that an exchange of products between the two countries would make Canada an adjunct of the United States. This argument had its origin in prejudice, and found a ready market at the time among men of

low intelligence and high credulity. But after the experiences of the past four years I feel confient that even this class will regard it as out of date and refuse to accept it. It was never contended that the reciprocity agreement was not a fair bargain: its opponents frankly admitted that it was absolutely fair. Besides, it contained a clause enabling us to withdraw from it at any time we . saw fit to do so. Still, with all these precautions, certain hon. gentlemen opposite, of whom the leader of the Government (Sir Thomas White) was one, professed to be alarmed about our fiscal independence. It does not take much to frighten some people. It has not been forgotten that a few years ago some hon. gentlemen opposite used to smell annexation and treason in every potato or codfish that crossed the boundary line. Why? Was it because they did not trust the United States, or was. it that the United States, being the stronger, would take an unfair advantage of us? The fact that since that time the Finance Minister went to Washington, hat in hand, to get leave to borrow $100,000,000 in New York shows that he did not really fear any of these things and that the campaign of 191| was nothing more than a hollow sham. Besides all that, a nation that has been compelled within the last year to submit to the humiliation of depending on the United States navy to protect its coast and its commerce and its fishing fleet is hardly in a position to harbour suspicion as to the good faith of that same power in regard to less important matters of trade and tariff. There is no serious opposition today among the rank and file of the Canadian people to reciprocity with the United States in natural products. There is no lerious opposition to it even by the Government; as witness their recent decision to place potatoes on the free list. I doubt if there is a single narrow-gauge statesman in Canada to-day'who is prepared to raise the old, worn-out cry of "No truck or trade with the Yankees"; it has been buried in the same grave as their opposition to a Canadian navy and to the British preference. The attempt to stir up ill-feeling between Canada and the United States in 1911 had all the appearance of a skilfully-contrived German propaganda.
Who made the first proposal in 1911 for the annexation of Canada to the United States? Was it not made by American speakers?

I never heard of any proposal being made for the annexation of
Canada to the United States; it is all news to me. I was saying that the campaign of 1911 had the appearance of a skilfully-contrived German propaganda, and we all ought to be thankful that the conspiracy failed and that our relations with our great neighbour to the south have never been more friendly than they are to-day. Time has amply vindicated the policy of my late revered leader in regard to reciprocity with the United States as well as in regard to that very vital question, the establishment of a Canadian navy.
The question of the franchise has been mentioned in the Address. This is a matter of vital importance. Three attempts have been made in the history of Canada to gain an unfair advantage by legislation in connection with the franchise. The first was what is called the gerrymander of 1882. The second was the Franchise Act of 1885, providing that a revising barrister be appointed in each constituency in Canada to compile the electoral lists. The third was the WarTime Elections Act of 1917. I am happy to say that those three attempts to gain an unfair advantage by legislation in connection with the franchise were all made by the same political party. One of the most serious charges to be laid at the door of the Union Government is this War-Times Election Act-it is known in my province as the War-Time Tammany Act. The leader of the House told us yesterday that this Act was not to be repealed until something else had been provided in its place. I trust that the other thing which is to be provided in its place will be fairer and more respectable and decent than the War-Time Elections Act. This Act is a disgrace to Canada arid should be repealed at once. It is customary for the police, when the row is over, to confiscate the sling-shots and the sand-bags and the brass knuckles; why should there be any distinction in this case? The Act should have been repealed last year; every day that it continues on the statute book of Canada, it serves to perpetuate our disgrace. Frankly, I was disappointed last year when I saw man after man, each a Liberal-Unionist, stand up in his place and vote for the continuance of this Act; I thought that there would be some conscientious objectors among them. What is the situation up to date? We on this side of the House stand for fair elections; hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House stand for the War-Time Elections Act. These positions are as opposite as God and mammon; no man can hold to the one without despising the other. I dislike as much as any man to refer to

these matters, but it is our duty as representatives of a free democracy to challenge the methods by which hon. gentlemen won the election of 1917.
I want to lay down the principle that absolute fairness in the use of the ballot is the first requisite and the only safety of a decent democracy. Fair play has always been the biggest word in the Anglo-Saxon's creed, and when men outrage that principle, they must take the consequences. It is as much our duty to hold these people up to the public gaze as it is the duty of the Allies to expose the Hun outrages of the last four years. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that red-letter day in the history of Great Britain, when, in November last, a string of German naval ships twenty miles in length steamed slowly up through the North sea and surrendered to Admiral Beatty in the Firth of Forth. No ceremonial courtesies of any kind were paid to the vanquished enemy. Admiral Beatty gives the reason. The following contains an extract from the official order that was flashed across the sky from the flagship of the Grand Fleet the night before the surrender:
At midnight Admiral Beatty signalled that while courtesy toward the enemy was obligatory, the methods by which the Germans had waged war should not be forgotten, that no international compliments should be paid.
In the same way, it is obligatory upon us to keep before the Canadian people the method by which hon. gentlemen opposite won their seats in 1917. We on this side of the House will follow the example of Admiral Beatty. There will be no ceremonial courtesies so far as the War-time Elections Act is concerned.
Let me quote an editorial from an Australian paper to show what our great sister Commonwealth thinks of the conduct of the election by which this Government came into power:
Canada stands in the unhappy position of having had her ordinary constitutional government overthrown by what is practically a military revolution.
The recent elections in Canada were simply a farce and a fraud from a legal and constitutional standpoint, as they were conducted under war precaution regulations, which permitted great numbers of unqualified persons to vote, and denied the franchise to large numbers of legally qualified Canadian citizens.
The ordinary Canadian electoral roll was set aside, and a manuscript roil compiled by specially appointed officials acting under military regulations, was used.
An election controlled by military despots, and carried out in defiance of electoral law, Is something quite new in the annals of British constitutional history, and by no stretch of imagination can the present Borden ministry claim 
to be the constitutional representatives of the people of Canada.
It must he apparent that, from a legal and constitutional standpoint, the recent Canadian election is null and void, and the Parliament so elected has mo constitutional authority for its acts.
Our local conscriptionist politicians are now bewailing the fact that they did not adopt the tactics of their fellow-conspirators in Canada, but it would be a dark day indeed if the frauds perpetrated there could be repeated here.
Canada now stands as the shocking example of what organized force is capable of, even in a British community, and emphasizes the good sense of the Australian people In their refusal to exchange constitutional government for military despotism.
Considering the distance from Canada at which this editorial was written, it is surprising how correctly the writer was informed.
Having said so much about the sins and follies of the Government, let me say that the fact that during this session on which we have entered we have to deal with the present and the future rather than with the past, is obvious to us all. We on this side fully recognize that the task confronting the Administration is not an easy one. The returned soldiers have the first claim on the gratitude of the nation. They must not want for anything that the country can do for them. The dependents of the brave men who have fallen in our service must also be tenderly cared for. The claims for pensions must be adjusted in a generous spirit.. Labour problems must be dealt with. Taxation must be fairly and equitably levied in order that money may be found to meet the enormous financial obligations of the country, and it is the duty of every member of tne nouse, I care not on whicn side he sits, to contribute everything he can to the solution of these problems. But the Government must of course take the lead. The first requisite? of an Administration is initiative; the second is efficiency. If the Government fails in those, it fails in everything. The collapse of initiative on the part of this Government is proved beyond doubt by the resignation of the Parliamentary Under Secretary of the' Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Why did the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) resign? He resigned, first, because the Government had failed to grapple with the problem of the returned soldier; second,, because the different departments of the Government failed to work together. My hon. friend from Colchester has been careful to use diplomatic language, but his real meaning is that the Administration is incompetent, and he refuses any longer to be-

responsible for its failure to do its duty. The returned soldier is the greatest problem before the Canadian people, and if the Government cannot grapple successfully with that problem, then it should make way for some Government that can.
So much for initiative. We come now to the question of efficiency. You say that this Administration is an efficient instrument to grapple with the grave problems that are confronting the country at the present time. We say, judging from its past record, that it is not. That creates an issue, and the. burden of proof is on you. I submit that in all the speeches that we have yet heard from hon. members of the Government, the proof is not forthcoming. A good example of inefficiency and drift is pointed out by my hon. friend from Colchester in his letter of resignation. When the question of soldiers' pensions became urgent in 1916, the Government had no solution to offer. When pressed to take action, they appointed a committee of private members to take evidence and report. This committee did its duty well and made a comprehensive report which, according to the hon. member for Colchester, the Government pigeon-holed and up to the date of his resignation no more was heard of it. The hon. member for Colchester is not a man who would say or do anything reflecting on his party without having ample and serious reasons for doing so. It is, therefore, for the Government to explain-and it has not yet done so-what justification the hon. member fo>r Colchester had in the action he took.
'With reference to the efforts of Great Britain in this war, the remark has been made that in the old land they did every thing but talk. The opposite is the case here. This Government talks, but very little else is accomplished. Everybody knows that there is nothing that weakens a Government so much as bold talk and feeble action. We have been putting our trust in Boards, Committees and Royal Commissions. What we really need is men at the head of affairs who can do things themselves and who have the courage to take the whole responsibility. Nearly every important matter that comes up, instead of being dealt with by the responsible minister, is turned over to some irresponsible commission of busybodies who in turn travel the country, collect information and make a report which is duly pigeon-holed and forgotten while the country has the pleasure of paying the bill. Let me give a few examples:
1.	The Trade Mission to London which should have been attended to by the trained experts of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
2.	The National Advisory Council for the employment of labour. Where, let me ask, is our Department of Labour?
3.	The Royal Commission on Wheat Supply. Have we not a Department of Agriculture in this country?
4.	The Department of Public Safety. Has this country ever been so dangerous a place to live in that the Department of Justice could not protect the citizens?
5.	The National War Savings Committee, consisting of fifteen men from different parts of Canada selected to deal with the question of thrift stamps. 'Surely this is a matter that should be dealt with by the Finance Department. What do we keep a highly paid staff of experts in the Finance Department for, if we have to resort to a committee of fifteen from the outside to attend to such a simple matter as thrift stamps?
These are only sample bricks. There are hundreds of these so-called commissions. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) himself informed us in the House that they were as thick as blackberries, and the number is increasing day by day. If everything is to be turned over to irresponsible commissions, what is left to the twenty-one ministers of the Crown and their departments to do? When these gentlemen were elected, the people of Canada who voted for them expected them to be useful as well as ornamental. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) is smiling at that, but that is a. fact. Lord Macaulay was right when he said that war could not be carried on successfully, by a debating society. The same is true of Government. If the Government of this country is to be of real service to the people in the anxious period that confronts us, efficiency must be the watchword in every department. The work must not be turned over to irresponsible outside committees
Permit me to say this, that the party that will do the greatest service for this country in the future will be the party that will stand above all for good faith and honesty, and public honour. We have talked so much of late years about tariffs and bonuses and bounties and shipbuilding and wheat and steers that we are apt to run away with the idea that these are the principal things and to neglect the weightier matters, such as faithfulness to our pledges, and even-handed justice be-

tween man and man. In my judgment no party can any more succeed in this country that seeks to serve itself. The people will demand not only sincerity on the part of its representatives, but also a frank recognition of the rights of the ordinary man.
1 was much struck with a paragraph in Lloyd George's recent election address referring to labour and capital. Permit me to quote:
I say to Labour: You shall have justice; you shall have fair treatment, a fair share of the amenities of life and your children shall have equal opportunities with the children of the rich. To Capital I say: You shall not be plundered or penalised; do your duty by those who work for you, and the future is free for all the enterprise or audacity you can give us. But there must be equal justice. Labour must have happiness in its heart. We will put up with no sweating. Labour is to have its just reward. And when the whole nation sees that wealth lies in production, that production can be enormously increased, with higher wages and shorter hours, and when the classes feel confidence in each other and trust each other, there will be abundance to requite the toil and to gladden the hearts of all. We can change the whole face of existence.
We can do the same here. Precisely the same task awaits us here in Canada, but when we speak of labour we must include not only the workmen in the factories and the mines and on the railways, but also the tillers of the land and the toilers of the sea. Surely it is not beyond us to develop a system of government by which quiet, industrious men can live and labour and enjoy the fruit of their own industry.
Mr. Speaker, before taking my seat, permit me to say that, representing a constituency that in common with others has made great sacrifices in this war, I am here to support any proper measures looking towards reconstruction. My constituents will expect me to demand so far as lies in my power, honest and progressive administration, and fair and generous treatment for the men who have survived and for the dependents of the men who have fallen in the great struggle.
The only desire of members on this side of the House is to guard the public treasury, to see that Canada plays her part with honour, and to assist in such measures as will establish on a firm foundation in this free land of ours the principles of democracy that our soldiers fought so bravely to maintain.
Hon. J. A. 0ALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization): Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I desire to congratulate the mover and seconder of the motion for an Address in reply to the

speech from the Throne. The task that was assigned to them was a difficult one. As every member of the House knows, the atmosphere in this Chamber in the early days of the session is just a little tense, somewhat frigid, and the task of breaking the ice, so to speak, under those circumstances is by no means an easy one. I am sure every hon. member will agree that the choice made in selecting these two young men to undertake this responsibility was a very happy one. They had both seen service overseas; they had come in contact with conditions "over there," and their experiences I am sure were such as will enable them to speak with authority on many of the questions which must be considered by the House during this session. I am sure we ail feel that their addresses will be exceedingly helpful to us in the work of the session.	-
'I wish also to express my thanks to the other hon. members who have spoken both on that side of the House and on this. The session now under way will, I think, prove to be the most important session of Parliament ever held in the history of Canada. The problems that are now staring us in the face are in my judgment the most difficult problems Canada has ever had to deal with, and for that reason it is very desirable and very important that we should have at this early stage of tire session the viewpoint of every one on the prevailing conditions. It is quite true we may not agree with all that has been said by our hon. friends opposite. Nevertheless, I think it is very desirable, _jn order that we may lay down proper foundations for our work this session, that we should have their views, that they should state to this House quite clearly and definitely whatever criticisms they may have to offer, that they should tell us the feeling in the country as they see it, and state whether in their opinion the work that lias been done by the Government has been done properly or not. That necessarily is very helpful, and particularly helpful to the members of the Government.
I have been connected with public life, not here but elsewhere, for a period of some fifteen or eighteen years, and I have never during all that time objected to criticism -or attack. I like attack to be fair, and I like criticism to be constructive, not merely destructive, and I am sure it will be helpful to every hori. member who is desirous of carrying out the responsibility cast upon him at this crisis to get the views of other hon. gentlemen in the House.

Naturally, our friends opposite, particularly the last speaker, have drawn a pretty dark picture. He in particular dipped his brush pretty deep in the browns and the grays and the blacks. To him all is gloom; the whole horizon is filled with dark clouds, with scarcely a gleam of light anywhere. Well, I hope before I get through to say something that will at least assure our friends on this side of the House that all is not so black, that there is a little light somewhere, and that the people of this country may reasonably hope for something.
The great war is ende'd. Thank God for that! I say, thank God, not because "the light is in the window and the latch string on the outside of the door," but because the curtain has rung down on the greatest tragedy in all history. I am not going to take up your time, Mr. Speaker, in dwelling upon the misery and suffering and sorrow	of the last four	years. I
shall not deal with the causes of the war or the ideals for which we fought. Much as I would like to speak of our own boys and what they did, the battles they fought, how they fought their way through from Ypres to Mons, I am not going to deal with that matter to-day. Those questions have been dealt with by previous speakers. The mover and seconder of the Address dwelt upon them and spoke more fittingly than I could. I wish rather during the time at my disposal to speak of what lies ahead, of the work that confronts us, of the tasks that we members of Parliament must undertake during the months that lie before us. The armistice was signed on the eleventh day of November. Hostilities ceased suddenly. It was not thought that the war would come to a conclusion s'o early. There may have been a few, very few, who understood the conditions and knew exactly the situation, but, so far as the great majority of the people of this country were concerned, they little expected the war would end last year. I well remember the conditions in Europe when I was over there in the midsummer of 1918. The Acting Prime Minister referred to those conditions yesterday afternoon. When we landed in London in the early part of June, you would scarcely meet a man anywhere with a smile on his face. I never saw such dejection and despondency in my life. In all the circles of government over there, where they had a clear knowledge of the situation on the continent, there was not much indication of the end of the war then. Hon. gentlemen will remember how the fifth army was
smashed. You remember the talk of the Huns breaking through to Calais and Paris. That was exactly the situation. The men who were responsible for the conduct of the war at that time were seriously considering the problems that would arise when the Huns did reach Paris and the channel ports. That was the situation then, and was the situation during the whole six or seven weeks I was over there. I went on board the ship, and we were two or three days from shore when we got the despatch that the Germans had renewed their attack towards Paris, and a few days later we heard of the Allied offensive and their successes in driving the Germans back. There was not a soul on that ship who was not very much surprised, and when later on we received the news that the Hun was being beaten back, those of us who had been in England in June and July, knowing the conditions which had been depicted to us, simply could not believe that these things were actually taking place. With our knowledge of the situation " over there," as we saw it in England, and as we were told about it, it seemed to us impossible that there should be any end to the war in the year 1918. At that time the whole energy of the British Government and qf the French Government was devoted to devising ways and means to prevent the Hun from reaching the sea, the channel ports, and Paris. So there was not very much talk at that time about preparations for after the war, and we must not be very much surprised in this country if, in that respect, the whole duty of the Government was not completely performed.
There were other things we had to consider, as was the case with the other nations who were very much in the same position as we were. Our Government was intent at that time on doing all they could do in supplying the sinews of war. While some work iwas done in preparation for peace I must admit frankly that all was not done jjhat might have been done. But hostilities ceased much sooner than had been expected. There is another thought that was also given voice to by the Acting Prime Minister yesterday. The problems that now stare us in the face are, in my judgment, more difficult than the problems of war, and I will tell you why. It took something like four years for Canada to build up her war machine. We were working month after mcftith and the machinery was being added to all the time, growing in size, and it became a huge machine. In the process of making it the people of this country were affected directly

and indirectly in a multitude of way®. The problem that now faces us is the unravelling of the conditions created. We must remember that that problem came upon us all at once, and I can assure my hon. friends that the problem is not by any mean® simple. From my knowledge of the situation at the present time, I am thoroughly convinced that the problems that this nation now have before it, in connection with the unscrambling of our military organization and the re-adjustment of conditions which have arisen as a result of four years of war, are very much more difficult and complex, and the result much more far-reaching than the problems that had to be dealt with during the war period itself. I am absolutely convinced of that, and I desire to impress the fact upon every member of this House. The immediate problems.that are confronting us now, staring us squarely in the face, will not wait. These problems, in my judgment, are the most difficult problems which a nation has ever faced, and if they are not attended to properly, unless we find proper solutions for these problems, well, God help Canada; no man can tell what the consequences may be. We have a little unrest and some dissatisfaction, and there is great pessimism in some sections of the country, and it may mean something very much worse. I do not wish to frighten anybody and I do not wish to be over-pessimistic, but right here in Canada we have conditions that are akin to conditions that exist elsewhere, and it is very necessary that every member of this House should understand his responsibility in relation to the solution of these problems.
Very shortly after the armistice was signed, and our people began to think of this new situation, there were a great many who began to wonder, as my good friend from Antigonish.Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I suppose, must have been wondering, as to whether all was well at Ottawa- whether the Government had made plans and preparations to take care of this new situation. As you know, there were all sorts of rumblings and rumours about our muddling along, drifting along, not being prepared, and all that sort of thing. I do not wonder at that. It is really not surprising that ignorance should exist in the country, as to the actual work of government when we find responsible members of the' House making statements such as we listened to yesterday and to-day. We can hardly blame the "man in the street."
The Government from the very first was seized of its duty. We always understood

that the war was going to end, that it would not last forever. As I stated, the end came suddenly, but, nevertheless, a good many preparations had been made and a good deal of thought and study had been given to many of the problems that would naturally come up when the war would close. There had been much spade work done. Some of the foundations were laid and in some cases even the superstructures were erected. In other words, we were not all adrift. Something had been., accomplished.
I am not going to take up your time to-day in attempting to cover the situation, because that would take too long. Nor am I going into details, but I simply wish, by way of illustration, to mention some of the matters that had received attention before the end of the war came and to touch very briefly ujjon the relationship of these matters to the problems now existing.
In the first place, as regards demobilization itself. The demobilization of our forces is by no means an easy matter, and careful thought had to be given to the methods by which tha,t could be carried out and the machinery which must be set in motion. We do talk about these things very glibly; we are all inclined to do that. We do not know what the job actually means. Personally, I do not begin to know what demobilization means in the way of creating machinery and seeing that that machinery is operated in such a way as to cause the least possible trouble. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn), and his officials, spent weeks over that problem. They went overseas, consulted the British and French authorities and spent further weeks in working out all these details in anticipation of what would eventually happen. You know what has happened. As far as I have been able to learn, the plan has been so well worked out, and the machinery has run so smoothly, that there is practically little or no criticism left in the country as to the manner in which the work is being done.
I am speaking now solely and only of demobilization, of actually getting the men out of the army. The Minister of Militia told me the other day of an instance that occurred within the last three weeks in which some 500 men had been returned. They were taken from the ship to the dispersal area, and within half an hour after these men had arrived at the dispersal area they walked out as civilians once more. That was by no means an easy task. It involved grave study and a careful arrangement of the details in order that it might be done.

We had this afternoon and yesterday some little slam at one of the departments that was created at our last session. I refer to the department of Soldiers Civil Re-Establishment. It was created for a very specific purpose. It took the place of the Military Hospitals Commission. It has been at work for something over a year. Its expenditures for the past year will amount to something in the neighbourhood of $12,000,000. We had a mild intimation to the effect that it was created very largely for the purpose of providing salaries for somebody. That is the usual, old criticism. We have heard it a great many times. I have used it myself. It will be used as long as parliamentary institutions exist. No, that department was not created for that purpose. It was created for a very definite, a very specific purpose. It was created with the object in view of caring for every disabled Canadian soldier who came back to this country. The work of the department has two sides, one medical, the other vocational. As a result of the work, in the first place, of the Military Hospitals Commission and later of this department, we have now, scattered throughout Canada in every province, something like one hundred and fifty institutions. I need not go into the details. The members of the House are just as familiar with them as I am, and they know where these institutions are and what they are doing. Something like 2,000 or 2,500 young Canadian boys, who were " over there " and who were disabled and maimed as a result of the war, have come back, have gone through these institutions and have been refitted for life as far as it is humanly possible to do so through medical treatment and vocational training. Those 2,500 young men are now back to civil life in this country as a result of the activities of that department. In addition, there are something like 2,000 or 3,000 men actually undergoing treatment in these institutions at the present time, and there are some thousands being fitted for new employment. I am now speaking of men who cannot, on account of their disability, their injuries, their sufferings, go back to their old employments. Thousands of them are now undergoing treatment at these institutions.
I do not wish to leave the impression upon this House for one moment that all is well with that department or with any other department of the Government. In the making of war, and in the dealing with * these problems of which our country had no experience and for which we were not at all equipped, it must not be wondered at that mistakes have been made. There
will be criticism, some of which will doubtless be ventilated here. Hon. gentlemen opposite have even hinted at criticism from within our ranks. Be that as it may, all I wish to do is to leave the idea with the House that the department referred to was created for a definite purpose, and in my judgment it has carried on its work well-not perfectly, but nevertheless well; -and if, as a result of our deliberations during the present session, we can devise ways and means whereby that department's operations may be bettered, I am sure the members of the Government, including the minister who has it in charge, will welcome any such assistance.	.
Again, Mr. .Speaker, time was taken by the forelock some two or three years ago in connection with another very important phase of the returned soldier problem. The matter was taken up a,t an interprovincial conference in this city called by the Federal Government, at which I was present as a member of the Saskatchewan Government. We sat here for two days with the federal authorities deliberating over the problem of the returned soldier to see if there was any responsibility or any work the provinces could undertake or carry on. After full consideration and full consent by the provinces it was agreed to establish what are known as Soldiers' Aid Commissions, and if I am not mistaken every province has by statute created a body of that character. These have been for some time in operation, and have done splendid work in connection with many of the problems that arise in connection with the returning men. I have visited some of these institutions, and the member for London (Mr. Cronyn) can speak of my visit to the Soldiers' Aid Commission in that city. I talked with the young man in charge, who has a staff of some six or eight persons assisting him, went through the office files, and saw the nature of the work which is there being carried on. Work of a similar character is going on throughout the length and breadth of the 'Dominion, and has been in progress for the last two or three years. These institutions have yielded splendid results. There is a great field of activity for them.
During the session there will doubtless be discussion on the question of soldiers' settlement, a very vexed and most difficult problem. If there was but one Government in Canada in which the ownership of the public domain was vested, the problem would be very much easier of solution, but hon. gentlemen know what the existing conditions are. There are nine provinces scattered over an enormous area,

and in these provinces varied conditions prevail, some owning their Crown lands, and others not. I can assure hon. gentlemen that the evolving of a satisfactory soldiers' settlement scheme under such conditions was a most complex and intricate one. I am not going to discuss the subject now, because ample opportunity for that will later on be given, but the problem was one which demanded from the Government very great consideration. We had numerous suggestions-I might say hundreds, and even thousands-from all over the country with respect to the matter; everybody had a scheme professing to afford an easy solution, but most of these suggestions were not very satisfactory because they were not very practicable. So far as I can see the Government have dealt with the question in the only practicable way that could be found.
It will be remembered that last session a Bill providing for assistance to the provinces in connection with the establishment of Labour Bureaus was presented. That action was not taken without due thought and reflection.	As a matter of fact,
at an interprovincial conference, called previous to last session, that question came up for	consideration.	It	was
only after thorough consideration by the premiers of the various provinces, who were accompanied in some instances by a number of their colleagues, it was only after the whole situation had been reviewed in all its aspects and the conditions likely to arise after the war reviewed, that the conclusion was reached, jointly with them, that the best way of handling the problem when it arose would be to make
5	p.m. provision for the establishment of bureaus of this nature throughout the Dominion. Hon. gentlemen opposite must not imagine that we forced this policy upon the provinces, or that we endeavoured in any way to interfere with provincial autonomy in connection with this matter. The subject was considered deliberately, coolly, and calmly with the provincial governments, and it was agreed, with the full consent of the various provincial authorities, to deal with the situation in the manner that I have described.
