In consequence, last session's measure providing for assistance to the provinces was submitted, and this year, on account of the conditions now prevailing, a very much larger assistance than was -anticipated at that time needs to be provided. Speaking broadly, about fifty of these bureaus are at present in existence and all our work in connection with finding employment not only for [Mr. Cal-dcr. 3
the returned soldier, but for the civilian in Canada as well, is concentrated in these organizations. The danger was that if some action of this kind had not been taken we would likely have had chaos in this country in regard to the. employment problem. While the system may^ not be working to the entire satisfaction of everybody in this country, nevertheless, so far as I have been able to judge from the representations made to me, it will reasonably meet the existing situation.
We must not forget that in this country- and the Government were thoroughly cognizant of the fact-there are- a large number of organizations, patriotic and otherwise, that were simply sitting waiting, willing and ready to undertake any work that might be placed upon them just as soon as the nature of the problems requiring treatment was made manifest. Very shortly after the armistice was signed, the Government realized that the whole situation had changed, and that -it was necessary to deal at once with the new conditions which had arisen. As hon gentlemen know, a new committee of the Cabinet was constituted.	In this connection I may say	that I	am
not afraid of committees or of commissions. If you have a reason for doing a thing, do not be afraid to do it simply because some one talks about it. We have had a number of committees and a number of commissions, and the great majority of them have done very useful and very necessary work, work that no government and no member of a government could carry on during these strenuous times. Very shortly after the armistice was signed we cieated a new committee of the Cabinet called the Repatriation and Employment Committee, which was appointed for the purpose of co-ordinating the work of the different departments of the Government and of all the various organizations outside of the Government machinery that had to deal with this problem. We had a pretty busy time for a while; during some six weeks we had a great many meetings. I am free to admit that there was a good deal of overlapping; that a good many toes were being tramped upon, through nobody's fault, by different organizations and by the departments. This committee and those associated with it found it necessary clearly to define the work of the various agencies that were brought into being to deal with the problems of demobilization and repatriation. I have had something to do with the work of this committee. I know a little

of its organization and of its administrative activities, and I think I can say truthfully that we have in Canada from ocean to ocean an organization handling this problem of repatriation such as does not exist in any other belligerent country in the world. It is a very complex organization; thousands of people take part in it- it is very necessary that that be so.
There has been a good deal of talk in some countries with regard to this problem. Much has been put down on paper and many fine reports have been got out and committees and commissions formed to enquire into and deal with the subject. We have had to make inquiries as to what is being done elsewhere, and we have gathered some information. When I say that we are well in advance of the other belligerent countries in this work, I think I am stating just what the situation is. The work is not perfect; many mistakes have been made, and perhaps more mistakes will be made. There will still be a good deal of criticism, and there will likely be room for it. There has been no work just like this in history; consequently we have had very little to guide us: The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) referred this afternoon to the great war of 1812, but that war was simply a baby as compared with this giant. You cannot look into past records and get much assistance from them, because the world has never experienced a situation such as this. This war has had far-reaching consequences; it has touched practically every home; it has touched practically every aspect of our national life. To say, therefore, that in dealing with matters arising out of these new conditions mistakes should not be made or cogs should not slip-well, after all, the Government and its agencies and the private organizations that are dealing with this problem are merely human, and these things will happen.
The immediate problems which confront us naturally fall under two headings, reconstruction and repatriation. The term "reconstruction" as used in Europe at present has a somewhat different meaning from that which it has here. Something has happened over there that has not happened in Canada. A smashing and demolishing of things has taken place; there has been a devastation over there, that we have not suffered. I have only to picture in my mind what I saw in the neighbourhood of the Somme to have some little realization of what the building up of that country means in the way of labour and expenditure that will be necessary
during the next few years. But the term "reconstruction" has a real meaning to us, a very deep and a very significant meaning. While it does not mean to us what it means to the people over there, nevertheless our people have learned some lessons from this war. They have learned that all is not well in the world; that some reforms are necessary. Our people clearly understand that work is ahead of this nation in that regard. In my opinion reconstruction, as applied to Canada, embraces the adjusting of the affairs of the nation so as to meet the new social and economic conditions that have arisen as a result of the war. Do not make any mistake about it, new conditions, social and economic, have arisen in our country as a result of the war, and we must adjust the affairs of the nation to meet them. Reconstruction involves also a national stocktaking of all our policies and laws that affect the well-being of our people, with a view to placing the nation in the position she should occupy as a progressive, democratic community. Every member of the House will place his stamp of approval on that statement. Reconstruction further means the taking of a long step forward through the adoption of measures and policies truly conceived and effectively and honestly administered in the interests of the great mass of the Canadian people. Reconstruction, if it means anything to us, must mean the adoption of higher ideals of citizenship, the searching for measures that will have an ever increasing tendency to unify and harmonize our many conflicting interests. They are here; we have heard a little about them so far, and I may touch on them myself before I sit down. Above all, reconstruction involves the creating of such social and economic conditions as are necessary to the comfort, happiness and prosperity of our people as a whole. Reconstruction means a going forward, not a standing still. It means progress, not stagnation.
I am but a young member of this House, and I naturally hesitate to give advice or even to voice a warning; and yet I feel that, I must do this if I am to discharge the responsibility that I bear as a member of the House and as a member of this Government. Many people in this country have the idea that our problems consist in getting back to the conditions that existed prior to August 1, 1914. Any man who holds that idea has failed to learn the lessons of the last four and a half years. I have stated on the public platform at two or three meetings that I have held, that Canada will

never again be the same old Canada. The people of this country by the thousands, aye, by the hundreds of thousands, have suffered during the last four years. The lessons of this war have been burned into their very soul. The people of Canada as a whole are thinking differently, and let us not make any mistake about it, they are going to act differently when they have an opportunity.
Some 'Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

I might just say, in conclusion, that I did not last session avail myself to any extent of the opportunity of speaking in the House. I think I probably acted wisely in adopting that course. Being new here, I was very anxious to get to know the members and to learn a little about the atmosphere and all that sort of thing. I must thank the House for the indulgence that it has shown to me to-day and the attentive manner in which it has listened to my very rambling remarks.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO PLACE COASTWISE AND INLAND WATER VESSELS UNDER RAILWAY COMMISSION.

speechtext: Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 6, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO PLACE COASTWISE AND INLAND WATER VESSELS UNDER RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO PLACE COASTWISE AND INLAND WATER VESSELS UNDER RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
This Bill is for the purpose of compelling the boats on our inland waters and coastwise trade to come under the control of the Railway Commission. At present the only boats that are under the control of that commission are those that are connected with the large railway corporations in our country. They are compelled to file their rates, tolls, tariff grievances, with the Railway (Board, while the other 4,500 boats-because there are 4,500 boats on the Canadian Register-are allowed to charge whatever rates they please, call or not at any dock or port as they please, and are a law unto themselves. When we take into consideration the fact that the people of Canada have spent nearly $350,000,000 in deepening our waterways, buoying and lighting our harbours and rivers, building our docks, piers and canals throughout the country, and then find themselves without any control
so far as Government control is concerned, we cannot help realizing that we are placed in a somewhat humiliating position. This is, however, practically the only public utility in Canada that is not under some form of Government control, and Canada is practically the only country in the world that has not absolute control over her shipping on inland waters and coastal trade. I hope, when this matter comes before the House, hon. members will give it every consideration and that it will become law at the earliest possible date. I understand that a Bill for the consolidation of the Railway Act has already been introduced into the Senate, and I hope it will come before the House in the near future. If it does, I trust I shall be allowed the privilege of placing an amendment in that Bill containing the principles contained in this Bill which I have now laid before the House.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to bring to the attention of the Government a question of national importance. In the Montreal Gazette of to-day, Thursday, February 27, there appears this cablegram from its resident correspondent in London:
Canada's trade handicapped in favour of the United States. Trade Commission lodges protest with Lloyd George. Change unlikely soon. Until brains of country get back on jobs discrimination will continue.
London, February 26.-Until the Peace Conference is over, and the brains of this country are back on their jobs again in Great Britain, there is little hope of the discrimination against Canada in the matter of imports being removed, declared I. N. Jones, member of the Canadian Trade Commission, to-day.
In support of this opinion Lloyd Harris and Mr. Jones have addressed strong representations to Premier Lloyd George and Sir Albert Stanley, president of the Board of Trade, showing clearly where discrimination exists.
I wish to know what is the nature of this discrimination, and whether Mr. Lloyd Harris and Mr. Jones have authority from the Government of Canada to make such representations to the Prime Minister of England direct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The news item in question was drawn to my attention only a few moments ago by my hon. friend. I have no official information in confirmation of the report,

and I must take the liberty of doubting that Great Britain would discriminate against Canada in favour of the United States or of any other country. My experience in the negotiations which the Government has during the past few months been conducting with the British authorities respecting the purchase of our agricultural and other products has been such as to assure me, if assurance were needed, that Great Britain is doing everything possible to facilitate and promote the trade of Canada with the Mother country. I am unable to say whether Messrs. Jones and Lloyd Harris made any such representations or not. Their powers and duties are defined by the commission which appointed them as Trade Commissioners Overseas. From time to time they take up with the British authorities matters relating to trade, but not having any official information as to the particular matter in question, I am unable to make any further comment. I shall he glad, however, to look into the matter.
On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
On the front page of the Ottawa Evening Journal of yesterday, under the heading, "All deserters appear again for heavy fine-minimum fixed at $250, and the new law is to be retroactive" there appears this statement:
It is further understood that this order in council will be retroactive, that is to say, that any deserter who has already given himself up and been let off with a fine less than ?250 can be re-arrested and re-fined at least to the minimum amount fixed in the new order. This will mean that hundreds of Quebec deserters who have been let off with a five dollar fine are liable to re-arrest and re-fine.
I should like particularly to know whether this is a proper representative of the Order in Council, and whether under its provisions those who have already been tried will be subject to re-arrest and re-trial.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Order in Council to which the extract refers does not provide for the punishment of any person who has already been punished in accordance with the law. There is a class of cases, however, of those who registered and were refused exemption who subsequently failed to report on being ordered to do so, and for whose cases, in the opinon of the Justice Department, as to which I think there can be no

dispute, no provision was made for a fine at all. The only punishment appearing in the regulations which it was open to magistrates to inflict in the cases was imprisonment. It is stated with regard to this class that there have been in many cases convictions where fines have' been imposed. The Order in Council is designed to enact that wherever in such eases fines of sub-tantial character have been imposed consistent with the magnitude of the offense- and the limits are fixed at $250 and $5,000 -those convictions are ratified as legal. The Order in Council does not go beyond that to ratify any conviction as legal, nor does it make illegal a conviction which when it was made was in accordance with law.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East) for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Wednesday, February 26th.

Mr. Speaker, before
entering upon the ground I wish to cover this afternoon it is my intention to make two preliminary remarks. First of all, I wish to tender to the Government of this country, and especially to the Acting Prime Minister, my sincere thanks for their broadmindedness in honouring as they have done the memory of our late beloved Chief. They have sympathized with us fully in our sorrow, and it is only right that we should proffer them our gratitude.
I also wish to tender to the mover and the seconder of the Address my congratulations for the able manner in which they have performed the arduous task that was allotted to them. Not wishing to risk a breach of the rules of the House by falling into tedious repetition, I shall confine myself to endorsing all the good things that have been said of these two hon. members. Their speeches, which were delivered with masterly skill, showed marks of deep thought.
Coming now to the subject before the House, I shall first answer some of the statements that have been made by two hon. ministers of the Crown, namely the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) and the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder). The Minister of Public Works informed us that numerous complaints were reaching the Cabinet every
day about after-the-war conditions, and his message to the people of Canada was to do away with unemployment in Canada. By this remedy, I suppose, he expects to avoid the complaints which threaten to overwhelm the Cabinet, and that peace will replace unrest. Is that a real remedy for the evil? Taking the picture he drew so vividly, with Canada called upon to borrow from $100,000,000 to $125,000,000 for a number of years to come, and with a net debt of two billion dollars, does he believe that his remedy will put a stop to the complaints which are pouring into Ottawa from all parts of the country? Does he believe that the feeling- of unrest will cease in view of the policy of extravagance which he has offered to the House, involving an expenditure of money by the millions of dollars? According to his statement, we shall be compelled to borrow every year the enormous sum of from $100,000,000 to $125,000,000.
I say, Sir, that we knew the evil as well as he did, but I regret to be compelled to confess that I do not believe the remedy he is offering will cure the situation, or that peace will replace the unrest that he told us existed in this country. This Minister of Public Works made a statement to which I have listened with a great deal of attention. I find, in perusing Hansard this morning, that the sentence he uttered in this House has been altered. It may have been a slip of the tongue, but I cannot, on account of those who heard the statement and who have not read the report, let it pass. I must enter my protest, and I must say to the House that I felt offended to hear an hon. minister of the Crown, on his own responsibility from his seat in this House, telling the members that he had read in the press that France intended to repudiate part of her war debt -France who has done so much for humanity, France with her indomitable courage, with all the losses she has sustained, France who has always been in the vanguard, fighting that right should prevail against might. If she were repudiating a single part of her war debt, she would not be the France we have known, the France we have loved, the France who has been the bulwark of civilization in the tremendous war which has just closed. There was another statement from the Minister of Public Works which has amazed me considerably. This statement I find in Hansard this morning, and I must take it as I lyaard it yesterday and as I have read it this morning. The hon. Minister of Public Works said last year that ships were more necessary than

anything else. In fact he is reported on page 50 as saying-
A year ago shipping was more vital to winning the war than were men or shells or anything else.
Well, Sir, if this statement is true-and I believe it to be true because I have heard it before in this very Chamber-why did we have conscription? Why did my hon. friend leave his party on that very question? And if my hon. friend thought, according to the advice that he had received from men in high office, that he was led into error when he was told that ships were not more necessary than men, but that men were more necessary than ships and we were compelled to have conscription, how is it he now contends that ships were more necessary than men, and how can be explain his remaining where he is to-day? My hon. friend, in his desire to defend his new friends in the Government in which he holds such a high position, has been compelled to let the truth fall from his lips, as the Book of Wisdom says, "Iniqui-tas mentita est sibi," "Iniquity has been a witness against itself."
We come now to the other minister of the Crown, the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder). He has invited criticism, and I shall avail myself of his invitation, and I shall try to answer as briefly as possible. The hon. gentleman has uttered a sentence that can be applied to the speech he delivered to the House yesterday. He told us that there had been a good deal of talk by the opponents of the Administration, but there had been nothing done. Here is a statement issued by Mr. Daly, director of repatriation for the Repatriation Committee. It is in regard to free medical treatment for ex-soldiers and sailors. I regret to have

to read such a document. It is contrary to the method in which I generally make speeches in this House, but I hope I will be allowed, for once, to depart from my rule. This is in answer to the assertion of the hon. minister, and, in order to be complete it must be read in its entirety:	It
reads:
Those discharged soldiers or sailors who become ill or disabled again as a result of some disease or injury suffered during war service receive free medical and surgical treatment.
This service is provided by the Medical Branch of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment.
An ex-soldier or ex-sailor who has a recurrence of a war disability should, if he is not too ill, go at once to the local medical officer of this Department.
If he is too ill he should have that medical officer notified at once.
Should he be taken ill in a place where there is no representative of the Department, he should call in a local physician to give him the necessary immediate treatment and ask him to communicate immediately all details of the case to the nearest medical officer of the Department.
The name of the authorized medical representative of this department for each locality is given alongside.
Treatment at the expense of this department can only be secured through these representatives. The Department cannot pay any bills for treatment which have not been authorized by the department.
If the medical officers recommend it pay is given to patients and allowances are granted to their dependents by the department^ during the period of treatment.
The established scale of pay and allowances that may be granted depends upon the extent to which the treatment recommended by the medical officer of the department prevents the patient from doing his regular work.
Arrangements for special care of patients of the department have been made with hospitals in all the larger towns and cities from coast to coast.
Sanatoria for treating tuberculosis under most favourable conditions are operated in every province under the direct supervision of the department
H. J. Daly,
Director of Repatriation.

If you take the list you will find that out of 49 medical officers there are only 16 who so far as my information goes are not friends of the Government. I do not accuse the Government of appointing their friends as medical officers for ex-soldiers and sailors, but what is the use of a minister of the Crown coming into this House, speaking from his seat in Parliament on his own responsibility and affirming that partisanship has disappeared, or is about to disappear? The document says that additions are being made to this list constantly. If we take it in the same proportion, we will see that out of over 100 medical officers appointed by this department two-thirds of

them are friendly to the Government. I do not object to that; I admit that it is fair, but virtue should wait before praising itself too highly when the Government has such a record as this. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization has also told us that he has been in public life for fifteen years, anu he has artirmed that the self-seexing politician is a danger to Canada. I suppose the hon. gentleman knows whereof he speaks. That is his statement. I do not challenge it. He has the experience. He is known as a public man from one end of the country to the other, and when he makes such a statement T believe the statement is true, coming from such a man.
The minister has informed us that the armistice was signed on November 11, 1918. This Government was elected as a win-the-war Government. Now, the war is over. I never could understand that, having beaten the Huns as we have, the world should be expected tp accept the camouflage of saying that what was signed on November 11 was an armistice when it was in fact an unconditional surrender. We have absolute proof that Germany, in signing this armistice, was surrendering and that when she signed it the war was over.
If it is true that the problems following peace are more stupendous than those which preceded it, and if it has taken this Government four years to build up their war machine, as the minister has said, do they want to take four years more to build up their peace machine? Why did they not call Parliament together before now? Why have the Government waited three months and why have they shouldered responsibilities that they had no reason to shoulder at all? They were elected to win the war, they believe they have won the war and that should be enough for any set of men even such an honourable body of men as our ministers are. Why had Parliament not been called upon before a few days ago to do its duty and to shoulder its part of the responsibility? I suppose the Government, having built their war machine, want to build, according to their own ideas, the peace machine to be put into operation when the war is over.
The hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) said to the House that there was a feeling of unrest in this country. Could it be otherwise? In a country like Canada, with the peculiar kind of government that we have, is it extraordinary that there should be unrest? Not at all. I shall explain what I mean. Having the confidence I have in the institutions of this

country, even if I were alone, I would stand up and make the statement which I shall now address to this House. This Government has been elected by a majority of the people. Whether the lists were right or wrong, we accepted the challenge; we lost the fight, but we are game enough to acknowledge that the ministers represent the majority of those who voted. But, they had a duty to perform. The first duty of all was to call Parliament in session when the war was over because they were elected to win the war and Parliament ought to have been consulted. The charge that I make against this Government is that they have waited for three months after the armistice was signed when they should have proceeded immediately to call Parliament together.
The Minister of Immigration and Colonization has told us that the members of the Opposition are like the man on the street. I have no objection to being likened to the man on the street. The man on the street is a citizen of this country. The man on the street is a voter if he has not been disfranchised by the Government.
The man on the street belongs to the common people. He bears the burden of taxation in peace time, and he risks his life in time of war, and he is entitled to the respect of even of a minister of the Crown. The man on the street, Sir, though he may be humble, modest, poor and even destitute has always been defended by the party which is now sitting to your left, and I am not ashamed to be compared to him. The man on the street is the backbone of the country when he is well treated, but when covered with scorn he is apt to lose his patience anu to crush those who think they are powerful because they happen to be temporarily holding the reins of power in the country.
The hon. minister (Mr. Calder) also told us that " he was still a Liberal and that nobody could put him out." I really think, Mr. Speaker, that nobody can put him out of the Government, which he seems to control. The hon. gentleman announces that he is still a Liberal, that he was a Liberal when he entered the Cabinet, and that he will remain one. I shall not enter into any discussion with him on that point. I shall not discuss his motives for leaving the party, it is no business of mine. But speaking for myself, I tell the hon. gentleman I do not regret his exit from our ranks. When the fruit becomes too ripe, Mr. Speaker, it falls from the tree which has given it life and which has brought it to maturity. The tree still continues to grow and to give its own life to

other fruit, but the fruit which has fallen to the ground is destined for destruction.
Every hon. gentleman occupying a seat in this House will agree with me, I suppose, when I say that in order that this country may be happy and prosperous we must have stability in Canada, and to have stability our people must have confidence in those who govern them. I submit, Sir, that the present Government is a peculiar one. It was elected to win the war, and the Government still remains in office. It is a Unionist Government without union. Free traders live under the same roof with ardent protectionists. Ministers are the target for the poisoned arrows of their followers and supporters; there is division in their ranks, and the majority of the people of this country who had confidence in this Government when they elected it will,
I believe, lose that confidence if something is not speedily done' to solve the problems which confront us. To judge from the speeches delivered yesterday by ministers of the Crown, there appears to them to be only one problem to deal with, and that is the problem of how to remain in office. Let me tell these hon. gentlemen that the country is not at all interested in that problem. The inaction of the Government, and the divisions which exist within it, have created that feeling of unrest in the country to which the Minister of Public Works yesterday made allusion.
Among the problems that confront us I find that there are three which require immediate solution, and it is the duty of the.Government to submit to Parliament a remedy which will cure the evils which threaten us. It is no use, Mr. Speaker, trying to avoid a solution of the problems which are calling for attention; it is useless to try and postpone the consideration of them. Now is the time for this Parliament to face the situation and to apply the remedy. The three problems in question, to my mind, are: first, the demobilization and reinstatement of our soldiers in civil life; second, the settlement of the question of capital and labour, and third, the agrarian problem. This Government was elected because it raised from one end of the country to the other the clamour that it favoured our boys at the Front. Do you not believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time to take care of the boys who-are coming from the Front? Do you not believe that those boys should be shown whether those war-time speeches were the true expression of sincere feeling? From my seat in the House yesterday I heard members of the Government telling us what they were doing in the way of meeting the existing problems. Admitting,
for the sake of discussion, that the Government is doing all that it can, that it has announced its actual policy in that regard, nevertheless, if that policy fails of results let the ministers have recourse to another. Mr. Speaker, when the boys rallied to the colours we promised to look after their interests. Well, the war is over. If the Government was able to supply ships to send our boys to the Front, let it with equal promptness find ships for transporting them back to their native land. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that it is a vexing problem, but a Government composed of the giants of the two political parties must surely be clever enough to overcome this difficulty in a satisfactory manner. Anyway, let it make an effort to do so. The policy which it has been pursuing has given rise to criticism and complaint. In all the large cities we hear it asserted that nobody is looking after the interests of the soldiers when they return from the Front. I repeat, Sir, that it is the imperative duty of the Government to provide in a speedy and satisfactory manner for the demobilization of our soldiers and their reinstatement in civil life. They have done their duty at the Front, and they are coming back covered with glory. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Government does not want our soldiers to feel ashamed because it is not performing its duty as well as those gallant fellows did theirs on the field of battle.
The second problem to be dealt with is that relating to capital and labour. I was very much interested yesterday upon hearing the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvelll) tell the financiers and the industrial corporations of this country: " You have made money by the war; put your money into new undertakings even if you do not receive any profit therefrom." Is that a remedy, Mr. Speaker? Capital is timorous; capital wants to feel its way before entering into any new undertaking. Because they have made money, does the Government believe that the financiers should invest that money in new undertakings at a time when the industrial market in Canada is one of such little stability? Not at all. Before plunging into new enterprises, capital wants to know the exact condition it has to face. Our captains of industry have been wise in the past, they are wise in the present, and we rely on their wisdom for the future of our country. It is bad counsel for a minister of the Crown to tell the financiers of Canada to spend their money without looking for any return.
The workingmen also are confronted with a situation the details of which they must

understand. I admit that the transformation of our war industries into civil industries is a more or less difficult problem. I admit also that the workingman may not have been as provident as he should have been during the time of war; he was making a large salary and should have saved for the future. I am told, however, that the savings of the workingmen do not amount to much and that during the period of the transformation of our war industries into civil industries, they will have to rely on the credit extended to them by the grocer, the baker, and all those who supply the necessaries of life for them and their families. If the Government does not tackle the problem of capital and labour, the workingmen, when they have lost all credit, will be looking for trouble. It is just as well not to be afraid of what is coming. It is our duty, as a minister of the Crown has told us, to inform the Government of what we know, in the expectation that the Government will do what it should do. The cost of living ought to be lowered. Profiteers should be called to account; they should be punished, not knighted. But I suppose the word of these men is listened to with more careful attention than are the words and the voice of the poor workingmen of Canada.
The third problem is the agrarian problem; it is the last but not the least. The farmers have responded wonderfully to the appeals of the Federal Government and the provincial governments; men have gone back to the farm and have worked to intensify their production. But just at the moment when the farming industry was at its height the war was terminated, and now the farmers are looking for a steady market in which they can sell their produce. They must have this market. The Government is appealing to the soldiers to settle on farms when they return to this country. Many who had been attracted from the farms to our large cities went back to the farm. Is there any sense in appealing to our people to take up farm work, in asking our soldiers to settle on the farms and our young men to remain on the farm, when the agricultural products of our country find no market? The farmers deserve to have the market; there is no use in postponing a settlement of this ques-4 p.m. tion; it ought to be settled immediately. This postponement cannot relieve the situation; I affirm, with all due respect to any members of this House who do not agree with me, that the postponement of the solution of such a problem as this is an economic error. ttMr. Gauthier.]
Having regard to these troublous problems which confront the country, may I be permitted, without indulging in flattery, to say to the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) that his day is coming? The affairs of the country require wise direction, and the people hope that the hon. gentleman will prove that he has the intellectual, the moral and the political stature to find and offer to the people a solution of these pressing problems which will bring contentment and satisfaction to every home in Canada. This no time for postponing settlement of these questions; a policy must be pronounced without delay.
Notwithstanding the words that fell from the lips of the two ministers of the Crown who spoke yesterday, I contend that in this as in any democratic country a parliamentary Opposition is necessary. We on this side intend to do our duty as the Constitution requires us to do it. We have lost our late chieftain; he has gone beyond the Great Divide, but he has left us his spirit, which still dominates our deliberations; he has left his teachings, which we still hear ringing in our ears, and we have his gospel embedded in our hearts. It is a gospel of tolerance, of justice, of equal rights ajid of democracy; its foundation is the human soul. That gospel must at the end triumph. It may happen' that the men of our generation will not see the hour of the triumph, but the triumph will come, because that gospel appeals to the mind and to the heart of every free man, of every lover of democracy.

Mr. Speaker, as a young and new member of this House, I wish in rising to continue the debate to pay my compliment to the mover and the seconder of the Address, and to congratulate the. Government on selecting two returned soldiers for that onerous and responsible duty. Not only was I very much impressed by the magnificence of their effort and the manner in which they discharged that duty, but I felt proud that amongst our soldier men we had two who could, upon the floor of the House of Commons, so vigorously, so ably, so splendidly, and with such refinement, in moving and seconding the Address, present the feelings prevalent in this country. The more particularly am I pleased because in the person of the seconder of the Address I have an old professional colleague and friend, one whom I have [DOT] watched and admired and respected ever since the first

day he entered as a student on the study of medicine.
Having siaid this, I am compelled also to remark upon the conditions under which to-day this House has met and the conditions under which we met last year. Then it was indeed a dark day of deep anxiety for the Empire. Men from this House of Commons went forth upon the streets of our capital with deep concern to study the bulletins outside the newspaper offices so as to know what was the next thing that had occurred, anxious as to what might he the outcome, some doubting, all hoping, yet restless, worried, I may say; and that feeling was but a mirror of the condition throughout the entire Dominion. Those who were not only concerned with Empire but deeply concerned and anxious regarding their loved ones who were in the thick of the fray-'aye, night and day, without exaggerating, they were there, living through the very mental anxieties almost of the lost, watching through the night, wondering if the next telephone ring might not bring some sad news, as it has done to many members of this House, to tell them that their dear loved one had unfortunately paid the full price of his devotion. To-day we meet under far happier circumstances. We meet, glorying in the realization that the Allied armies of the world have achieved a great and wonderful victory. We are proud too as Canadians that, in all the fighting, in all the struggling, in all the disasters, in all the uncertainties, in all the trials, the Canadian nation has played a man's part; a part equal to the best in this great, titanic struggle.
To-day we meet to make, in all seriousness, with every impartiality, a plain, honest, retrospect of our progress up to this hour. The hon. member (Mr. Gauthier) said that this Government was elected as a win-the-war Government. That is undoubtedly true and I want to express here my conviction that never before since Confederation has there been a government of this Dominion confronted with such a herculean task, confronted with such multitudinous and Protean difficulties, and that has come out with such a magnificent Tecord of achievement as has the present Government. And, Sir, I am convinced, notwithstanding all the criticism that that is the unanimous conviction of practically all the people of this country.
I desire to say a word or two in the way of kindly admonition and advice, so far as I am able, regarding the work left as the aftermath of this great war and which it is the legacy of this Government still
to wrestle with. I conceive it to be the bounden duty of every member of this House of Commons to shed any light that he can upon the difficulties so admittedly numerous which confront us to-day. The great work immediately before us as a lawful and legitimate legacy of this great war is the work of reconstruotion. ' I have listened with a great deal of attention to the arguments that have been put forward from both sides of the House as to the specific proposals upon the question of reconstruction. Whilst the needs and the difficulties have been dwelt upon, I must confess at the outset to some difficulty in laying hold of tangible suggestions, suggestions into which one can, so to speak, get his teeth, that he may know what we are going to do next. I purpose, in my humble way, to offer one or two suggestions.
Our first duty is to the returned soldier.
I do not think there is in this House a single man who is not desirous of doing all he can and all the country will, in his judgment permit him to do for the returned soldier. When the soldier comes back, welcomed as he is by his friends, flushed with victory and pride, hailed by his fellow citizens and received everywhere with open arms, may we not, as we cheer him and grasp him by the hand, have something in the hand to help to make his homecoming beneficial to him? For that reason, the first suggestion that I am going-to offer to this House is the wisdom of considering an increase in the pensions for the returned men. I believe I am correct in stating that at present the pension for total disability figures are somewhere around $600 for the private soldier, and that a difference is made between the pension for the private and that for the officer. At the outset, speaking for myself, I very seriously douut the wisdom of creating any such distinction. Whilst I give every credit to the officer, yet I think the magnificent work, accomplished by all our troops has been accomplished equally by the private as by the officer, and the same is true in regard to their record of suffering and sacrifice.
I will face this question fairly and squarely by asking myself, what would I be satisfied with as a pension for total disability so far as the country reasonably can provide? I know there are difficulties in doing all we desire, but after all is $600 under present conditions a very liberal allowance for total disability? Conceive what total disability is ! I saw a returned soldier in the city of Toronto who had lost both legs and his left arm. I presume that man

would not be ranked as totally disabled and would not receive the pension for that class. Yet what condition is that man in to face life? Would any man take $600 or $6,000 per year and go through life under those conditions? And yet we commence by awarding a pension that is based on total disability, and then our Pension board figures the degree of disability according to their conception of total disability, and total disability is an uncertain quantity. Some one may say that figures cannot lie. Well, I do not wish to say they cannot, but I know that some figurers can, and I know that when you want to obliterate the truth or cover up a patent and obvious defect, the best way to do it is to ta.se a percentage basis of calculation; and calculating a man's degree of disability on that basis you can start with a very serious handicap and figure it down almost to nothing. I think that is where there is danger of dissatisfaction creeping in almost without the knowledge, and certainly without the intention, of the Government, and it might be held up by some as something which was not creditable and which did not represent an honest endeavour to deal justly by the returned men. For that reason I want to offer the blunt suggestion of raising the total disability pension from the present rate up to $1,000 a year. iSome may say: You will bankrupt the country. Not a bit of it; because the number of total disabilities will be comparatively small, and I am convinced that if my suggestion were adopted it would not add a very great amount to our Pension Bill. But it would be a great satisfaction in the future to know that an earnest, honest effort had been made to discharge as far as we legitimately could our duty and obligation to the men who have so gloriously distinguished Canada among the nations. And, Sir, no matter to what height the tidal wave of our generosity may rise we still remain a debtor to our men who by their service have given us that protection which Canada can never fully compensate for.
The next question I wish to deal with is the question of the aliens. The alien question is a very serious one in many of our cities. It is a very serious one in the city of Toronto. Aliens are divided into two classes: the enemy alien, and the ordinary alien. The enemy aliens-and theie were, and still are, a number of them resident in the city of Toronto-are individuals, we can hardly call them men, who have come into our midst and fostered the ideas of the Teutons. They have done all they could

to injure the loyal citizens of my city; they have connived in every intrigue that they could possibly conceive. They have houses in some cases, and have sheltered within them enemy aliens until they were discovered by the police. They have propagated that rotten system of espionage which has honeycombed the civilization of the whole of this continent. They have been forced into concentration camps, they have been surrounded by guards, they have been threatened with the pointed bayonet, and to-day they are waiting and anxiously hoping that now the war is over they may creep back again and mix with loyal, honest, and patriotic Canadians. I want to say with all the emphasis at my command that I believe I am speaking for the whole of this country when I say it, that the best policy to adopt regarding enemy aliens is *to pack them all aboard the first outward-bound ship and see that they go back to the countries whence they came.
While on this question, I am forced to refer to the War-Time .Elections Act. I am glad the Government intend to bring down a measure which purports to make permanent some of the provisions of that Act. I hope they will see to it that none of the enemy aliens at least, whether or not they have been implicated as active enemies, will be placed on the franchise rolls of this Dominion for the next twenty years. We can do without them. It was one of the master strokes of this Government, an act which carried with it the commendation of all loyal people, when they decided in the great effort of this war to proceed along the lines of the old British people who came here and laid the foundations of our institutions. II think we can sometimes take a lesson from the great republic to the south of us, and upon this question 'I agree with the policy of (Roosevelt, who declared that as far as he was concerned, speaking as an American citizen, he believed that a country that was good enough to live in was good enough to fight for. I like that sentiment, and I say it is a good one for the people of the Dominion of Canada to adhere to.
But when we have disposed of the enemy alien, we have by no means disposed of the whole alien question. Besides enemy aliens, we have many other aliens in the city of Toronto. We have aliens who have been exempted from military service for international reasons, very largely, and have continued to do business and to take advantage of the situation. I had the privilege when the Military Service Act was

being enforced to sit upon one of the exemption tribunals in the city of Toronto, and I will give a concrete case to illustrate my meaning. A young man who was conducting a grocery store in the city of Toronto applied to that tribunal for exemption. His father was an old, feeble and infirm gentleman who had put all his capital into the business in the hope that the son would be permitted to carry it on. The son was of military age, and applied for exemption to the military tribunal on which I sat. We discussed his case very carefully and thoroughly, but we decided that, although his business might be ruined, he would be compelled to go to the Front. As a result of our decision the store was closed, and he had to make the best of the situation. Wishing to know the true facts of the case,
I visited the locality, and I was astonished to find that an alien had rented the store next door and had started the same kind of business. I asked him when he came there, and he said: " Oh, I came just now;
I know you, doctor; I have no vote, but I do not care about having no vote, if I have the business." There are plenty of men in the city of Toronto who have received, in a smaller or larger degree, an advantage exactly under those circumstances and conditions, until now I think I am within the mark when I say that a large proportion of the small businesses in the city of Toronto are controlled by aliens, I do not say by enemy aliens, but aliens, men who have come into this country within the last few years. Forty per cent of the small businesses and many of the larger businesses are conducted by these people. Incident to the war, their businesses and their profits have increased enormously. We were told by one of the ministers that about 50 per cent of the active young men of fighting age from Canada have gone into the service. Well, you can see what remains. It gives, and has given, these aliens a magnificent opportunity, and they have taken the fullest advantage of it. What I want to say to the Government, and what I would respectfully suggest for their consideration, is the conception of some proper and practical method of taxation, so that these business increases which ensue as a result directly of the war, could be investigated, and the profits that have accrued, shared in by the country; to the end that when the men return and apply to be reestablished in civil life, they will not be confronted by aliens who control the business which they wish to enter, men perhaps who very imperfectly understand English or speak it not at all. It is disappointing for 6
them to find that, on their return, after having fought for the liberties of the people, these liberties are being enjoyed by men who are not possessed of British ideals, and who are not in the true sense Canadians.
While on this subject, I wish to say a word or two regarding our immigration.
I am not speaking particularly of immigration as administered since this Government came into power, but the immigration system under previous governments. They have, so to speak, permitted the doors to be opened, and everybody who likes can come into the country without question, hesitation, selection, or inspection. I saw not very long ago a statement in one of the Toronto newspapers that there had been a special arrangement by which Mennonites were admitted into the western provinces of Canada, exempt from military service. I do not believe the statement; ll am sure it cannot be true, and I do not believe that any member of the present Government would approve of such a thing. Do we not know Mennonites? Are they not essentially German? Have they not German traditions, German literature, German legends? Are they to be permitted, after being hounded from the United States of America, to gain admission into Canada exempt from military service? No, no, hon. gentlemen, I do not believe the Government made any such arrangement, and I do not believe that the Government in the future would be justified in giving any privileges to anybody coming into Canada which the native born Canadian himself cannot enjoy.
I want to say a word or two regarding the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Department, and I make my statement particularly as the hon. gentleman on the other side (Mr. Gauthier) said he considered it was only an organization for the distribution of patronage. If at some time the hon. gentleman would come to the city of Toronto and would visit the Davisville hospital or the Hart House or any one of several institutions I can give him names of, he would not only see that it was not for the distribution of patronage, but that it was marvellous in its achievements, magnificent in its ideals, splendid in its efforts, and in the work it has set out to accomplish. I can show him there, where soldiers who had been disabled for two years in the English hospitals have come home, have been placed there under the directions and guidance of masseurs, trained calis-themc directors, and under treatment the paralyzed muscles and the palsied limb have been restored, and the cripple has gone out of the hospital astonished at the



splendid results which have been achieved under skilled and scientific direction. I can go further, and show you that in every department of civil life they have, from the ordinary private soldier, evolved experts for almost every line of work. We ' have stenographers, typewriters, skilled machinists, expert electricians, mechanics, wood carvers, all developed out of soldiers who knew nothing about these trades before. Our men have been more encouraged and more benefited by that work and the examples which they have daily seen developed before them than by any work for the benefit of the soldier that has been done, I venture to say, by any country in the civilized world.
I congratulate the Government upon stating that they had at last decided to establish a federal Department of Public Health. This is to me no new idea. I read a few years ago a most able speech by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) which he made in this House, a speech which wa? commended very highly by the members of the medical profession throughout the whole country, a speech to which my attention has been drawn since I was elected to this House by no less than 20 medical men in the Dominion of Canada, irrespective of politics or party, and residing in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Therefore I am more than gratified to see that a Federal Department has been at last resolved upon, but, if I understood the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) correctly, he said he could not understand the use of it; he could not see what was the sense of sending a medical man of the federal government to interfere with a medical man of the Provincial Government. Well, if that is his conception of a Federal Health Department work, I am sure, (adopting the words of the last speaker), he will have to linger long upon the boughs of the apple tree to which he is attached before he will on that question be anywhere nearly ripened so as to fall to the ground in the amplitude of his maturity.
I can conceive at this juncture of no department of the public service which any Government could institute more replete with opportunities beneficial to all classes of the community than, a public health service, rightly and justly administered.
Let me just, en passant, give you a few thoughts that have occurred to me with regard to that work. First and foremost, it is a great work in connection with the Department of Immigration. We have had in the past, rushing into this country, without

restraint, inspection or restriction, the diseased, the mentally defective, the criminal, the unhappy, the uncertain, the infamous. They have come in here to do what? To work? Not a bit of it. They are absolutely incapable of working. They are not skilled workmen, they are not farmers -they never were-and they are not artisans. They have been in many cases chased from one large centre of the civilized world to another, until they have embarked en route to the new world. Probably they have tried the quarantine station at New York, they have been hunted from there, and then they creep around by the sea and come into Halifax. They have done that in the past. I am not blaming the present Government for that; that is a legacy that dates away back, to the time when people of this class were allowed to come into the country.
I have reason to know whereof I speak, for I have had occasion to act in many of their cases. Not only have we to care for them, but we have the legacy which they leave. We have the epileptic, we have the mentally defective. The defective engrafts his progeny upon Canada, breeds in his turn other mental defectives still worse because with every generation the trait intensifies, until, as a result of imperfect and unscientific inspection, we have innumerable cases occupying our asylums, our jails, our reformatories and our prisons, which have entailed upon the Dominion of Canada a cost of untold millions. All you have to do is to study the catalogues and indices of psychologists and those who have checked up the subject to see the percentage of mental defectives amongst our imported population. Tnat is one feature.
Another feature that I want to refer to has reference to the epidemics which occasionally come in this country. We have had an illustration of one in the ravages of the "flu." "Flu" has been very severe in some localities. I was speaking on the subject with a medical man, a Canadian officer, who was located at Gibraltar. As far as he knew, the first case of 'flu in the south of Spain came under his observation and he told me of the investigations that were being made by the French and British Governments when the epidemic broke out. While I admit that no department, under present conditions, is in the slightest degree to blame for the ravages throughout Europe and this continent of such an epidemic, I merely cite that illustration to strengthen the point I have to make regarding this matter. They knew how these epidemics spread and developed and

they were able in a large measure to take preventive means which, I am quite convinced, restricted the further ravages of this disease. Would it not be a profitable thing for the Federal Government to have a scientific bureau of investigation where trained men would be able and competent to investigate all these sporadic and serious infectious maladies so that we would be able to deal with the situation before the advent of the infection and thus prevent the wholesale and general infection which is apt to follow if these diseases are not thoroughly and scientifically understood.
There is another point directly in line with that to which I would draw attention. There is the control and supervision of all kinds of quack nostra for the cure of all the ills that flesh is heir to. The men who sell and manufacture them know little of medical science and they care less. All they know is that it pays to advertise and that their sales are proportionate to their advertisements. They have indices of every disease to which flesh is heir and they have a remedy for each. The poor unfortunate invalid as he struggles tottering to the grave is on the list of the charlatan who has a cure-all to sell him. Is it not time that the Government of this Dominion should control absolutely and rigidly the manufacture and sale of patent and proprietory medicines? Is it not time that they tested in the public laboratories of the country every curative that is to be put upon the public market? Is it not time that they left the manufacture of serums to the provincial authorities whose laboratories in the main are excellent for the development and manufacture of these products? Yet they do not.
I want to give to you, Mr. Speaker, by way of illustration, an incident which occurred under the last Government. I am informed that the laboratories of the Public Health Department of the province of Ontario were ready to make Salvarsan, or as it is known, 6-0-6, as a serum cure for syphilis. Before they could distribute that amongst the medical men of the^. country, they required a Federal license and the officers of the Provincial Board of Health of Ontario came to Ottawa for the purpose of obtaining that license. They were not permitted to get it. They were absolutely refused the license which would have permitted the Provincial Board of Health to manufacture and distribute that curative product. They were opposed by what we may call the interests, by certain men who
6}
were engaged in the introduction of other so-called cures for the same thing. Now, I contend that these things should not be and that there is a splendid opportunity for a Federal Department of Public Health which will regulate all that kind of thing. We have been agitating about this matter in the Province of Ontario, and the Provincial Government has appointed a commission for the purpose of investigating venereal disease. The one thing which makes that malady more terrible than it really is, is the hope existing in the mind of the infected that he can secure a cure in privacy, and that by entering his cloister with some patent nostrum and shutting the door he can regain his health, with the result that the last state of that man is worse than the first. Now if these things are true about the human organism, they are equally true about another branch of the animal kingdom, viz: cattle and other domestic animals. They are equally liable with ourselves to infection, and they are equally liable to conditions and troubles which can be cured by scientifically and wisely directed effort. So also in connection with the vegetable kingdom. There are infectious maladies in the case of fruit trees, and various other species and varieties of vegetation, with which it is the bounden duty of the Dominion to deal, and not the duty of any particular province. I am fully aware that health affairs ought to be left to the provincial governments very largely. True they are to a great extent a matter of locality, or are very often modified by local conditions, nevertheless, it is wise that we should co-operate to the fullest, and assist to the utmost of our power in the work, the pioneer work, which has been so splendidly done by the provinces in the domain of public health. But that is begging the question entirely: there is st'll a large field of activity awaiting the attention of a federal health department. Moreover there are legacies, directly traceable to this war, which the federal health department must needs deal with. There are cases of tuberculosis, there may be cases of venereal disease, there are cases of mental aberration, there are cases of shell shock, there are cases of chronic nervous maladies which will be with us for ten or fifteen years to come, the treatment of which is not a burden belonging to any particular province but should rest upon the shoulders of the Federal Government representing the country as a whole, and should be scientifically and intelligently dealt with. I will not weary you any more by dwelling upon what I might narrate upon this line

I am leading up to the point which I want to impress upon you, that if we are going to have active, energetic, and proper service from this department, which the country needs, we must have a medical mind at the head of it. There is in its administration, as much technicality, as much minute detail, as much complexity as there is in the conduct of the Department of Justice; and yet would any member of this House entertain for a second the thought that a doctor, or a layman could administer, as Minister of Justice, that legal department with any degree of common sense or satisfaction. And yet the Minister of Justice has to deal with man-made laws, whereas in the Department of Public Health the administrator is confronted with the great complex and obscure laws of nature, which it requires long training to apprehend and even then they cannot be understood to the fullest degree. These laws can only be realized by a study in the greatest laboratory of all, in the hospital ward, where we see the varied phases through which the sick are passing, and where we are able, with gentleness and kindness, to make every allowance as we approach with a keen desire to help those cases which command our patience, our sympathy, and our regard. It is for that reason that I urge upon the Government to begin right, to place at the head of the Health Department some man who will command the respect of the whole of this Dominion; a man who is skilled and expert in medical knowledge, so that he can administer that department with the same efficiency and the same comprehension as is displayed in the administration of the Department of Justice. Some hon. gentlemen may say: You are extravagant in your ideas for the period of curtailment and economy which has been suggested by the ministers of the Crown. For my part, I am not altogether convinced that economy is the wisest policy at this juncture. It all depends of course on how we practise economy. The cheapest thing is not always the best, it may be cheap and yet very dear in the long run.
I was somewhat impressed with the speech of the Minister of Public Works (iMr. Carvell), and I am sorry he is not in the Chamber at present because I wish to say one or two things about him. First of all, the hon. minister said he was not a pessimist. Well, it is hard for me to believe that he is an optimist, and in his speech he drew rather a sombre picture of the future conditions in this Dominion, as to what we were to do for revenue to keep
[IMr. Sheard.]
going. To my mind he mixed up his accounts; 'I would like to have a professional audit of the statements from a financial standpoint. The hon. minister incorporated the expenditures for capital and permanent purposes with current expenditures, as I understood him, and forecasted an outlay something like $110,000,000 per annum. This is the estimate he gave us of the sum which would have to be raised. There was to be a Government building in Montreal, a Government building in Toronto, and I think he' said a Government building in Calgary-these, amongst other things, were to be the subjects of outlay. I do not suppose the Government intends to go on erecting great public buildings annually, and I think therefore there was probably an over anxiety on his part in considering the expenditures incidental to the present year. I have great confidence in this Dominion, as we progress in our national development. I have great confidence in our resources, in the agricultural richness of Canada, in its mineral and timber wealth, in the value of its inland seas and fisheries; and I believe that if we wisely direct the development of our resources and see that they are not wasted, we need have no apprehension or anxiety regarding our ability to provide for all that is needed, or for all that the country imperatively desires. At the same time I am not in favour of exempting the great interests from the Business Tax. I know it is very popular to tax incomes and to say: ''Let the man who has the money and the income take the taxes. Everybody says: there are few who have it, and therefore if we tax the few we will probably have less complaint from the great majority." But let me ask you as a professional man-and you know that doctors never make any money, they are one class of the community that work night and day and die poor- let me ask you who have been the makers of the great fortunes realized ever since the commencement of this war. I met a man the other day who had made, since the beginning of the war, no less than two and one-half million dollars. There are men who are engaged in certain industrial works to whom war-time conditions brought greatly increased trade. The Government has in the past taxed them, and I hope it will continue to do so even in peace times, because their profits were unduly and excessively large. Let us adopt a broad and equitable policy, so that every man will pay his share. I like a man who will always do his part, who will lift his share of the load, who will pay his share of the taxes,

who will carry his burden in common with the rest of us, so that we can all pull together with confidence up the slope, and in due course land the load on the top of the hill.
Now, I want to say a word with regard to the Civil Service Commission. Last session- on the floor of this House I supported the Civil Service Commission; 1 thought that there were great possibilities for good in it. I have not changed my mind; I am still going to support the continuance of that commission. I do not say that it is perfect. I do not say that we cannot make improvements in it. I do not say that it always does the wise thing. There are certain things I want to know. First, I propose, if some one else does not do it, to put a question on the Order Paper with a view to finding out how many appointments made under the Civil Service Commission since it was established were given to returned soldiers. I want to see how in the total sum the returned soldier figures, because I have known instances where he did not get a good show.
I am an old examiner. I have been at the business for thirty years, and I know all the tricks of the trade. One time I had to do with an appointment in Toronto where there were tremendous crowds and very strong influence on both sides, and the appointee had to be a lady, so you can guess what difficulties we were in. The matter should have been dealt with by the municipal council, but the municipal council balked when they saw the beautiful faces and winning ways of the ladies' delegations; so finally, after shifting it from one committee to another, they landed it on my shoulders and said: Let him do the work. Then the deputations began to come before me, and I must confess that several of the recommendees left not much room for choice among them. They all appeared to have splendid qualifications, and I spent some time and many weary hours of thought in studying out what kind of problem I should put up to get the one that pleased me best. I am not a card player, but I understand that the card players say: When in doubt, play trumps. Similarly, when you do not know which side to please, please yourself. That, I think, is a good policy, and it is my policy. Well, in this case I had my own ideas. Some sections of the press were recommending one person and other sections were recommending another, and I said, I will hold an examination and decide the question on its merits. And then the examination proved exactly to go my way; I appointed the one whom
1 desired to appoint, and everybody was satisfied that the best girl won. I am not saying that the best did not win, nor am I saying that this is what always happens with the Civil Service Commission. But I will give you another illustration.
In London a student who was to he examined at the 'College of Surgeons had been a special pupil of one of the examiners, and this student was excessively stupid. This professor said to the student: " James, I want you to study the symptoms and pathology of cirrhosis of the liver. Do not bother with anything else, but
5 p.m. study that so that you can say it backwards and frontwards until you know it thoroughly." The pupil agreed to do this. In the College of Surgeons in London the examiners work in pairs; one man asks the question and the other puts down the mark. So when this candidate was called in the examiner who had been teaching him said to his co-examiner: " I will ask the question now, if you do not mind, and you can mark him." So he was trotted in and the first question he was asked was: " Now, sir, just tell me the symptoms and pathology of cirrhosis of the liver." Of course, he excelled himself in the readiness of his answer. He did so well that he completed the whole thing before the time limit, and the examiner scratched his head, and, assured that if he asked the candidate anything else he would prove his ignorance, said: " You have done that so well, would you please repeat it?" So I say that examinations are not always a real test of a man's fitness, and when you come to test by examination a man who is already qualified for a technical position you are apt to get just where you do not want to get.
Apropos of this, I want to read a letter which illustrates exactly the question that I am discussing. A Canadian veterinarian of considerable ability who had seen service in Egypt, the Mediterranean, France, Belgium and Britain, who had qualified in the Ontario Veterinary College and had been four years in the war, was desirous, now that he had come home, of carrying on the work that he had given up when he went to the front. He came to me and spoke about applying for a position in the Government. I said: "I have nothing to do with it; you had better write to that Civil Service Commission." I do not know whether there is a place in the Government service at this time for a veterinarian, but this is the answer he got from Dr. Roche- this to the returned soldier, to the experi-

enced veterinarian who had seen four years' active service overseas:-
I have yours of the 5th and am enclosing you a temporary position form, which kindly fill out and return to the Commission, so that we may have your name on file in the event of the Agriculture Department placing a requisition before the Civil Service Commission for additional help in your line.
He did not see that that was going to get him anywhere, so he wrote again, this time to the Secretary of the Civil Service Commission. Apparently more consideration was given to his application this time and a fuller letter was formulated. The next letter he received from the Commission was as follows-remember, this is a case of a returned soldier, a professional man:-
With reference to your application for employment in the Civil Service of Canada, I would say that the work in which you are Interested or for which you appear to be qualified, comes under "Special or Technical Positions," usually thrown open to competition and for which an examination is sometimes necessary.
Evidently they have not any fixed rule in the matter. (Reading):-
As a rule such vacancies are not of frequent occurrence, but when they do occur and are not filled by promotion, an advertisement thereof appears in the Canada Gazette. In order that you may receive copies of these notices, your name has been placed on our mailing list.
Well, I think I could have given him my copy of the Canada Gazette and not lost a great deal. However, I do not wish to criticise too severely the Civil Sendee Commission. They made two splendid appointments of considerable importance in Toronto. They appointed a postmaster and a deputy postmaster in the city of Toronto, and I do not believe there have been two appointments made by any Government since Confederation which have, to so large an extent, received the approval of the people, one and all. They took as their appointees in those particular instances men who had devoted their whole lives to the service. The man who was made postmaster was the former deputy postmaster who had grown up in the service, who knew every wrinkle in the whole office, who knew the very men that were employed there. Even although I was not consulted in regard to the appointment and did not know who the appointee was until after he got the job, I am glad that he was made postmaster. I congratulate the Civil Service Commission and the Postmaster General of this Dominion on making that appointment, because I know that almost irrestible efforts and pressure were exerted by certain political parties in order that that appointment should not be made. Not
[OMr. Siheard.]
only was the postmaster appointed in that way, but as deputy postmaster they appointed a man from the ranks, a man who had grown up in the service, a man who had a magnificent and perfect record behind him, a man who thought that by devotion to the service of this country in a civil capacity, he would be justly dealt with and would receive advantages and emoluments which would be worth while. I wish, on the floor of this House, to offer my testimony and express my satisfaction in regard to those two appointments, to encourage the Civil Service Commission and also the ministers by showing them that when they are making good appointments, such appointments will not be forgotten. There is another thing I desire to add to this. A few days before I left Toronto I saw the newly appointed postmaster, and while I was congratulating him upon his work, I incidentally said, " Well, how is the salary now? Is it the same as before the war?" I really do not know what the salary is. " Why," he said, " the salary is the same as it has been for twenty years, but the work and the business have increased over a hundred fold." I have had some experience in work and in getting good service, and I think the poorest policy one can adopt is to underpay ofiicials that have responsible duties to perform. While I am speaking about the post office in the city of Toronto and the whole postal service, I want to say that the postmen are scandalously underpaid in the cities-I do not know anything about outside. I say they are scandalously underpaid, because they cannot live on the pay they get.
It is 100 per cent worse in the country.

I heard the discussion on the floor of this House last year in reference to the rural mail carriers. I heard it stated by hon. members that contracts were actually let at prices that would not pay for the horse feed. I believe that was, to a large extent, true. It ought not to be so. You will never get satisfactory service unless you pay a reasonable fee for it. It is all very well to say: Well, they get so many hundred dollars a year. In all this discussion of labour, somehow or another, people do not appear to have grasped the cardinal thought of the purchasing price of a dollar. A man's pay must be proportionate to the purchasing price of a dollar. What is the use of giving a man $950 a year as a postman in the city of Toronto, when that sum will not pay for his house rent, clothes and fuel-those three essentials? You cannot expect him to be

satisfied. We had serious trouble last year. The postmen made representations, so they told me, time and time again, and they did not get any satisfactory answer, so they went on strike.
