We came down here in the interest of the city to try to get the Government 'to consider their case. The Government did consider their case; they went into it very thoroughly and exhaustively. I had hoped that they had kindly and generous hearts in the Council, but unfortunately when the returns came in, we were disappointed to find that the Government had given an increase which I think was given with a very mean and stinting hand. I am convinced that it would be good policy to go through the whole Civil Service administration from top to bottom. Let there be a portion of the work of reconstruction applied to it. Let us weed out the useless rot; let us take out the weed crops; let us take out the old decayed roots from the structure, and let us revitalize that which is retained and give strength and character to the Service by paying a decent, generous, liberal wage to the men who have to assume the responsibilities of carrying on the government and administering the work which is, after all, for the benefit of the people. Let us in that way make them satisfied in the knowledge that when they devote their talents, time, energy and years to public trust in the public service, they are serving an honest and good Administration, and will not have to spend their declining days in a workhouse or a home. That is the policy which I would suggest to the Government if I were touching on the Civil Service question.
Unless we can use our public moneys in a proper manner, we may find that we are suffering from the troubles referred to by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell), when he spoke of people who lived beyond their incomes, and some governments have in the past been very wasteful. I was impressed by the speech made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) last year, when he referred, speaking in connection with the Canadian Northern railway, to the tremendous, extravagant expenditures which were made to liquidate the liabilities which had been manufactured by Mackenzie and Mann. Let us exercise prudence, forethought and foresight. Let us economize by not assuming burdens that are unnecessary and that will undoubtedly be unprofitable. Let us economize so as to give what we all desire, namely, assistance to the soldier in every way. Let us rise and give him our place if need be.
Let him understand that the country is not unmindful of his great sacrifices. We are apt to lose sight of the prospect of capitalizing the greatest asset we have from this great war, that is the patriotism and devotion to service which those men who went overseas, evince. They went without compulsion; they went voluntarily; they suffered, as we know; they come back imbued with the same love of country, if not more so, as they had before they went. They come back sure of their belief that Canada is of all countries the best place to live in, and we want by generous and kindly treatment to develop in that particular an asset of value in them, to make them emissaries and missionaries in every hamlet and town so that they may extol the great advantages of this vast country which belongs to us, the country we live in, the country we love.
Those of us who have had their sons and blood at the front know what I mean, when as I look back upon the war I refer to it as those four long years of hellish night, and we are apt to ask now of our watchmen upon the tower, "Watchmen, what of the night?" The answer comes back: if we have confidence, the night is not so black as it was; there are streaks on the horizon's verge; there is mist in the valley, the sun is rising, there is dawning upon this country and upon this people a new day, a day of peace, prosperity and happiness. Let us all join together with a united effort, without regard to party politics and their narrow divisions, and hand in hand, as one broad-minded, generous, devoted, energetic and hard-working people pray God to grant that in the new day now dawning Canada may be blessed above and beyond all nations, that glorious Canada may rise Phoenix-like from the fire of this great war, triumphant as our boys have been triumphant in Europe, and let us all as Canadians say, God be thanked.

Mr. Speaker, among the hon. gentlemen who have paid a tribute to the memory of our beloved chieftain (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), few perhaps have suffered as deep a loss as we younger members of the House.
From our very youth we had grown accustomed to admire the noble and grand figure of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and to follow the advice he was wont to give our seniors; we had made up our minds to do as much, when our turn came, but unfortunately the fatal hour has struck; he has passed away and bid adieu to this world where

he played such a glorious role and we, the young members, are left alone to steer the course so well marked out by him, with those great principles of harmony, humanity, union and tolerance. We shall certainly be called upon to put those great principles into practice, and there will be no more striking tribute paid to his memory by the younger members than their faithful adherence to the virtues preached by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We shall endeavour to follow in his footsteps by promoting the welfare of the country and helping our fellow-citizens, no matter what their language or their race, and to make of Canada a country worthy of the Twentieth Century.
Let us set to work, and to satisfy him of our sincerity let us remain faithful to duty to the very end; let us walk in his footsteps and history will tell that the broad-mindedness of the younger generation was worthy of the broad-mindedness of their beloved leader.
It is now my duty to tender to the mover and seconder of the Address to our beloved Sovereign my warmest congratulations for the manner in which they have performed their task. They have departed from the beaten track of their predecessors and shown real independence of thought.
They have shown themselves the fearless and gallant soldiers that they are. They are entitled to our congratulations and we, the younger members of this side of the House, are happy to express to the younger members on the opposite benches our appreciation of their courage and their eloquence.
Let us hope that in the future they will also walk in the footsteps of our great leader who has passed away; that their minds and hearts will be constantly attentive to the promotion of the welfare of this country and let me assure them that in following this straight and narrow road they will have us with them.
From the very beginning of this session, Sir, we have shown that we were willing to follow in the wake of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We have accepted with enthusiasm the lead of our present chief and shall endeavour to prove to him that we are the worthy sons of that great patriot, Sir Wilfrid Laurier; we will follow him as thoroughly, as frankly and as fully as our English-speaking friends, for upward of thirty years, followed our great Chieftain who has passed away; we will render him the homage that he, in company with his English-speaking associates, tendered to our own leader by remaining with him through thick and thin. He can count on the younger members as

well as on their elders; these last, moreover, have already shown their willingness to do his bidding.
After listening to the speeches delivered so far I have wondered-in company with many others-whether all the speakers were not quite of one mind in demonstrating that the present Government often lacked decision in the decisions it was called upon to make. It seems rather impossible to find a decision which is lacking in decision, but really we have had ministers tell us that they have given the greatest care and attention to our national problems, that they would give more care than ever to the problems brought about by the war. But, Mr. Speaker, during the present session we shall be called upon to, work out the difficulties of re-establishment and to decide in what way we can help our returned soldiers to resume their status in civil life. The hon. ministers talked a great deal, for hours at a stretch, to tell us that they had accomplished a lot; unfortunately, they did not tell us what they intended to do later on.
We have not even learned from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) how many acres had been granted to our returned soldiers; nor how many veterans had applied with the intention of settling on this fwonderful land that was promised them. It is all very fine to promise the soldier land, to make a farmer out of him ; but, Sir, the offer is conditional: the condition is that the soldier pay full value for what he gets; he will have to pay, in common with all other farmers, the biggest part of the taxes levied after his return. If my information is correct, the Government lends him, to start with, a few thousand dollars, payable in fifteen or twenty years; but the Government, of course, has the prudence to take, as security, all that the soldier-farmer has, so that even he will be unable to get under way immediately. Everything will be mortgaged. And that is their idea of re-establishment.
Have you ever considered, iSir, what it would cost the country if only one-half our returned soldiers asked the 'Government for the $7,500 it is proposed to lend them? Did you ever consider that the country would have to pay out, a few months hence, between $1,500,000,000 and $2,000,000,000?
At the time of the last Victory Loan the hon. Minister of Finance had many misgivings about its success; but he may feel sure that when he comes again before the country to ask for such fabulous sums he will meet with complete failure because he

will be unable to grant to the most exacting any exemption from customs duties such as the people of this country are clamouring for.
He won't perhaps be able to pass Orders in Council exempting from taxation the tractors required by the Western farmers for their ploughs or to enable the farmers of the great provinces which produce potatoes to export them to the United States; without which expedients the loan would have proven a failure in those provinces. It is all very fine for the Minister to have succeeded in financing his loan by such means; but when the question will be to borrow some hundred million dollars for rounding up the budget and the other hundred millions to be loaned to soldiers for buying land and stock and farming implements, do you think, Sir, that the country will still be able to advance so much money? If the Government intends giving effect to this programme of Soldier Settlement-in the West alone, I suppose-it will require at least half a billion, and we may very well ask ourselves if the financiers, if the agricultural classes will be able to supply these funds; with this mind, and in an attempt to shift the burden, the Government invited all the provincial premiers to a conference. They made a decision without deciding anything. This conference took place in Ottawa; it lasted for a few days. The papers informed us that a few of the great premiers had made formidable suggestions, that they were going to get the Government out of the mess it was in. We have as yet been unable to find out just what these suggestions were, or whether the 'Government saw fit to make use of them, for the Teason that we have still to witness any result of this conference. The two Iron, ministers whose speeches preceded ours in this debate, told us nothing about it. I suppose that the hon. Prime Minister of Ontario, as well as his hon. colleague from Quebec, offered lands for Soldiers Settlement, too. Mr. Speaker, can you see the position the returned soldier would be in if the Ontario or the Quebec Government gave him land to settle on? Gan you see these men who for the last four years, in some cases only three years, have had to dig themselves a hole in the soil of Flanders for shelter against enemy fire, coming back to this country, where, thanks to the present Government, we'll change the spade for an axe and make our soldier into a pioneer; we'll put him into the forest where, on his arrival, his first care will be to throw up some kind of a shack t.o live in while he is
waiting tq spread out more and hoping that, after two years or so, he will be able to afford a little stable for his horse and a cow, yes, after two years! Isn't this, Sir, the acme of re-establishment. The Government is full of divine kindness towards the soldiers.
Were not the provinces consulted, Mr. Speaker, as to what they could do to accommodate returned soldiers at home, and if both these provinces-I am speaking of these two only-adopt the idea of giving land to the soldiers, the hero will shoulder an axe, exclaiming:	"What a kind Providence we have in this Government. '
But that was a neat trick, to have the provincial governments decide what was to be done for the soldier. Unfortunately, here in the east, we have no cleared land; so, the soldier will have to hie himself to the west. In the West, we hear, there are immense stretches of land held for years by certain companies for speculative purposes. We hear a great deal of talk about the generous idea of expropriating these holdings and putting them into the hands of the soldiers. But, Sir, isn't this merely a move to prepare public opinion for the expropriation of lands in the hands of notorious speculators whose gigantic shadow sometimes hovers over the Government. This shadow would leave the great railways and go farther north, towards Lesser Slave Lake, towards Bear Lake, I believe it is, so as to work other lands, not to work the surface- the surface is too remote to be worked in the ordinary way-but to work what is below the surface; and then perhaps we'll need a Minister of Public Health in this district, in accord with the wishes of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Sheard) so as keep an eye on the cases, not of shell-shock, but of shell-game, that would begin to develop on another scale.
I have just alluded to a word of my hon. friend from Toronto. There are likely many others that I should single out for attention.
In his opening remarks he used an expression so striking that I wish to repeat it here: he said that once more the Government had, during the present war, "played a man's part." I would have liked him to add just what the Government's part has been; probably that of a stripling and not that of a man. He was seeking to protect the Government which claims to have done so much for the soldiers. The morale of the soldier on the firing-line must be excellent, but it must be backed by the morale of those who remain behind at home. Evidently, if we are to judge the morale of
i

our troops at the front by the morale of those who stayed at home, those who supported the man behind the gun by supplying him with all he needed, this morale must needs have been excellent, for the hon. member from Toronto told us a moment ago that he had come across one of our greatest citizens, who, during these four years had amassed $2,500,000. There you have an excellent morale, the morale which supported the Government so as to uphold the morale of the man in the front trenches.
The hon. member also said that the Government had frequently to face herculean tasks. They have had to move the rock ol Gibraltar out of the way in order to get anything done in the country.
Certain papers have spoken of a certain rock that certain people want to move, not out of the way, but into one of the important harbours of New Brunswick.
Some ministers refused to pass the contract; then, it seems, the present minister took a hand; we have got the rock as a wharf, the thing is done; and there you have a herculean task; the people pay.
Now, .Sir, the hon. member said moreover that the development of this country does not require alien enemy hands; but I wonder where we are going to look for our immigrants if we turn away from the countries whose people we have been wont to consider as our enemies, but whom President Wilson asks us to welcome as our brethren. If we are to put into practice those great principles which are being applied to-day at the Peace Conference, these men, stranded in a ruined country, will want to move to some other country. Therefore if we continue to look upon them as enemies, then ours will be a closed country where only those already within our borders can prosper.
The speech from the Throne tells us that we must recruit immigrants. We shall get them from Europe or from the United States. We must not forget that we shall have to close our doors to certain American citizens whom we consider alien enemies. We can turn to England who has lost a great many of her sons at the front. Undoubtedly we shall witness no great flow of immigrants from Great Britain. There are so few Belgians left in Belgium that those who remain will not care to come to our shores. As regards Germany, her people would perhaps make dangerous citizens. France has never been much given to emigration. Italy might 'furnish a few; but Italy is entering upon a period EMr. DechSne.]
of self-development and she will need all her people. Where, then, are we to look for the immigrants mentioned in the speech from the Throne, the immigrants that the Government is after? This is a problem that demands very serious consideration and the hon. ministers in their indecision will either have to decide for once, or give the matter up.
Mr. Speaker, there is something else about our Government which must be brought to your notice; something which is a direct result of their indecision. When a man is at a loss where to turn he tries to get somebody else to decide for him and very often in so doing he has to observe certain niceties; the gentlemen who are at the head of affairs in this country, who make up the Government which exists theoretically if not actually, have found this to "be the best means of governing Canada.
We have a great many commissions which exist for the sole purpose of being commissions-naturally, they can be nothing else-and commissioners are appointed so that they may draw commissioners' salaries. A great many of these commissions have shown, so far, that their usefulness went no further. There are no more political parties; everybody is a Whig or a Tory; we all belong to the same party;-it is a pity, however, that nearly all the commissioners are Tories. No party spirit there. The Government is merely protecting itself.
Mr. Speaker, no doubt you will allow me to ask you a question: how comes it that in several of these commissions appointed for the promotion of Canadian trade, for the public administration of the State's resources, there are so few representatives of the different jjrovinces?
There is the Canadian Northern Commission. I must admit that it no longer represents the Canadian Northern; but that it has become the Canadian National Railways Commission. The Government could not be so unmindful of the very great services rendered it by this railroad as to forget them in such easy fashion, and so as to have them ever present to the memory and constantly before it's paternal gaze, the Government could do no better than to give to this commission which administers these railroads as nearly as possible the same initials as those which still stand for this notorious railway. Hence the commission was styled C. N. R., or Canadian Northern railway. These things are all one; the same commission administers for others.

The thought was sublime; nothing better could be found.
There is another commission which has just been appointed. The supreme commissioner, the grand commissioner, is the man of petty measures. I do not mean to say that the measures he submits are not broadminded ; no, far from it!-in fact, I wish to say just the opposite: they are very broad. There was talk last session of bringing everything under the same system of measurement; of reducing everything to a general standard. There was to be a standard in this country for bags of cement; another for liquids, still another for wood. Well, Sir, this year we are introduced to another standard which had not been discovered last year. I refer to the standard measure for electricity and we have-this is likely to provoke laughter-we already have on the Order Paper of Parliament a certain thing which is styled about like this: "An act respecting the Units of Electrical Measure. ' Everything must be measured-the better to tax it later, I suppose. That is self evident.
If wre want to tax properly later on, we must begin by knowing just what we have on hand. Well, when the electrical unit has been measured, I wonder just what tax will be levied on it? It is possible that it will suffer no taxation, for it is not the common people, it is not the helpless ones who own the unit; they pay for the unit, but it is the wealthy capitalists who sell electricity by the unit-an irresponsible way of not giving us what we are entitled to-they glance at all these little figures and then say: "Here's the amount of your bill." Exactly like the Government. Just like the hon. Minister of Public Works who was saying a moment ago: it's going to take a heap of money to run the railroads; here's what you owe; fork over.
Mr. Speaker, could you tell me, or some member of the Government in your stead and through you-for it seems that we must speak through the Chairman-just what boon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is going to bring back to -us when he returns with the remainder of the Government which is on the other side of the ocean? No doubt we shall learn that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has become enamoured of the metric system and that, next year, once electric units have been measured, he will impose the metric system on us so as to sell to the French things that he would not try to have them buy from us.
Isn't it surprising, Mr. Speaker, to see a Trade Commission leave for Europe so as
to look after the commercial interests of this country while the Minister of Public Works was telling us yesterday that he was quite willing to do something for trade but that the commerce of this country should first of all take care of itself.
This Trade Commission, presided over by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce himself, intends visiting France and Belgium, finding out from these people what they need from us, and informing us what we can supply them with. But, Sir, to reach an agreement, in a matter of business, it is necessary to speak both languages; and haven't you wondered why, at least, in this matter, one of our French-Canadian leaders of industry in the province of Quebec was not chosen to represent the French people of this country, so as to allow the province of Quebec, a part of Ontario, even a part of New Brunswick, where French is spoken, the privilege of being represented on that commission by someone who could talk to the folks of these countries in their own language, who understands their way of doing business, and could thus have given an impetus to trade with France and Belgium for the period of reconstruction? Well, Sir, those who were sent can speak nothing but English. And how do you expect them to reach an understanding when they are concerned with systems of measurement with which our English speaking fellow citizens are more or less acquainted not having had to study them as we have?
Is this, Sir, a deliberate slight to those of our inhabitants who speak French exclusively and who go to make up three out of the seven millions of our population; is that the way to strike after the prosperity of our country and obtain for us the share we are entitled to in the trade of those foreign countries when it comes to supplying their needs for reconstruction and for, building over their ruins?
Well, Mr. Speaker, I maintain that this is another instance where the Government lacked foresight and that those who represent it on that commission are there for the sole purpose of concealing responsibilities behind which the Government itself is trying to hide.
Mr. Speaker, while I am on this subject of overseas affairs you will doubtless, permit me to take exception to the words of the hon. gentleman who is our Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) yesterday when he said, with a good deal of emphasis, that without a doubt we would receive a war indemnity to bolster up our finances and enable him, our grand treasurer, to

meet his liabilities. That, Sir, was the last thing that I expected to hear on the floor of this House from the lips of the hon. treasurer of this country.
If the newspapers, if the Associated Press, if the Canadian Press, supported by the Government, if the correspondents whom the right hon. Prime Minister brought with him to Europe so *as to keep us informed back here, if these people have really told us the truth about what is happening at the Peace Conference about what is happening in England, we must come to the conclusion that there will be no war indemnity unless it be, perhaps, the indemnity foretold by the official correspondent of the Canadian Press when he wrote that to fill the coffers of our hon. treasurer we would receive- Greenland and its fields of ice.
Well, Sir, let Denmark keep Greenland; we need no ice in this country save perhaps, to cool-oh, not altogether-to cool off the zeal of certain financiers who are constanly dancing attendance on the treasurer,-attracted by his handsome eyes, no doubt-maybe, by something else besides.
Sir, this brings me to another feature of the Government's policy. The hon. member from Toronto told us a moment ago that he had seen people make millions out of politics; others took advantage of the wholesale exemptions granted by our hon. Minister of Finance so as to entice them, in a roundabout way to loosen their purse strings; still others turn to their advantage the tariff barrier which protects their industries; but the common people have had nothing at all.
If, (Sir, we wanted to delve deeper into this feature of our politics we would find, not a policy of partisanship-because the hon. minister has told us that such a thing does not exist-but, at least a policy of favouritism. Why was it, Mr. Speaker, that the Government took such pains to have the wealthy citizen, the man with bulging pockets, subscribe for the treasury bonds which were already paying a handsome dividend, and were so attractive that they persuaded everyone to subscribe, that had the whole country as security, and were supported by all our natural resources- which to-day we boast of as immense, as boundless-why was that little stamp affixed which exempted thesq bonds from taxation, if not to encourage the big financier to stuff his pockets with them? Because the plain people of this country, the toiler, the man behind the plough, because, Sir,' the petty clerk behind the counter, have not been accustomed to buying bonds, because 
they do not alw>ays have a few cents to invest; but they knew, moreover, that our mighty business organizations, our high financiers who are well known to the Government-we are aware of that-would appreciate the value of a bond which could be tax-exempt for fifteen or twenty years >and would subscribe to the limit so as to shelter their fortunes from the income tax while we, the plain people, while the farmer behind his plough, the housewife in her home, the school teacher in her class-room, the clerk in the store, the street labourer-who is despised in certain quarters-would continue to sweat taxes all of the time.
And the soldier hack from the front who will work hard for his salary; when this, added to his pension, reaches $1,200, he will have to pay an income tax on all revenue exceeding '$1,000. The returned soldier, I repeat, will have to bear a share of the taxes while those who stayed ,at home, making munitions and filling their pockets continue to rush into the money markets of our country to sweep into their vaults all the tax-exempt Victory bonds they can gather so as to enjoy their income in all security. The plain people are the ones who will pay; and the soldier will be called upon once more to bear his share. This man won the fight; he lived through filth and misery in the trenches; he is disabled for the rest of his life; and, Sir, [DOT] once he has returned to this country and has put away his rifle he will have to get into harness with the rest of us poor people, us plain people, so as to ensure the success of future loans and especially to help pay the billions of faxes that the Government will exact from the people of this country. At six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I was just saying, when you announced the hour of six, that the policy of the present Government is a policy of favouritism, I mean a policy which favours the vested interests and makes light of the wishes of the common people. The vested interests were given tax-exempt treasury bonds so that they could invest their tremendous fortunes to good advantage. Very few among the working class, very few among the farming class were able to invest a lot of money in these bonds and profit by this exemption. The income tax levied by the Government, and which was increased nearly one-third last year is borne almost exclusively, therefor, by those who are pos-

sessed of lesser fortunes and those who earn their livelihood by laborious toil. Since these wealthy gentry, these millionaires- and the Government has quite a few of them among its friends-are safe from this tax, are immune from paying this part of their income tax, the others will necessarily have to furnish the funds required by the country both for the expense of government from day to day and for the payments of interest and principal on our tremendous debt.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is not only- what a sorry admission to make on the floor of this House-it is not only those who work and who worked all during tire- war in this country, who will have to bear the burden of these taxes. Is it not unfortunate, Sir, that our returned heroes themselves will have to undertake a large share of these payments if they wish to enjoy certain privileges that the Government offers theim and accept the loan of $7,500 that will be made them to set them up on a farm.
Have you ever figured out what enormous sums they will have to pay back in the course of the next 25, 30 or 40 years? We, and they, in common will have to pay not only the debts accumulated through the war, but they will also have to pay back the -amount they borrow; and we shall all see ourselves forced to pay a national debt of nearly four billion dollars; this means, Sir, that those who won the war, those who shed their blood, will be worse off than if they had lost the war.
The big interests have been promised, so as to enable them to meet their liabilities, that the tariff, that barrier which prevents imported articles from competing with their products, would be strengthened. It is fitting that customs duties should provide enough revenue to permit the Government to honourably discharge its obligations; but these tariff duties must not be made into an impassable wall which altogether shuts out imports.
I remember one of the famous speeches of Mr. Thiers before the National Assembly of France, after the great defeat of 1870. The delegates to the National Assembly had been asked to find the necessary revenue for paying off the five billion francs demanded as an indemnity and to each and every proposition M. Thiers made answer:	"But is
this article you want to tax able to support even a penny tax without putting a stop to imports?"
We must always keep in mind when levying customs duties the fact that these should not put a stop to imports. M. Thiers' advice was to make each and every article pay to
the limit of its capacity, but never to lose sight of the fact that if you shut out imports you kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. And this will be the inevitable result if the tariff is made still higher. If customs duties are increased merely to please a few big manufacturers imports will cease and instead of enjoying larger revenue we will be faced with a growing deficit.
Several of those who spoke before me talked of lowering the tariff, especially to the advantage of the agricultural class. We on this side of the House, Sir, are in favour of tariff rates which will allow the agricultural class to increase production and get some return for their efforts. But we are in favour of this reduction in rates, Mr. Speaker, merely because it pleases a few people. We advocate these reductions because we know, we have proof, that the wealth of the farming community, the wealth of the plain people is the only real wealth on which the country can rely in time of stress. What made France so strong, Mr. Speaker, during the war just passed? To what, in fact, do we owe our own strength, if not to the wealth of the people themselves?
It is not the millionaires, it is not the magnates of big business who are the backbone of the country; for, when a crisis comes, they stop, they stow their millions of dollars away somewhere and the country can't touch them. But when a crigis is upon us the country can always turn to the farmer, to the workingman, and ask him for money. And we are astonished- you yourself were astonished at the time of the last Victory Loan-to find that there was so much money in the province of Quebec, which is entirely an agricultural province; that Quebec had irfore money than any other province of the Dominion. You refused to believe it, Sir, when we told you on the floor of this House that Quebec was the only province which, during this crisis, had not availed itself of the moratorium; that it was the only province where you could always demand the payment of what was due you, whether it is a mortgage, a note, or what not. Why? Because the Government of Quebec, because the people of Quebec, ever mindful of their ancient origin, did not forget that they were the descendants of the sturdy French race and that the first care of the French peasant, the farmer t>f the mother-country, is to pile up money at home and not in the banks; not tremendous fortunes, but little savings so that when bad times appear and they are forced to tighten their belts, they always have gold in their pockets. There

always has been gold in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, if the Government wanted to he honest with the agricultural class when they published the report of the last Victory Loan, to show the proportion of subscriptions in our province which represents the farmers-they would have given us the amount subscribed by the city of Montreal, which they somehow never put into their statistics. Certain English counties were included and the figure of their subscription credited to Ontario. All this was done so as to cast a slur on the province of Quebec and in thus discrediting Quebec they are discrediting the entire agricultural class. This is an insult to the farmers and we wish to register an energetic protest against it.
Now we come to another consideration. We demand the revision of the tariff on all farming implements, on everything that is a help to farming and to the farmer; we must never forget that it is the man with the hoe who amasses the real wealth of the country, the wealth which does not scamper away to the other side of the ocean once the pockets are full, there to bask around the desks in the War Office or in the quarters of the big English cabinets. That kind of people run away with their millions; but Canada desires its real wealth from the pockets of its farmers. We do not want to see our wealth crossing the ocean. That is why we are criticising the Government to-day for its policy of favouritism towards the big capitalists. In the words of the hon. member for Brome {Mr. McMaster) this policy is most pernicious for the country.
We have to do not only with a policy of favouritism, but with a policy of despotism. We work for the big fellows, we work for those who are well off, for those who have large fortunes, hut what do the poor people get? Nothing. What are they promised? Bosh, soap bubbles. They are promised the moon, but they never get a thing. That is the lot of our poor people; that is what this Government's policy leads to.
Mr. Speaker, we ask the Government to put aside this notorious policy and to remember that the people exist; that these gentlemen are governing for the people and not for a few privileged interests.
Every means have been tried, during the last three years to turn our social fabric upside down, with this policy. We have seen a cataract of laws falling in such rapid sequence and with such suddenness, that we did not have time-even we who are

accustomed to keep a close watch on our laws to kpow just wfiat was the law of the country, because just as soon as a law had been passed it was immediately succeeded by another law. And what a law! For instance, the notorious Conscription Act. Things that had never been seen, even in Germany, became a part of our life in this country where the Government showed more severity than the very potentates of Germany. Indeed, to our knowledge, the kaiser himself had never acted in such a fashion.
Mr. Speaker, if we want the^ people to submit it is high time that this state of affairs were a thing of the past; if we do not want the entire working class to rise up in revolt and have a repetition in this country of what is going on in England where strike succeeds strike, and one fine day wake up to find the country we are working for thrown into the abyss where the Bolsheviki have thrown Russia. If things came to that pass we would find in this House leaders who could very well call themselves Trotsky and Lenine.
Were I allowed to offer suggestion I might make a few, but the hon. Minister of Public Works told us that he has had so many that he doesn't want any more. The reason is magnificent! He doesn't know where to turn.
As the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Sheard) said a moment ago: when these gentlemen are in doubt they play trumps. But, Sir, when they play "trumps " the people pay; there you have the biggest proof of their indecision.
The hon. member for 'Toronto-I feel bound to pay him this compliment-gave to the House some very pleasant and very useful notes that could very well have come from the few ministers who have had the floor.
Since the beginning of the session we have been told that a Department of Public Health is to be inaugurated. We all wanted to know what was meant, and what the emergency was now that the epidemic has passed, and someone made the guess that it was to prevent an outbreak of epidemic among the members of the Government, and that having seen the candle in the window of the Liberal stronghold and heard the murmur that so-and-so w,as thinking of leaving, some one guessed, I say, that this Department of Public Health is for the purpose of curing all those erring sons who are willing to return; curing them of influenza. Really if the " flu " should break out in their ranks they decidelv would need an energetic Minister of Public Health to

prevent the complaint from spreading because they are already suffering from a rather severe attack and the Government itself might well be the first to die.
But this Public Health Department, as stated by the hon. member will cover many other diseases beside influenza, and after the epidemic has been stopped, they 'will have to watch its consequences. The hon. member also referred to matters which, at first sight, I did not think would come under the control of a department of Public Health.
The Minister of Agriculture is having considerable sums of money voted each year, towards checking certain plant diseases and destructive insects in our forests, but according to the hon. member, it appears that it will be within the functions of the Minister of Public Health to do away with all the insects which cause plant diseases. The hon. member may be a vegetarian and for this reason he would like the minister to look after the matter. Do you fancy our Minister of Public Health running through the fields to destroy all the little bugs which are eating up our crops and which, in some of the provinces where they grow a lot of potatoes, practically destroy the crop? Do you fancy him sending engineers in our forests to destroy all the flies that are liable to injure balsam, spruce or white pine trees? Mr. Speaker, is that what they call the public health. The plants as well as the bugs will have their Minister!
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, there is one of the remarks made by the hon. member for Toronto that struck me more particularly. Evidently the Minister of Public Works is not in luck's way. This afternoon somebody told him most disagreeable things which made him frown and grow nervous; now the hon. member for Toronto tells us that the Minister is all mixed up, mingling the assets with the liabilities and the revenue with the interest. But nobody told us where goes the money which we are paying.
Mr. Speaker, did you ever ask yourself, as some of the members of the Government, and specially of the Opposition do, what was the result of such policies.? Of course the first conclusion we may draw is that this policy is one of demoralization.
Fortunately the war is over. There is no one, Mr. Speaker, who had a deeper sense of regret at the death of so many brave volunteers in his home town than I, and I must say that out of 45 of our young men who went voluntarily to the front, 42 were killed-forty-two dead who may have had no decorations, but whose death we mournand that those who came back are disabled for life. Hail these gallant men and the others who came from the surrounding parishes. Hail these farmers' sons who left the plough to fight in Flanders and died on the old isoil of France whence came their ancestors. No one glories more in their supreme sacrifice than I do, neither does any one regret more than I do the futility of their sacrifice. Of what use is it for them to have gone and fought overseas, to have spilled their blood for the land of their birth and for Old France and for their country of adoption, Great Britain, if those who are coming back after winning the war have lost peace at home.
The policy carried on by the Government will necessarily bring about this demoralization. As to the promise made by the Government to the returning soldiers that they would give them the best positions or at least, as .a last expedient, the positions which they held before enlisting, we know, at home, what that promise is worth. It means to the returned man that he is sent from one commission to another and delayed until the time when there is nothing to be got. Is it not regrettable to notice how vain are these promises?
I myself happened to apply to the authorities on behalf of a wounded returned soldier who was asking to be re-instated in his former position on a ship. It is with a deep sense of regret that I had to tell him: " My friend, the Government who promised you would get back your job say that they will give you another one on the new boats they will build next summer." Is this the way of re-establishing the soldiers? Here is a man who did his duty, and who is told when coming back wounded:	" To fulfil
our promise to you we shall wait until next summer when our boats are launched."
How many soldiers received the same reply! They are sent from " Dan to Beer-sheba," and the unfortunate ones have to struggle without getting anything. Will this help in strengthening the morale of these men? Or is it not rather calculated to [DOT]raise their indignation against those who remained here and to whom they will say: " While we were working hard, while we were fighting and giving our blood, you were busy making money without providing for us; we had the promises and you had the real thing; now that we are back, we have not even the satisfaction to say that you intend to keep these promises."
A time will come, Mr. Speaker, when these gallant men will be able to speak out, and when that time comes, the hon. ministers who, to-day, are living happy,

will be glad to go back to their mansions. Indeed they will be fortunate if the soldiers do not fetch them there and force them to give an account of their conduct.
Hail the Canadian army which showed such valour in the fighting on the various battlefields! Hail the brave ones who h ave left us, who have sacrificed their all for the triumph of their country of adoption and of their mother country. But, Mr. Speaker, how will you ask them to respect the laws? How will you ask them to abide by the various Orders in Council, when they know that these laws do not represent the wishes of the people for *whom they fought? They come from the people, they want the people to rule, or else they will have a hand in it. If they do, we shall help them and the people will have their revenge.
Hear, hear.

That is the first difficulty, I think, encountered by the hon. leader of the Opposition in carrying out his "repatriation" policy, and I think I can assure him that there will be many more difficulties met with before it is successfully carried out.
Our armies overseas faced difficulties and overcame them; our people at home during the four years of war have faced difficulties and overcome them. With our army returned, and with our people at home united, as they will be, after demobilization, I indulge the confident hope that whatever difficulties arise in this country within the next few years this combined after-the-war army will successfully cope with and overcome. It is gratifying, I am sure, to us on this side of the House, and, I believe to the great majority of the people of Canada, to know that demobilization, repatriation and reconstruction are being carried out by a Union Government. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) this afternoon made the statement that there was no one to look after the returned soldier. I would remind him that Union Government looked after the soldier before he returned and that Union Government looked after the soldier last spring when he was badly in need of assistance and reinforcements. The returned soldier is being looked after by that same Government now with the same spirit and the same success.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe also made a remark referring to the Liberals on this side of the House and compared them to fruit ripened and falling from the tree. I would like to remind him that the ripening of fruit is not the only reason for it falling from the tree. Fruit falls from the tree when the tree becomes blighted, fruit falls from the tree when the tree dies, and is unable to give the fruit that vitality that it requires in order to remain upon the tree.
We enjoy Union Government on this side of the House for many reasons. One reason especially is that we have the privilege of criticising the Government. Hon. gentlemen on the other side cannot appreciate what that means but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the great majority of those who are supporting Union Government feel a freedom that they never enjoyed when they belonged to either of the two old parties. We are free to criticise and in so doing we are free to retain the freedom of men thinking for themselves. I believe that the day of the infallible governments has passed. We have had many of them in Canada. Every government, in fact, has been infallible while it remained in power especially in the eyes of its own supporters. We have not an infallible Government, I am glad to say, and I hope we never shall have another.
I want to refer to one question that is before 'the Government at this time and which was referred to in such excellent terms this afternoon by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard)-the Public Health Bill. The previous speaker (Mr. Dechene) made the remark, if I understood him, that a Public Health Bill was not warranted by the circumstances. I hope, Sir, that when the discussions which will take place on that Bill during the session are ended, my hon. friend will be fully convinced that the circumstances do warrant the establishment of a Public Health department. He also made the remark in connection with this Public Health department that when the Liberal influenza gets hold of the people it cannot be checked. That may be true, but when it gets hold of the people I believe it will prove just as deadly as the influenza that has passed over Canada during the last few months. I am rather gratified that the Government have at this session announced their intention of organizing a Public Health department. For two years I have brought the matter before the House and it is gratifying to know that at last the efforts that have been made in this House on many occasions are going to bear fruit and 'that we are likely to get the department which is needed. This is in line with what I believe this Government, as all governments in Canada, will have to do in the next few years-give greater attention to social problems. After all, -the importance of our country is determined by our people, and unless we have a vigorous, virile, healthful people, we cannot have a



country of the first importance. Universal health conservation is, to my mind, the duty of the nation. Sanitary science has placed within the hands of the State facts which, if applied to the protection of the health of our people, will produce a greater and better nation. The physical care of our people determines to an important degree the mental and imoral development; and all combined, the physical, mental and moral, are required to make the best citizens. In Great Britain much attention is being given to the subject. In his first speech of the campaign in the general election of last fall, Premier Lloyd George made this statement:
The recruiting- statistics have revealed terrible conditions as regards the physical health of the nations. This is due not to poverty but to neglect. The health of the people must be the special concern of the State.
The British Labour party have adopted as the first principle of their platform:
The securing to every member of the community all the requisites of healthy life and worthy citizenship.
What can be done in Canada? In these days we hear much of the burden of taxation which is going to he put on the people of Canada as a result of the war. Every person is looking for a means by which taxation can be lightened. I want to give to this House a possible method by which the taxation of Canadians may be greatly lightened. Irving Fisher, in his work on " National Vitality," estimates that sickness costs each family in the United States on an average $110 per year. If that rate is applied to the people of Canada, it costs the people of Canada $220,000,000 each year for sickness and $100,000,000 at least of that can be saved, or the part of that cost which is due to preventable sickness; sickness which, under an efficient department of health, can be prevented. This tax falls heaviest on the working man.
It is estimated that on the average each working man loses nine days per year from sickness. In Canada we have a million and a quarter working men, which means that eleven and a quarter million days' labour are lost to the country on account of the sickness of the workingmen, a loss in wages alone of at least $35,000,000. Then there is to be added to the wage loss the cost of the sickness, and the cost of the deaths. Not only that, hut sickness brings unemployment, which we are all striving to prevent. Unemployment is followed by poverty, poverty is followed by destitution, 
and destitution is followed by either charity or crime. In Canada, there are every year at least fifty thousand deaths which are unnecessary. This is a tremendous economic loss; let me give you some figures to illustrate. If ten thousand of those who die are wage earners, and each wage earner is worth to the country at least $10,000,- so it is estimated-then, Sir, the unnecessary deaths of wage earners occurring in this country each year means an economic loss to Canada of at least $100,000,000. There is an opportunity for a modern, up-to-date, live Government such as we have to-day in Canada to save that immense burden of taxation to our people. Not only have we great unnecessary loss among the wage earners from deaths, but every year in this country there are dying fifteen thousand infants under one year of age, who can be saved to the state. The blackest page in the records of Canada is the page which contains the records of infant mortality, because that record is due to the neglect, indifference and ignorance of the Canadian people. When a child dies people are often heard to say, "Providence has taken another little one home." It seems to me it is almost criminal dishonesty to place on the shoulders of Providence what our own ignorance and neglect are entirely responsible for.
We have talked of conservation for years, and along some lines conservation has greatly advanced, but we require conservation and yet more conservation. We have for years been applying conservation to our agricultural problems, but why, Mr. Speaker, may I ask, should we conserve the fertility of the soil and not conserve the tillers of the soil? Why should we conserve plant life and not human life? Why conserve animal life and not child life? Why conserve our forests, our iron, our coal, our water-powers , and neglect our people? Thousands are spent every year to destroy the parasites which prey on plant and animal life, but how miserly we become, how miserly the Government has been in the past, when asked to spend anything to protect from similar parasites the citizens of our land. Horses, cattle, hogs, fruits and vegetables, all receive due attention, but thousands of infants are allowed to go to early graves, thousands of wage-earners are allowed to die or become disabled, without any attention from the State, and so generation after generation the health of our people goes neglected.
We have for the past few years been fighting to maintain democracy in the world.

The Canadian Army preserved Canada as a democratic country. Our soldiers made their contribution for democracy; now it rests with the people of Canada to make their contribution by rendering Canada a democratic country fit for a democratic people to live in. Why expound the benefits of democracy to a poor citizen with tubercular chest, slowly fading, knowing well that within a few months, or a year or two, his little family will be left to depend for the essentials of life on the cold charity of the world? Can we interest in democracy the wife or children of a man who can leave as his only legacy to society another illustration that the sins of the fathers are visited on the children unto the third and fourth generation? The only democrat who can appreciate Canadian democracy is he of clear eye, pure blood, robust frame, and well-functioning brain, enabling him to fully enjoy the privileges and liberty which that democracy bestows upon him. To protect our people from the conditions which I have been describing, is to perform work of the highest and most patriotic character, work worthy of the attention of any Government.
To secure the greatest industrial production and development, it is necessary to maintain at the highest efficiency the health of the farmer, the industrial worker, the transportation employee, and all other workmen on whom depend the production and distribution of agricultural and industrial products. For this reason I think the Government is to be commended for its announcement that it is going to give aid to the highways of our country. Great changes have taken place with regard to the Highways of Canada in the last thirty or forty years. In the pioneer days practically the only people who used the country road were a few farmers who lived within a mile or two of it. Then we reached the stage where the town or city dweller began to use the roads to a limited extent, and it was found advisable that the counties and the provincial authorities should come to the aid of the farmer in constructing and maintaining in repair the roads which he had previously had to keep in condition solely by his own taxation. But we have passed awaj from even that stage. The good country highway to-day is a national highway; it is used not only by the farmers living in the district through which it passes, not only by the citizens of the villages and towns or nearby cities, but by citizens throughout the whole country. It is even used by citizens from the land to the south of us, and therefore I say
7i
it is becoming that at this time the Dominion should step in and say: We recognize that the main roads of our country are national highways now, and therefore we feel it incumbent upon us to come to the assistance of the farmer in constructing those roads and keeping them in repair.
The speech from the Throne announced that a Bill would be brought in dealing with immigration matters, and I am glad of it. In this connection the Health department can be of very great service. I hope, Sir, that in future only the immigrant of healthy body and sound mind will be admitted into our country.
The great problem of the feeble-minded in Canada to-day has arisen chiefly because our Dominion authorities have been permitting great numbers of feeble-minded immigrants to come into this country. At the inspection of immigrants in New York City it has been found that four out of every 1,000 people applying for entrance into the United States are feeble-minded. I doubt not that the percentage of feeble-minded among those who have been applying for entry into Canada in past years has been quite as great. If so, it means that every year, for a considerable period at least, from 1,200 to 1,500 feeble-minded persons have been admitted into Canada. Let us pause and think of the enormous burden that this places upon our people. Remember, too, that 80 per cent of the offspring of these people will be feeble-minded. As we make this calculation we find that the Dominion, through laxity and carelessness, are admitting and have been admitting into this country every year large numbers of people who ultimately will be a tremendous burden upon each of the provinces. So that from a provincial as well as national point of view it is important that immigration regulations shall be stricter and the inspection of immigrants more efficient.
But in our immigrants we require not only healthy bodies and sound minds; we look for more than that. We have been entrusted with a great country. Perhaps in the past we have been allowing ourselves to run to commercialism. No question today would more readily excite a discussion than that of the tariff, and this shows that our minds are still largely centred on commercialism. To my mind, the tariff that was made for Canada in 1878 probably requires a great deal of remodelling in order to make it thoroughly adapted to the Canada of 1920. But this has nothing to do with immigration, about which I was speaking. As a result of the war and of our war

work, there is imposed upon Canada the necessity of making of this country a great. British nation where. the English language shall prevail and where law and [DOT]order must be recognized. There is no room in Canada for Bolshevism, notwithstanding the apology made for it by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) the other evening. I should like to read to the House a summary of a report which was made on some of the deeds of Bolshevism, as published in this morning's papers. In a despatch through the Associated Press from Copenhagen, February 26, there appears this statement:
An appalling narrative of inhuman crime is revealed in the official report of the Esthonian authorities on Bolshevik atrocities committed in Bsthonia, especially Wesenberg and Dor-pat.
The graves of those murdered at Wesenburg were opened on February 17 in the presence of the town governor. Three graves were found to contain 82 corpses. Skulls were shattered, bodies hayonetted and even eviscerated. An eye-witness of the execution Who escaped, described the terrible scene when the victims were placed on the edge of the graves and shot indiscriminately, trampled into the graves and finished with the butts of rifles. The vicinity of the graves was littered with torn clothing, brains, fragments of skulls and hair, while the grass was covered with congealed blood.
Similar bloodthirstiness was evinced at Dor-pat, where the murdered victims were dropped into the river through holes in the ice. Recovered bodies revealed many arms and legs broken and one with the eyes put out.
The prisoners captured were robbed of clothes and valuables, led to a cellar and killed with hatchets and bombs. Examination of the cellar showed bodies piled up thickly in unnatural positions. The walls were splashed with blood.
Bolshevik fury also raged against the peasantry many of whom were mutilated and murdered. Thirty women were killed at Narva by stones being tied round their necks and being thrown into the river.
Those are the deeds of the people for whorp the member for Brome, the other night, tried to enlist the sympathy of this House, and for whom he made
9 p.m. a partial apology. There is no room in Canada for Bolshevism, and if there are any evidences of it to-day, we are but reaping what we have been sowing in our immigration policy. We have seen people in Canada during the past four years who have been profiting by the protection of the Canadian flag and of Canadian law, whose hearts were turned against Canada during that conflict, and who were openly professing sympathy with our enemies. I hope that in future our immigration policy will be such as to guard this country against' the man who comes to exploit Canada. In the past the desire of
£Mr. Steele.]
the foreigner has been the deciding factor; in future we should have the assurance that the foreigner desires, when he comes to Canada, to become a good Canadian citizen. We need immigrants, but we do not need them so badly that we must accept any one and every one who desires to come. I do not sympathize with the view that in future our immigration policy should be limited only to the Anglo-Saxon countries; I believe that there are many good people in continental Europe who will make most desirable Canadian citizens if our people do their duty by them when they arrive here. But in my opinion, none but those who are able to speak English or the French language should be granted the rights of citizenship until at least eight years after their arrival here. I believe also that every immigrant should be registered on his arrival and that he should be required to have in his possession a registration card such as our own people had to have during the last few months of hostilities, so that a check can be had on him at any time. The eight years should be spent as a period of probation, and if at the end of that time the immigrant has not been living as a well-behaved, law-abiding, industrious, loyal Canadian citizen should live, and if he has not in those years been successful in acquiring a reasonable knowledge of the English language, he should at the end of that time be invited to return to the land wdience he came and not be allowed to carry with him all the wealth which he has made in this country. Every one who leaves the land of his birth to settle in another country should feel that by so doing he indicates a willingness to relinquish the language and customs and ideals of that land; and when he comes to Canada he should come with a willingness to adopt the language, the customs and the ideals of this country. Only by the recognition of this principle can we develop a citizenship which is one hundred per cent Canadian.
We should not blame former immigrants for the condition of affairs which has been shown to exist in Canada of recent years. They came here on invitation; they were almost constrained to come. But when they landed here they were ignored. No further attention was paid to them. If blame is to be laid on any person, it should be laid on our Governments, on our municipal authorities, on our educational authorities, on our public men, and especially perhaps on our aspirants to public life who are too often willing to cater to the foreigner in our midst in order to get his vote. Perhaps a share of the blame could be laid on the

shoulders of every Canadian citizen, for we have all sadly neglected the newly arrived immigrant. Many of them have left their own countries and have come to Canada in order to- escape oppression and to enjoy the liberty which Canada offers them. We desire that they shall enjoy that liberty, but the liberty which they enjoy in Canada must be Canadian liberty, they cannot be permitted to enjoy the liberty which they imagine they might enjoy if they had remained in the land of their birth. Canadian liberty entails a responsibility, and the immigrant coming to this land should be made to understand that. That responsibility is a responsibility to the State, and amongst the responsibilities to the State is the responsibility to defend the State when the State requires defence.
We are at this time emerging from trying experiences. Victory has come to our armies overseas. Victory has also come to our people at home, because we will all, I am sure, admit that the efforts of the Canadian people at home have resulted in splendid industrial and agricultural victories. The combination of these two forces will, I am certain, result in our people courageously facing the difficult national problems of the next few years. Together they will successfully overcome those difficulties, and the achievements of our after-the-war army in industry, commerce and agriculture will be such that there will result a greater and more prosperous Canada than the most optimistic at present can even hope for.
Mr. WILLIAM C. KENNEDY (North Essex): Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me have extended their congratulations to the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Redman) and the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) on their speeches on the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. May I be permitted to concur in those congratulations, feeling sure that the House will agree with me that in the speeches they have delivered they have given us information, facts and figures that will be not only of service to the House but of great service to the country.
The speech itself was a typical Union Government production replete with promises. If there is one thing more than another that hon. gentlemen opposite do well, it is to promise. In fact, it has been said that no government that has been formed in Canada since Confederation has been so long on promises and so short on performance as the present Union Government. There is, however, one promise
that I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will implement, and that is the promise with reference to the War-time Elections Act. That Act should be repealed without delay. There may have been some excuse a year ago for hon. gentlemen defending that measure. They may not have had an opportunity of knowing all the facts and details in connection with the voting overseas, but surely there is in this House no hon. gentleman who has returned soldiers in his constituency who does not now know the disgraceful story of the elections that were held in England in 1917. I am not speaking from hearsay; I have had in my possession the documents dealing with the matter, documents that at all events some gentlemen on the other side of the House have been privileged to see; and I hope, before the session is over, an opportunity will be given not only to the members of this House but to the people of this country to learn the names of those implicated and the methods employed to place this Union Government in power.
The people of this country are to-day in no frame of mind to accept a franchise Act whose only object is to continue in power hon. gentlemen opposite. Not only the Government of the country but the form of government are on trial with the people of Canada. The people are seriously asking themselves if some other form of government would not be preferable, and if a form of government, which, through Orders in Council, permits a small coterie of men to impose their views and wishes on the people of the country, is not inconsistent with responsible government and the spirit of democracy so necessary to our national existence. Let me say-and I am only reechoing the words of the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair), who spoke yesterday-that in so far as the people of my part of the country are concerned, no halo goes with the position of a Cabinet minister. The Cabinet ministers of this country are the servants of the people and not the masters, and that is a good thing for Cabinet ministers to remember. It is important in the interests of the people that the proposed franchise legislation should be fair and just, so that it will appeal to all irrespective of party.
Amongst other matters dealt with in the Address was one that I thought would perhaps have come in for more attention. I refer to the visit of our distinguished Premier (Sir Robert Borden) and his fellow diplomats across the sea. So far as I have

heard, no explanation has been given by hon. gentlemen who have up to the present addressed the House as to what has transpired in Paris or in Versailles, what the Premier is doing, or what he hopes to do for this country. All the information that the members of this House can obtain is what they can gather from the public press. Fortunately, it seems the Premier is well supplied with correspondents because we are able to keep to some extent in touch. I wish, however, to congratulate . the Premier, as other hon. members have done, on his finally obtaining some definite standing abroad. I am free to confess that I am not aware just what that particular standing is. The fact remains, nevertheless, that it seems to be perfectly satisfactory as a matter for congratulation, and in these congratulations I desire to join. I notice that the right hon. gentleman is in Paris; I notice also that the President of the United States is in Washington, that the Premier of England is in England, that the Premier of France is incapacitated, and that the Premier of Italy is in Italy. We, therefore, really are represented at the conference, and I trust with credit to this country.
I should like to say just a word or two with reference to the personnel accompanying our premier on his trip across the sea. These gentlemen are probably, from yearns of experience, distinguished diplomats, and I have no doubt they will reflect great credit upon this country. But may I say that, in view of the trip overseas that was taken last spring by other hon. gentlemen in this House, there was not a little surprise, throughout the province of Ontario at least, that one other hon. member of this House had not been chosen to accompany the Premier on this trip. Those who read the newspapers must recall the magnificent work accomplished by the hon. President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) and the gentlemen who were with him when they were over there last year. I know the papers were replete with information as to what the President of the Council was doing, and how well he was doing it, and it - seems to me there must be some very good reason for his having been left behind, or else some very great mistake has been made'by the Premier in leaving him off this delegation. Many reasons have been advanced why he did not accompany the Premier. I have heard it said that when the President of the Council was over there last year his presss agents were perhaps a little too vigorous and there were times when the people were not quite

sure whether the Premier was in England or in Canada. I likewise heard that he was being reserved for the leadership here in the absence of the Premier. But we see these were all mistakes. The matter did not disturb me at all, because I absolutely knew the reason through having read early in July last year a press despatch from across the seas dealing with matters over there,	and	I at once	saw
that it was out of the question for the gentlemen who accompanied the Premier last spring to return with him again this year. If the House will bear with me I will quote part of the despatch: I shall not read it all, as it might prove embarrassing to the hon. gentlemen who are mentioned, although I do not see any of them present at the moment. The despatch appears in the Detroit Free Press of Sunday, July 28th, 1918, and deals with the visit of our distinguished group of diplomats. It describes how busy these gentlemen were in London, and incidentally I am glad to note the landing in England of the Minister of Colonization (Mr. Cal-der) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). It is reassuring to see that they sailed and landed, because beyond that very little is said in the despatches about them. The despatch reads:-
They entered into a self denying ordinance on their arrival here.' They declined the ordinary social engagements except those directly connected with the operations of the war, refusing almost every offer to speak-
There, Mr. Speaker, was self-sacrifice of a high order. They absolutely refused every offer to speak.
-despite insistent demands from every part of England. Frequently at the close of a laborious twelve-hour day the ministers would visit some hospital a considerable distance away, talk with the wounded, dine en famille with the staff, and reach home at midnight. Their appearance gives physical evidence of the heavy nature of their work. Mr. Rowell looks years older than when he arrived.
There, Mr. Speaker, you have the reason. Out of consideration for his colleague the Premier refused to add more years to the hon. gentleman's life. A few years, of course, in the young life of the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), or the Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) means nothing. The members of this House must surely be indebted to the Premier for his consideration for the President of the Council, and speaking for myself and on behalf of the Liberals of the province of Ontario I desire likewise to thank the Premier, because the Liberals of the province of Ontario are

anxiously waiting for the time to come when they may have an opportunity of showing their love and affection for the President of the Council. It seems fitting that the author of this despatch should have the privilege of being named in this House. I think the gentleman who could pen such a despatch is worthy of that distinction. I am sorry to disappoint my hon. friends, but the despatch was not written by Donald Hunt, it was not written even by Main Johnson, but by a gentleman who by a strange coincidence is named McKenzie, and if I am any judge of names he is a Scotsman. And yet there are people who say that the Scotch have no sense of humour ! it. is about time that the Government took the matter in hand themselves. It is about time that the Government had a Department of Trade and Commerce that could look after the affairs of the country without the assistance of outside commissions. If hon. gentlemen will bear with me for a minute I will read a letter which I have received from the secretary of the Board of Commerce in our city in connection with this matter. He

encloses me a copy of a letter received from Mr. F. C. T. O'Hara, Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, which says:
I may say that we have always had much trouble in supplying- information with regard to the British and foreign tariffs, for as you know, all tariffs are subject to Treasury decisions and changes of which we frequently are not advised for months afterwards. Prom our own knowledge of the Canadian Customs Tariffs you will know that experts in the Customs Department of the country itself alone are able to give information in many cases. Since the outbreak of war all our International Customs Bureau publications which were issued at Brussels have ceased, hence many of our tariff's are out of date, and no means exist for obtaining this information at present for all the countries of the world, translated as before the war.
That does not apply to England. We have over in London paid officials of this Government. Surely there should be somebody there who would keep the Department of Trade and Commerce in touch with conditions over there, so that we could do business with that country. The letter continues :
Personally I have relied largely on Kelley's Customs Tariffs of the world, which is published annually but this department cannot hold itself responsible for any tariff information supplied respecting foreign countries.
We have another trouble to contend with, and that is lack of space and lack of a sufficient number of officials to compile such tariff information as we can from time to time.
It does not seem possible, if one goes through the buildings in Ottawa, to believe that there is any lack of officials. You simply fall over them, no matter which way you go.
