Yet, the hon. gentlemen who spoke on the Address told us about the magnificent efforts that were being made to extend the trade and commerce of this country. Surely, Sir, I am justified when I say that the time has come when some bright, progressive, alert, smart, business men should be placed in charge of the organizations that we have in connection with the affairs of this Government and of the country.
The right hon. the Prime Minister of this country (Sir Robert Borden) seems to

have come into a good deal of prominence in connection with the Russians that were to meet on Prinkipo in Prince's Islands. In this connection I want to say a word in justice to my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster). I listened attentively to his remarks the other evening, and I did not gather from what he said that he used language which could in any way be construed as denoting approval of the Bolshe-viki. On the contrary, I understood him to say that there were possibly two opinions and to substantiate his argument he quoted from the Manchester Guardian, which took the side of the question opposite to that taken by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell). I have here the report of the remarks of my hon. friend from Brome, as contained in Hansard, and I think it is only just to him, in view of what the hon. Minister of Public Works said, and also in view of what the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) said this evening, that his words should be repeated. My hon. friend from Brome said:
I am not sure whether the common view taken in this country ot the Bolshevik is altogether correct. I think that perhaps there is another side to the question, and as this is the great forum where truth and exact knowledge should be brought before the people, I take the liberty of referring the House to some articles which are appearing in the Manchester Guardian from an eye-witness from Russia.
That is not endorsing by any means the Bolsheviki, and I think it is unfair that my hon. friend should be placed in that position. So far as I am concerned, may I say that I heartily agree with the Minister of Public Works. I have exactly the same idea of the Bolsheviki that he has, and it was a matter of extreme regret to me to see the Prime Minister of this country placing himself in the position of opening communications with them and inviting them to meet decent people. I thought it was hardly fair to the people of Canada that they should have to assume that role. Anxious as some of the great powers were that there should be a settlement in Russia, none of them was willing to assume the responsibility of accepting a rebuff from one or other of the Russian parties. But, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada was made of sterner stuff, and, without a moment's hesitation, according to the despatch from Mr. Dafoe of the Winnipeg Free Press, he put forth the idea which he had conceived of inviting the Bolsheviki to meet at Prince's Island. Apparently the decent element among the Russians refused; so far there has been no meeting, and the matter has been dropped. I think it would be fair
for the Minister of Public Works and the hon. member for South Perth to communicate with the minister and give him their views in reference to the Bolshevikis in order to prevent anything of that kind occurring in the future.
Of course, it may be that the Prime Minister was better informed with reference to the Russian situation than we were. It may be that he had some inside information in reference to the matter. I am quite willing to admit that it would have been a wonderful diplomatic victory to have achieved if he had brought peace to Russia.
I can well imagine how the newspapers of the whole world would have acclaimed him as a great diplomat, and I believe that if he had been successful he would have been entitled to have been so acclaimed. It may be that the Prime Minister, with perhaps more vision than most of us possess, looked a little ahead and saw that in the event of being successful some recognition would come to him from the powers that be. In the olden times he would have been given broad lands, but now the League of Nations seems to have nailed the land down pretty well. There would be nothing left to give him but a title, and if he had been successful we in the Dominion of Canada could have had the pleasure and privilege of welcoming him back, not as the right hon. Sir Robert Borden, Prime Minister of Canada, but as the Earl of Prinkipo, because he would be entitled to that proud distinction in view of the great diplomatic victory that he had achieved at that island. The time has about arrived in the history of this country when some of the right hon. gentleman's colleagues should tell him that he was elected, and selected, to manage the affairs of Canada, in Canada, and that the seat of Government is Ottawa, not London, not Paris, and not Prinkipo. Somebody should tell the right hon. gentleman on one of his intermittent visits to this country that it is far [DOT] more important to the people of Canada to have the tariff settled satisfactorily than it is to have the boundaries of the Balkans settled. Somebody should tell the right hon) gentleman that it is far more important to the people of Canada to have the railway situation straightened out than it is to decide who is going to police Constantinople.
I would like to go further and say that the newspapers of Canada to-day are filled with stories of returned men who are not receiving the treatment they should receive. It is far more important to the people of this country that we should have

a government that is looking after Canadian affairs and far more important to them that the Premier should be here directing public affairs, which is his first and most pressing duty, than that he should determine who should have mandatory powers over the Hottentots. That is the position of affairs insofar as we are concerned, and the sooner the right hon. gentleman comes home, bringing his entourage with him, and permits the absent gentlemen to fill, even if only temporarily, the positions of Minister of Customs, Minister of Justice, and Minister of Trade and Commerce, the better it will be. Because that is what the people Of the country are paying them for. The Cabinet ministers are paid officials. It is not necessary that a man should be a wizard to be a Cabinet minister; the day for that sort of thing has passed and gone. The duties of Government consist largely of taking the money of the country and disbursing it wisely and well, of administering the affairs of Canada in the interests of its people. That is where hon. gentlemen opposite are falling down. They are in the clouds, their minds are given to everything but the duties of their offices; and the time has about arrived when somebody should direct the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada to come home-he was elected for a specific purpose, and the taxpayers of this country expect him to be here and attend to his business.
The Acting Premier (Sir Thomas White) said the other day in the course of his remarks, that there was absolute need for steadiness amongst the people of the country to-day. I quite agree with him in that statement, but I desire to point out that the lead must come from the Government. The people must have confidence in the Government, they must feel that they are being governed intelligently and well. There must be a return to responsible government-not government by order in council, but government for the people by the people. That was the obligation undertaken in behalf of the Canadian people when Confederation was formed. But hon. gentlemen opposite have not been carrying out that obligation, and that is the cause of the unsteadiness and unrest which prevails throughout Canada to-day.
I wish to refer to the subject of the Siberian Expedition, Canadians have not been vouchsafed very much light as to why they are being represented in Siberia. I could understand, Sir. that if we were still at war there might be need 
for the presence of a Canadian military force in Siberia, but I cannot understand why, once the armistice was declared, our soldiers should still be sent from Vancouver to Vladivostok. The people of Canada are equally at a loss to understand this, and it is one of the questions that hon. gentlemen opposite will find very difficult to answer when they appear before the public. Personally, I do not believe we have any more business in Siberia at the present time than we have in Mexico. Why should Canada be the policeman for the world? As a matter of fact, apart from the humanitarian reasons that are actuating some of the Powers, a good many nations are influenced by the fact that they have loaned large sums of money to Russia at extortionate rates of interest. That being so, why should we be the money collectors for Europe? Surely it is up to the creditor nations to collect their own investments.
There are certain other matters I wish to take up, and one of them has reference to a letter which I received from a returned soldier. Unfortunately I do not know under whose department it comes. It is difficult for a comparatively new man to determine just who is responsible for the administration of the many public departments of this Government. However, Mr. Speaker, with your permission I will read the letter, and if there are any ministers present who are interested in the department affected I shall be glad if they will take cognizance of it. If not, perhaps they will mention it to some of their colleagues, if it so happens that those colleagues are in this country. The letter in question is dated, "Windsor, Ontario, February 12th, 1919," is addressed to "William C. Kennedy, Esq., M.P., Windsor," and reads:
H. A. B. Aikman,
Formerly No. 7109-1st Battalion Can.
Board of Pension Commissioners, No. 13314.
Sir,-I have the honour to submit for your consideration the following- facts1 which represent an occurrence in which T figured in connection with the Board of Pensions Commissioners for Canada and the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Toronto.
In compliance with their request I reported in Toronto on Tuesday morning-, February 4th, 1919, at ten o'clock at the latter department, from which I was transferred to the (Military Hospital for medical re-examination, where I (with others), waited until about twelve-thirty, noon, when we were told to go away, get our dinner and report again in the afternoon. Two or three of us stated we had no money, so we *were given our dinner there. Probably about four o'clock, I, with others, was told to report again next day. I said that I, for one, would not report the next day, as I had come from Windsor, had already lost two days and to Windsor I was going that night and requested

transportation together with my expenses. The officer who Imparted the suggestion of reporting next day, did so in very crude language, had dishevelled hair, moved with uncertain gait and the expression of his eyes was such as I have seen produced by the immoderate use of liquor, and while X am not prepared to say definitely that that condition existed, his appearance implied such was the case.
It was then found possible to give me an examination, which occupied probably twenty minutes. At its conclusion I requested transportation and expenses and was told these would be supplied me at the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, where I had once before been. Reporting at this latter point again I was told that they could not supply my demands for transportation and pay and that I would have to go back to the Military Hospital for it.
I was suffering from lumbago, in addition to a shrapnel wound in the groin, the distance was between one and two miles and another trip was an impossibility for me. I thereupon flatly refused to do it. They then issued me return transportation to Windsor and, as is customary in the army, I signed a receipt for my pay and expenses, in advance. The clerk, who took my receipt, returned in a few moments, took my Windsor address and informed me cheque would be mailed to me the next day. This was eight days ago and I am still looking for this cheque, which I have already signed for, but have not received.
The amount involved is not large, but the principle of the thing, or shall X say, the lack of principle, is not only worth some consideration, but matters of this nature are things that we returned men in various stages of crippled condition, and impaired earning power, cannot financially afford to stand, especially when the amount is considered, of the pittance the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada sees fit to dole out to us.
Det me say further, that at the time of this visit to Toronto, I was informed that arrangements would be made for my return to hospital (Whitby being suggested), for further treatment, of which I am in need.
I am likewise still waiting for these latter arrangements to be perfected as well as for repayment for money and time expended by me.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
-	Tours respectfully,
(Signed) H. A. B. Aikman.
There is the story of a returned man, and that is one - of the matters that I refer to when I say that there is a feeling everywhere throughout the country that the affairs of the people are not being conducted by the heads of the respective departments as they should he; that we are not getting the government that the people are paying for, and that the time has arrived when hon. gentlemen should take charge of the departments for which they are responsible to the people, administer them in a businesslike way, and do away with these useless commissions that have been sapping away the financial life-blood of the country.
Another matter that I wish to take up is, perhaps, local in a sense, but it has a bearing on what I have said. Situated on the border, I have known many cases where men working in the ^city of Detroit were drafted or volunteered for military service and whose positions in various business houses of that city were reserved for them. Their employers said: You are Canadians; you are going to fight for your country. We honour you for it; you shall have your position as soon as the war is over. It was generous, and it was decent; but that is the spirit the Americans have always evinced-I say that after having lived for years on the border. Well, what happened? The armistice comes. Many of these boys who were drawing from $1,500 to $3,000 a year in the positions which they held before they went on military service, are working at $1.10 a day in London, filling clerical positions, some unimportant, and some important, perhaps. Their employers write them as soon as the armistice is signed, saying: The war is over; your position is waiting for you and we shall be glad if you can come at once. In the meantime the American boys who gave up their positions and went overseas are returning to the United States and if the Canadians do not come back and take their old positions, the first thing we know the Americans will take them and we shall increase to that extent the unemployment in Canada which the Minister of Public Works told us we were to spend millions to avoid. That was a case not of half a dozen men, but of a hundred men or more. When that situation confronted me I immediately took the matter up with the Minister of Militia. In justice to that hon. gentleman, I want to say that he met me more than half way. He appreciated the fact that my arguments were sound. I maintained that if the Government needed clerical assistance they should go into the, open market and engage that assistance, and thus avoid jeopardizing the future of these men by preventing them from taking the positions which they could never get again. The Minister of Militia wrote me very kindly saying that he had instructed the commanding officer of the London District to give heed to my suggestions, and, where possible, to meet them. I took the matter up with the Commanding officer of the London District, General Shannon, a very fine gentleman, and I found him kindness itself. He, too, was anxious to help where he could, and he wrote me to say that where it was possible to dispense with the services of these men he would be very glad to do it. But these

requests of mine were transferred from one department to the other and by the time the matter got back to General Shannon it was almost impossible to accomplish the object in view. In many instances I got .the men released; in many others I could not, and in many cases the positions were lost. But picking up the paper one morning I read about the Repatriation Committee, and decided that here at last was a place when I could obtain some relief, because they asserted that they were anxious to find employment for returned men. I wrote to the chairman of the Repatriation Committee, the Minister of Immigration' and Colonization (Mr. Calder) telling him what the conditions were. He wrote me a very nice letter agreeing that my argument was sound and that what I had suggested was absolutely the right thing to do. He said that he was 10 p.m. turning the matter over to the Secretary of the Repatriation Committee, who would write me later. In the course of a week or ten days I received a letter from the Secretary of the Repatriation Committee, in which that gentleman thanked me for the suggestion, saying that it was a very valuable one and that he would take it up with his committee and advise me at a later date. That was on the 20th of January, but unfortunately the committee, I take it, has not met since, because up to this time I have had no further word from the secretary. So you will see the way things are passed from one department to another. Nobody seems to be running the departments, and one can get no satisfaction from correspondence with them. You cannot get decisions and that is what the people want. What good is it to these boys who before going on military service had worked up to the point where they were of such service to their employers that they were getting $3,000 or $4,000 a year,-what good is it to them if I get a letter a month from now from the Secretary of the Repatriation Committee telling me that they are glad to comply with my request? The job is gone then. That is not what we want-we want action, and that is where hon. gentlemen are falling down in handling their departments.
I have other matters to take up, but I shall deal with them before the session is over when the issues with which they are connected come before the House. I shall not hesitate to express my views as to what I believe to be the proper thing to do in the interests of the country. I accept the statement of the Acting Prime Minister
L'Mr. Kennedy.]	.
that it is the duty of everyone to assist the Government, and to do what he can in bringing our country through the crisis that prevails to-day. I have done my share in every matter that has arisen in connection with the war and I propose to do my share in the work of reconstruction. I want to help, but I want to help intelligently. The people want to feel that they are receiving intelligent assistance from the men who-lead at this juncture and who compose the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot resume my seat without saying a word or two with reference to one who recently left us. Last year I had the first opportunity of serving under the stainless banner of our departed chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. To me it was a proud distinction, a distinction and an honour that I shall cherish to my dying day. His was always a fight for the people, and although he is gone, his spirit lives. In the words of Beecher on the death of Lincoln::
Bren he who now sleeps has, by this event, been clothed with new influence.
Dead, he speaks to men who now willingly hear what before they refused to listen to.
Our Chieftain is gone; but Liberalism is not dead, and I very much mistake the temper of the people of this country if, when the opportunity offers a*hd we appeal to them once more, they do not show their appreciation of Liberal principles.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join
in the congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the Address. It is a long -time since I have listened to what I presume we may dignify by the name of a speech by an honourable member such as we have just heard, because it strikes me as being an adaptation of the writings of the Fenian press of the United States in their attack on President Wilson for attending the King's banquet. I may, however, be doing the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Kennedy) an injustice, and lest I should do him an injustice in the budding moment of his distinguished career, I should like to ask him if he disapproves of Sir Robert Borden's accepting the invitation of the King of England and of the British Dominions overseas to that banquet to which he so caustically referred. Will the hon. gentleman answer me that question?
No.

If he had, it would have been about the only original part of his
speech. The rest I have read in the flamboyant Fenian press of the United States which has been forwarded to me at different times to show me what they could do along the border. I am inclined to think, to do justice to the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), that he will administer some slight and significant rebuke for that display of politics. The light which has been held out by the Opposition is, I presume "The Light that Failed." To me it is a very singular thing that the sum total of the brilliance of the Opposition, the attraction indeed for all those erring ones, should consist in an old candle stuck in the back door of the Opposition cabin. That, to my mind, is not doing justice to the attractive power of the Opposition, and it certainly does not look well in this country, nor does it look well to leaders abroad who will suppose that all that can be handed out by way of an attraction is something stuck in the back door of an edifice of that description.
I wish, however, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, to turn to something more important. The chief question now before this country, and, indeed, before the world, is reconstruction. I will, however, confine myself to one phase of that, namely, to the standard of living, to the living wage, to that wage which the lowest, simplest form of honest labour should receive in order that it may maintain the standard of life to which we all agree it is entitled. The wage earner has evolved from a long historic post. In the early days of England, he was a member of the family, when the work performed by the family was done in the family. By and by he became a member of the clan, when the work was done by the clan, by the blood relations. Afterwards this was extended to the guild, to those associations of men who united for the p'urpose of prosecuting industry. And so it advanced from time to time until the period of the plague in England in 1346-47, when nearly one-half of the people of England died of the plague, and this so Upset the industrial conditions of England at that time that the labourer as he was known then, wandered in an unorganized and indefinite way over the country, so much so that the Statute'of Labourers was enacted which compelled him to root himself once more to one spot and to confine his exertions to that area and which also compelled him to accept a certain specific wage. As time went on, however, the consideration of the people for each other changed. What was regarded as
strictly an economic question dawned upon the people as an ethical question. It was not so much a question of poverty as it was a question of life, and it has grown to be that more and more, so that we have to-day in England, in France, even in the United States, in Australia and in New Zealand, legislation of a character that has gone very far in elevating the condition of what is known as the common people. Canada has unfortunately hitherto lagged far behind. The reason of that is no doubt that we are a young country with great natural resources and much prosperity due largely to our abundance. That has probably not yet caused a condition which would warrant the measures that have been made use of in the older countries; but if the seeds of poverty, if the seeds of disintegration are here, it only requires time to bring them into growth, and it is well for us to provide against such acontingency by learning from the experience of other people. The most singular thing is that in a country like England, of such Conservative - tendencies, there should have been such haste to remedy the errors of the past.
The British people are, of course, a kindly, well-intentioned people, and so soon as it was brought home to them that it was necessary for them to improve the condition of the people, and to show some interest in them, they hastened to do so. We had, first of all, the Notification of Births' Act in 1907, by which for the first time in England it was compulsory, in all cases of births, for notice to be sent to the district medical officer, in order that registration might duly occur and some notice be taken of the birth. This had the effect of enabling the medical official, and through him the Government, to know exactly the condition in which those children were born, and to render the children and the mothers some assistance. This worked a miracle in England. Thousands and tens of thousands of children who would have died at this period through neglect and ignorance, were for the first time taken care of by an intelligent Government.
Then there was the Education Act, another far-reaching Act, under which the school children in the cities were provided for the first time with play grounds or breathing spaces. Then we had the system of national insurance, insuring people against unemployment, against sickness, and even against under-employment. I am citing these measures simply to show how very attentive the British people are at the present time to the elevation of the common

people from the low standard of life at which they have lived for so long. It is recognized now for the first time that the common people-the unskilled labourer, the man who is compelled to take what he can get-are entitled to something better. The lowest form of honest labour, if it is to be recognized at all, and it surely must be recognized, ought to receive some consideration on the ethical basis of a proper standard of life.
1 have here a report of the American Federation of Labour which represents the most intelligent ideas of labour in America arid, very largely, the ideas of labour the world over. Their ideas are summed up as follows:
There is no such thing as good wages without the cost of living in decency and comfort equalize the wages received. There must be no reduction in wages; in many instances, wages must be increased. The workers of the nation demand a living wage for all wage earners, skilled or unskilled, a wage which will enable the worker and his family to live in health and comfort, provide a competence for illness and old age, and afford to all the opportunity of cultivating the best that is in them.
It seems strange indeed that anybody should rise in this House and endeavour to call the attention of hon. members to the simple principle here enunciated. The principle, it is true, has been acknowledged in theory, has been made use of in disquisitions in the pulpit, but beyond that it has not been made use of at all. The principle of a living wage, of a decent standard of life for the lowest form of honest labour, has never yet been recognized in this country as necessary recompense of all forms of labour, but when that day comes it will mean something new for labour. It will mean hope. There is nothing unreasonable in the contention of labour, because once this zero mark has been ascertained, they are quite willing that labour above and beyond that mark shall be allowed to take care of itself. Above that mark wages will be paid according to the skill and competence of the labourer. That proposition seems to me entirely reasonable. Those who are below that mark are either weak or wicked, and have to be taken care of. They come under the denomination of the unemployed, the under-employed, the criminal or the wastrel. What is to be done with them is another matter; that is a question of reform in connection with detention farms and kindred schemes for their improvement. But that is not the question I am considering to-night, since it involves the consideration of the weakness of the

people, and that does not come under a business arrangement. If it is once practically recognized by the people of this country that the lowest form of honest labour is entitled to such a wage as will maintain it in efficiency and in decency, then the point is gained, and the greatest stroke of reconstruction that could be accomplished with regard to labour will have been accomplished. Permit me to repeat that it is such a self-evident proposition that it seems singular anybody should wish to call attention to it, but, practically, the principle has not yet been admitted. But when that time comes, in that one simple fact as set out by the American Federation of Labour, and as set out by all the recent authorities on political economy which I have been able to consult, will be found the solution of the problem. Trades unionism up to a few years ago was a criminal offence; but that the people should have the right to combine for the consideration of their own affairs and for their own protection was so self-evident that at last it was allowed. Then the time came when, to the wonderment of our people here, there was introduced in the old country by no less a man than Lloyd George himself the revolutionary measure of imposing a tax upon the site value, the unearned increment of idle land being appropriated by a supertax to the use of the state, in order that the fundamental principle of the worthiness of work should be finally recognized.
One thing more is necessary. I hove here a Bill passed by the Imperial Parliament prescribing a minimum rate of wages during a limited period and repealing certain provisions of the Act relating to workers on war munitions. A Bill of that description fixing a minimum wage would be considered in this country such a tremendous step in advance that it -would cause a great deal of trepidation. The minimum wage, however, has been discovered not to be the solution of the difficulty, for if a man receives ten dollars a day that is of no consequence if it does not provide him and his family of three children which is usually taken as the unit, with a proper standard of living. On the other hand, if he receives only one dollar a day and that provides him with the proper means of existence, it is enough; so that a minimum wage has really nothing to do with the case. The sole and only contention is that the lowest form of labour, since we must begin from some definite point, shall be considered entitled to a proper standard of living. That proposition

is not only economically sound, but surely all decent and Christian people will agree to it; and when it has been incorporated in legislation, as it undoubtedly will be in course of time, labour will have achieved what it has been striving for. It is trades unionism that is the hope of this world against Bolshevism. The trades unions are fighting Bolshevism. The trades unions are an organization of sensible labour men doing their level best. It was the trades unions that furnished more than half the men who fought the battles of this war. The Bolshevik would upset all organized labour of any kind. Therefore, it is time for the Government to pay due and proper attention to the contentions of the trades unions and endeavour to place them as nearly as possible upon a thoroughly sound and economic basis. But that basis must have in it the pure ethical spirit, for if it is going to be simply an economic system, if it is going to have simply the principle of taking what you can get-the old system of plunder-it is simply the curse of modern and industrial conditions known as profit. It seems to be a very absurd thing that anybody should speak against profit as I have done so many times in this House, but profit is the taking of that for which no equivalent is given, and the man who takes that for which he does not give an equivalent is a Bolshevik. We are asked to eliminate from the world these conditions, and to do away with that spirit of plunder, and in our dealing to restore, a fair equivalent in trade or exchange. The establishment of so simple a thing as- a standard of decent living for all honest, sensible men-for all these have to be fairly considered units of humanity, units in the industrial world-and the doing away with the desire to take what we can lay our hands on without regard to the justice of the case, means the making of a new world.

On the Orders of the Day;

Before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I desire to draw the attention of the Government to a matter of national importance contained in a special despatch published in yesterday's Toronto Globe, and to ask a question with reference thereto. The despatch in question reads:
8i
London, Feb. 26.-Overseas representatives are interested in John Bull's slashing article. "Shall We Lose Canada?" in which the editor protests against the price being paid for the support of America and condemns importation restrictions which give advantages to Scandinavia and the United States. The article contains a number of specific Instances which apparently could be obtainable only through official Canadian channels, and which give point to the renewed attempts of the Trade Commission to have the restrictions removed.
Canadian Feeling Bitter.
The Globe correspondent finds that the feeling among some of the Canadians is bitter. They are urging Sir Robert Borden to take official action to bring the situation to a crisis and have a general clearing up. But there is still hope that this can be brought about without a quarrel in the Imperial family.
There have been some ludicrous incidents, sudh as the refusal to admit certain business calendars for free distribution, the printing of which had been refused here owing to war limitations, and which the authorities were consequently compelled to print in Canada. On their arrival the British authorities decided they could not be admitted for two years, and the matter is still under consideration.
There are other instances, such as Canadian boots, wallpapers, and other articles which are refused admission, but American and Scandinavian goods are coming in without stay. Canadians feel that If the regulations applied generally to all there could be no protest, but as now enforced there is real discrimination against them.
I desire to ask the Acting Prime Minister if the Government has any information regarding the matters referred to in the despatch, and if so will the hon. gentleman impart that information to the House?

I would direct the attention of my hon. friend to my answer yesterday to a question asked by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Hunt-ingdon (Mr. Robb), dealing with the same subject. The Government has no official information respecting the matter in question, and I am satisfied, as I stated yesterday, that Great Britain has not discriminated and will not discriminate against the interests of Canada in regard to trade relations.
Has the hon. gentleman made inquiries since yesterday?
