Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session resumed from Thursday, February 27.
Mr. WILLIAM DUFF (Lunenburg.) In rising to address the House, Mr. 'Speaker, on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Redman) and seconded by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), I feel my inability to deal with the subjects contained in the Address from the Throne, but as a representative of the people of this country I feel it my duty to call the attention of the House to certain facts. Before doing so, Mr. Speaker, if you will permit me, I would like to add my word of praise for the able, eloquent and moderate manner in which the mover and the seconder of the Address placed their views before the House. Before proceeding with the subject matter contained in the Address from the Throne, as delivered by His Excellency the Governor General, would you allow me on behalf of the loyal citizens of Lunenburg county, which I have the honour to represent in this House, to convey to His Excellency the great joy expressed by the people of that county on the success of the Allied armies at the front.
May I also place on Hansard the deep and profound regret of the people of that district at the loss to the country of that eminent statesman, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. As so many fine tributes have been paid to his worth and memory by all classes and creeds in this great country, it is not necessary for me to reiterate what has already been enunciated. As has been well said, his life has been an ideal which every Canadian boy should endeavour to emulate, and if they follow his illustrious example the next generation will be a higher type of men.

During the past few days I have received a number of telegrams and letters from different parts of Nova Scotia, asking me to convey to the hon. gentleman from North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. D. D. McKenzie) the congratulations of the Liberals of Nova- Scotia on the honour which has been done them by his selection as leader of the Liberal party. In one of the letters which I received I find the folio-wing, which 1 think is worth reading to the House:
How sweet the name McKenzie sounds In every Liberal's ears,
It soothes our sorrows, heals our wounds, And drives away our fears.
There has been a good deal said in some of the reptile press of this country during the past few days as to what happened when the Liberal party assembled in caucus to select our leader. I do not wish to divulge the secrets of that caucus, but I wish to say that the stories in these papers are untrue. The utmost harmony prevailed, and I say-and I think I speak on behalf of the English speaking Liberals of the Liberal party of this country when I say it-that we feel that we owe to the French Canadian Liberals of this country a debt of gratitude for the action which they took at that caucus. I never shall forget the fairness, broadmindedness and sense of justice of these gentlemen, and I am pleased to call the French Canadian Liberals in this House my brothers.
Mr. Speaker, I now turn for a few moments to the speech delivered by His Excellency to the honourable gentleman of the Senate and the honourable gentlemen of this House and I wish for a few moments to discuss some of the matters contained therein. We are all in perfect accord with His Excellency's remarks with regard to the conclusion of the war. For more than four years the Empire was in the throes of the greatest war the world has ever known and the prayers of a thankful people went up to the Most High when the telegraph wires on November 11 conveyed to many anxious hearts the news that the armistice had been signed. Of Canada's part, ISir, in that great struggle, other honourable gentlemen have told' us and I am in perfect agreement with the eloquent remarks on this subject as expressed by the Acting Prime Minister, Sir Thomas White.
The Acting Prime Minister, in his well timed remarks, paid just tribute to the work of the British, French and Canadian forces, and his remarks especially with regard to the Canadian Expeditionary force were in good taste. I was rather surprised

however, Mr. Speaker, that no mention was made by the honourable gentleman of the great part which another nation took in this struggle, and it seems rather strange indeed that the Acting Prime Minister, speaking as he really did not only for the Government of this country but the people of this country, that he did not pay a just tribute to our sister nation to the south. Without being caustic in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the honourable gentleman has not gone back to the position which he took in 1911 when he did not desire "any truck or trade with the Yankees." The United States financiers treated the honourable gentleman with the greatest courtesy and respect when he was compelled to go to them a few years -ago to borrow money to finance this country and her war effort and I trust his omission with reference to the United States' part in the war was not due to the fact that the financiers of that nation at last refused to grant us further advances. Since the honourable gentleman has not dealt with the great part played by the people of the United States in the last few' years, might I, Mr. Speaker, for a few moments speak of what they have done. It is true there was some criticism of that great country, because she did not at once plunge into the war after the sinking of the great liner Lusitania w'ith the loss of so many lives. Previous to that, however, the United States had been doing a great work and in the first two years of the war and in fact during the whole period of the war, if it had not been for the whole-hearted support that that country gave the Allies in supplying them with munitions, guns, food, etc., the issue might possibly have been settled in a way which none of us desired.
It is not for any of us to criticise the actions of that great man and that great democrat, Woodrow Wilson. He had a difficult task to perform and when the time was ripe and when practically the whole nation was at his back, he gave the w'ord with the result that hundreds of thousands of gallant American lads were hurried to France to fight in the great cause in which the allied countries were engaged. We must take off our hats, Mr. Speaker, to that great country. I am not saying too much when I say that no other country in so short a time placed so many men on the field of battle. It is quite true that the first expeditionary force from England, the old contemptibles, was in the fighting line three weeks after war had been declared, and here I might also have
a word of congratulation for a previous Minister of Militia for the expeditious manner in which he despatched the first contingent from this country. To show the appreciation of the English people for the help given by the United States, I have much pleasure in reading the following from the London Morning Post:
The London Morning Post states that the arrivals of American troops during the past few days have eclipsed all records. It is a shipping feat which has never been equalled in maritime annals. General March, the Chief of Staff of the American Army, is the authority for the statement that there are now over eight hundred thousand American troops in France. That probably means that there are well over a million men overseas. The despatch of troops from the United States during the last three months has been limited only by the shipping capacity. Every ship that sails which is at all suitable for carrying troops is loaded down with soldiers. During a recent month, as many as two hundred and fifty thousand men were despatched from American shores, and American papers state that soon the last of the sixteen National Army Divisions will be overseas, or on the way. It is the knowledge the Germans have that this great army, the pick of America's young manhood, is on the scene ready to replenish the Forces of Freedom which is forcing Hindenhurg to make his desperate and costly attempts to win a decision.
Hhe above, Mr. Speaker, is only a just tribute to the people of that great country, and I only regret, Sit,-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I, with exceeding regret, feel it my duty to direct the attention of the hon. member to a rule of this House which is as old as the House itself, and which says that the reading of speeches is not permissible. I think the House will bear me out in saying that the Chair has always been inclined to be exceedingly lenient in the matter of copious notes being used by members, but the hon. gentleman is going far beyond the bounds in reading his speech verbatim. I must ask him to put himself in order and to adhere more closely to the rule of the House in this regard.

I submit to your ruling, of course, Mr. Speaker, but I have only been following the example which was set by the hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), who read closely from his written speech, and also the example of the mover and seconder of the resolution, who did the same thing. However, I shall endeavour, Mr. Speaker, to carry out your wishes as far as possible. I am only sorry that my capacity for public speaking does not permit me to express my thoughts in a manner which would do justice to the American heroes of Chateau Thiery and the other battles in France and Flanders in which the American armies took part. We

are proud to pay a just tribute to these gallant men and the people of both countries feel that the blood which was spilt during the last two years in France has cemented the English-speaking people in a bond which will never be broken. Of the noble part played by our own heroes in this great war enough cannot be said. Their efforts were appreciated by every allied nation and Canada has taken her rightful position in the sun on account of their gallant deeds.
It is gratifying to me, Mr. Speaker, as it is gratifying to every Canadian, to know that steps will be taken to properly protect 'these heroes. Especially should this be true of the wounded and sick who are coming home now on every steamer. It is our country's duty to see that during the remainder of their lives proper protection is given them and Canadians will vie with one another in placing these wounded heroes in a position where they will not feel that Canada has not appreciated their noble efforts. As to the boys who are returning physically fit, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that after conversing with a number of them I have come to the conclusion that they deeply resent anything which would tend to make the public think that they are objects of charity. These boys who have fought for four years in the muddy trenches of France have endured terrible sufferings and discomforts and are able to take their place in civil life with the best of us, and I feel confident that after they have been discharged and have returned to civil life that we may expect great things of them. " They have finished the fight, they have kept the faith," and they have made the world safe for democracy.
Before concluding my remarks with reference to the returned soldiers, I would like to address a word of advice to the gentlemen in charge of the department which has to deal with demobilization, and I do it not in a critical spirit, but in the best interests of the soldiers and our country. There is a great deal of complaining amongst the soldiers disembarking at the port of Halifax on account of the fact that they cannot get their discharge in a few days after their arrival on this side of the water, and this fact, Mr. Speaker, is creating more unrest than perhaps the hon. gentlemen of the Government realize. As a frequent visitor to the city of Halifax, I have come in touch with a number of the boys who have this complaint to make, and if you will allow me for a few minutes I would like to tell of one specific case.

Five weeks ago a young man returned on the Aquitania. He got permission from the authorities at Halifax to go to his home for a week. He came to see me about a business matter and said that he had a chance to purchase a business and that he was going to Halifax to endeavour to get his discharge. About three weeks after that while walking on one of the streets of Halifax I happened to see this young man and he was still in khaki. I asked him why he had not received his discharge and he said he did not know. He explained that he had applied to the authorities four times but he had got no satisfaction. It seems that the men were paraded every morning at nine o'clock, the roll was called and they were then free to wander through the streets of Halifax until nine o'clock the next morning. The business that the young man was anxioug to acquire was purchased by somebody else and to-day he is out of a position. Shortly after having spoken with this young man in Halifax, I happened to meet one of the officers who has charge of the demobilization and I made it my business to ask him what good reason there was for these soldiers being kept for three weeks or a month after they came home. His reply to me was: ''In the first place there is too much red tape. In the second place, sometimes when a steamer arrives the necessary documents are not on board, and we have to wait until the arrival of the next steamer from the Old Country." I said: ''That does not seem to me sufficient reason; is there any better explanation?" He replied: "There are other reasons," and he gave this as one of them: "Sometimes," he said, " the men when they arrive in this country have overdrawn their monthly pay, and they are kept by the Halifax military authorities in Halifax until such time as they have worked the overpayment off." Another case he told me was to this effect: A young man arrived, and when he reached the demobilization station he was minus his rifle, which was worth $35. The authorities kept that man there thirty days, and in addition to paying him so that he could reimburse the cost of the rifle, this country had to feed him. Mr. Speaker, is this not a ridiculous state of affairs to have in connection with the demobilization of our troops? I draw the attention of the Minister of Militia to these facts in order to see if he cannot speed up the present procedure.
The speech from the Throne announces that a Bill relating to the franchise for women, and conferring on them the privilege of sitting in Parliament, is to be in-

troduced. Such an Act as that, Sir, meets with my humble approval, and nothing will give me greater pleasure than to have at some future date one of the fair sex as a desk mate.
The leader of the Opposition in his remarks dealt in suitable terms with the Wartime Elections Act. I submit, Sir, that this Act should be repealed before any other legislation dealing with the franchise is introduced. Regarding the proposed Franchise Act, I am entirely in accord with the remarks made by my leader when he referred to the Franchise Act which was in force in Canada for a number of years previous to the enactment of the War-time Elections Act. That law has worked very well in the province of Nova Scotia, and if you will bear with me for a moment, Sir, I will explain to you how voters' lists are made up in that province. The lists are compiled in the towns, cities and counties	in	this manner. In
every town there are three revisors appointed, who may be one year in the proportion of two Conservatives to one Liberal, and in the following year in the proportion of two Liberals to one Conservative. In the rural districts the municipal council appoints a revisor for each district. As you know, Sir, in political matters in Nova Scotia we are pretty evenly divided, and consequently every year one party has as many revisors as the other. These men get together and prepare the voters' lists. When they have performed that duty the list is submitted and if there are any complaints, or if there is any person who wants redress, he can apply to the sheriff of the county, to have his name placed on the list, or to have other names, which should not be there, struck off. This system has worked very well in the province of Nova Scotia for the last twenty-five years. Indeed so satisfactory has its operation been that in my county I cannot recall any application in the course of twenty-five years to the sheriff for redress. Un,der the circumstances, Sir, to depart from such a system as that would, in my opinion, be a waste of public money. After the lists are made up by the local revisors they are placed in the hands of the municipal clerk for every county, from whom the Secretary of State receives a copy of the list for federal purposes. The county clerk receives for his trouble one-half cent per name, so that it is quite apparent that the prevailing system in Nova Scotia is a very cheap and effective method of preparing the lists, much cheaper and better than the method adopted in the last election. I respectfully submit, Sir, that a large amount of money will be saved for the tax-payers of this country if the federal authorities will adopt that system and I am sure tnat every citizen of this country, who is interested in safe-guarding the financial interests of the country will want to have this work done as cheaply as possible.
With respect to the announcement that a Bill providing for federal aid towards highways is to be introduced, I would like to say that any moneys to be voted by the House for this purpose should be gifts outright to each province, and that no string should be attached thereto. A year or two ago some of our newspapers were advocating the construction of a national highway. That, Mr. Speaker, might be a very wise thing to do under happier circumstances if the condition of the national finances permitted, but, in my opinion, nothing like this should be done at the present time. Any money granted by this Government to the different provinces should be expended' on the present highways in order that the great farming industry might enjoy better roads on which to transport their products to the different markets.
The speech from the Throne declares that Canadian financial and commercial stability has been well maintained. To that statement, Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to take exception. I feel that a great many people in Canada are not at all satisfied with the way in which the Government has handled the public money. In their minds unnecessary expenditures have been made, and new departments created which have not been a benefit in any sense of the term. A previous speaker has referred to the fact that an hon. member from a Nova Scotia constituency was appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, but resigned in disgust after holding the office for a few months. After tendering his resignation to the Government the hon. gentleman in question issued a statement which makes very interesting reading, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to have that statement placed on Hansard. It is taken from the Halifax Herald, and reads as follows:
Why P. B. McCurdy, M.P., Resigned His Position.
Too much delay and too little Progress made in preparing for Rehabilitation of our Overseas Soldiers and Solv-. ing Problem of their Return.
Halifax, November 28.-P. B. McCurdy, M.P., returned yesterday from Ottawa where he has been serving the government in various capacities. Formerly Mr. McCurdy was parliamentary

branch of a department, I do not know which. My attention was directed to this by an advertisement which I' saw in the Truro Daily News. When I received this paper I noticed that on the margin, close to the advertisement, the following words were written: " Can't you stop this nonsense?" I will read to the House this advertisement as it appeared in the Truro' Daily News, and probably in every other Unionist paper from Vancouver to Halifax, at considerable cost to the ratepayers of this country. It is as follows:
The ''Why" In Fish Prices.
''Why is the price of halibut so high?" The question is often asked.
The public is itself responsible. It has put halibut into the luxury class. Many people never bought red cod, flounder, plaice, witch or drill in their lives, nor asked for them.
Each of these is as delicate and as satisfying as the fish of their choice and habit.
From 30 to 40 per cent of the oatch on halibut lines is cod that has to he thrown away. The cost of a sea fishing cruise has to come out of about 70,000 pounds, where it might be spread over 400,000 pounds if all fish taken were used and eaten. Retail cost would slump at once.
You cannot blame the fisherman for throwing away cod and other fish for which the public do not ask. He has to gratify the public: it is a fickle master.
The 'Canada Food Board aims to end this waste by making facts known to the people.
Meanwhile "there's plenty of good fish in the sea."
Canada Food Board, Ottawa.
For the Government, through their Food Board, to issue such ridiculous nonsense is a matter of great concern. It shows conclusively that some person connected with the Canada Food Board has insulted the intelligence of the people of this country. Any one who ever heard tell of a codfish knows that it is one of the most valuable and most palatable fish caught in the Atlantic. The person in the employ of the Government who sent that notice to the public should lose his job within twenty-four hours; he is not fit to hold it.
I noticed also an editorial in the Yarmouth Herald referring to another statement sent out by this Food Board, and I think that this editorial should find a place on Hansard. The editorial reads as follows:
Recently a report was sent out, signed by a member of the Canada Food Board in which it gave the public the positive reason for the high cost of halibut and which displayed unpardonable Ignorance regarding that fishery. It stated that the sole reason why the price of that food commodity held so high was due to the fact that the fishermen in the prosecution of the halibut fisheries were very sorely hampered by the smaller fish such as cod, haddock and other shack, all of which had to he returned to the sea. In consequence only small fares of
halibut were taken at a trip and the high prices were necessary to assure the fishermen a paying return. That report was issued several weeks ago, and owing to the absurdity of the statement was probably thrown to the waste baskets with little or no comment. The report so published no doubt started a thought of just *where the officials preparing such statements may have come from, for it is hard to conceive of a man of Canadian birth signing such a statement. Yet it was done, and only a few days ago the following statement was issued by the Food Board, which also shows that the department is gaining little or no enlightenment re Canadian Atlantic coast fisheries:
"As an instance of difficulties under which the fisherman of Nova Scotia are working this winter," says a Canada Food Board statement, "the loss of gear on the codfish banks by trawlers catching their trawl nets on vessels sunk by German submarines last fall may be cited. Many cases have occurred since fishing was resumed on the codfish banks off the Nova Scotia coast, and fishermen are very bitter, as while the sunken wrecks remain, these banks will be impossible to fish. When trawls are lost in this way, it means an amount of about 13,000. Despite this discouragement, however, Nova Scotia fishermen are endeavouring to increase production of codfish this winter, and the Canada Food Board urges a greater consumption of this staple Canadian fish."
Can any reader, with the slightest knowledge of the fisheries, see through such a statement? Of all the vessels which fell victim to the German submarines, there were not more than ten acually sunk directly on the fishing banks, and even if they were, what difference would their wreckage make to trawl gear? Absolutely none whatever, yet the Food Board in ignorance of the real facts allows such statements to be published and given to the public. With such reports going broadcast over the Dominion the fishermen, we feel, have a stronger plea than ever before for the appointment of a Fisheries Commission to be composed of men who have all their years made a study of the fisheries, not only from a scientific basis but from a practical standpoint as well. Not until such is done will it be possible for the ministers at the heads of the departments to he in a position to deal with the many difficult problems which from time to time confront them on the fishery question. It is also a matter which the fishermen should most urgently demand, for the publication of such absurd statements as the above makes a huge joke out of one of Canada's most important industries.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the Canada Food Board has served no useful purpose, except it be the fact that for the last six months it compelled the people of this country to eat a great deal of bran and middlings. It is also quite true that they made a poor Chinese restaurant keeper in this city pay a fine of $100 for placing a bowl containing sugar before one of his guests, while they took no steps to reduce the price of the bacon which the restaurant keeper served to the same guest. " One law for the Chinese, and another for the bacon hog."	_
Then there is another department which is known as the Department of Public In-

formation. This department, a great many people are of the opinion, was created to boost the Government, and to show what some of the people of this country think of the work this department is doing, I read the following clipping from one of the Toronto papers:
" The Department of Public Information is another fountain of wisdom which showers blessings on a large number of unattached or lightly attached journalists. It began with large ambitions which have been considerably whittled by circumstances. It had no less a purpose than to hand out all the news to all the newspapermen-scientifically predigested, of course

and thus to control the press of Canada. What upset this little scheme, which had its origin in the teeming hrain of Leader Rowell, was the objection of certain newspapers to taking coloured news from anybody, and a similar objection by the Ottawa correspondents to this rubber-stamp way of doing their work. Moreover, jealousies arose in the Cabinet. The ministers objected to any one man, however pure, giving the thing his own slant.
So the Department of Public Information drew in its horns. Occasionally it makes a feeble gesture when it hands out a parboiled despatch from Argyll House, but mostly it contents itself with keeping a scrapbook for the Cabinet ministers and printing a weekly "Official Canadian Record" which nobody takes, although the subscription is nothing a year. The "Official Canadian Record" is made up of stale news scalped from the dailies, bum puffs of the Government, blue book hash, and rose-water statistics. Once in a while it offers a bit of owlish advice, as, for instance, the last number, which admonishes sufferers from the "flu" to keep their windows open. A good tip. Let us all keep our windows, our bowels and our minds open, and we shall be a happy, healthy people. Union Government or not."
Another costly experiment for the people of this country was the Canadian Registration Act. It was a useless expenditure of public money and had no beneficial results. This has been acknowledged by every wellthinking person in Canada, and I wish to place on Hansard the opinion of the Montreal Gazette with regard to this costly farce:-
Tlie Canada Registration Act has been suspended. Announcement to that effect comes from Ottawa. It will no longer be necessary to carry a registration card. Any man or woman happening to have one of those interesting souvenirs is at liberty to destroy it. The Registration Act, like the no-strike order, has, it is assumed, 'served its purpose.' The value of this registration business was questioned at its inception. As an inventory of manpower it was as useless as the previous count made by the National Service Board, and for the same reason, namely, that it provided no means whereby the information obtained could be put to practical use. There was, it is recalled, the sapient suggestion that the registration would facilitate the enforcement of the Military Service Act. The hope that it would so operate was based upon the theory that slackers who had determined to evade the draft would walk meekly into the office of the nearest registrar and confess their eligibility. One hopes that

this confidence was not misplaced. What is recalled of the registration is that it put the people of Canada to considerable inconvenience, that it created much confusion, that it imposed upon the population an extra and useless obligation at a time when necessary restrictions and regulations were sufficiently numerous, and that it involved the country in a doubtful expenditure when every dollar of public money was urgently required for war purposes. The people registered on the assumption that they were contributing to the country's war effort. They have yet to learn of any substantial practical purpose having been served by the registration. The suspension of the Act may have been necessary as a formality. It makes no difference otherwise.
This article, coming from such an important newspaper as the Montreal Gazette, a newspaper which supported the previous Government, that is the Borden Government of 1911 to 1917, and which has supported this Government since then, deserves serious consideration on the part of the Government.
The hon. member (Mr. Redman) who moved the resolution in support of the speech from the Throne referred to the fact that the Prime Minister was at present in France attending the Peace Conference. Conflicting reports have come to us as to the value of the services being rendered by the Prime Minister in this connection. I am not in a position to state as to what is the Prime Minister's status at this great conference, but it is quite evident 4 p.m. that some of the newspapers in this country are not carried away by the work which the Premier is supposed to be doing. There is a story in the Good Book which tells of a man who sat by a certain gate waiting for the " crumbs which fell from the rich man's table," and it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has been placed in that humiliating position by the memDers of this Government who are at present in Paris.
I supmit, Sir, that our case would be very much stronger if it had been submitted in writing by the Prime Minister to Premier Lloyd George, setting forth our claims, and that after he had discussed the matter fully with the Premier of Great Britain he could have returned to Canada and looked after and attended to the government of this country.
A short time ago a report was published in the newspapers that the Premier was engaged in settling the boundary lines between Greece and Rumania. That, to my mind, was no compliment to this great country, and it is to be hoped that the day is not far distant when the different members of the Government, who are at present

in a foreign land, will return and look after the business of their departments.
I was greatly interested, Mr. Speaker, in listening to the statements made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) in his speech on Wednesday, relative to public expenditures which are proposed by the Government. It is certainly a very large order, and in the expenditure of such large amounts I trust that the minister will act as the "watch dog" of the treasury.* Part of the programme as outlined by him, is one of shipbuilding, and I wish to protest strongly on the floor of this House against the Government's going into the shipbuilding business. It seems to me that they are developing political hysteria, as they would never think of such a project in view of the fact that it is doubtful if there is one member of the Government who has any practical knowledge of this great industry. I also doubt if there is one of the members of the Cabinet who knows the cathead of a ship from the dog watch, the cow's tail from the horse pipe, the ring stopper from the wheel box, the port watch from the chronometer, the jump stay from the stop water, the royal yard from the foot ropes, the ratlines from the mousings, or the cats paw from the thoroughfoot; and yet these hon. gentlemen propose to enter a business, a knowledge of which it takes years to acquire. Then, again they should remember that when the war started and when Lloyd George told us that the demand was for ships and more ships, in addition to the shipyards already in Canada, old shipyards were re-opened, and the business men and shipwrights of Canada proceeded to do their bit in winning the war by carrying out the wishes of the Premier of Great Britain. They did not ask for any favours from the Government, but they have established their businesses on a business basis, and have sold their ships in the open market. Is it fair, Sir, that after these people have invested large sums of money and established their business, the Government should now come in and propose to interfere with them? I would think that the bungling and the gross extravagance on the part of the Naval Department in the last few years, in purchasing ships, should have sickened the Government when one of their members made such a ridiculous proposition. I can only say, Sir, that "they know not what they do."
The Minister of Public Works, in outlining his policy, declared that his own idea was to provide work for the labourers of Canada. It is evident that he has had a change of heart since August last when he
threatened the mine and steel workers of Nova Scotia with the importation of coolie labour. The following is an extract from the Halifax Herald of Tuesday, August 30, 1918, from which it is quite evident that the labour people did not agree with the Minister of Public Works:
Halifax, August 30.-The labour leaders' attitude towards the pronouncement of Hon. Prank Carvell favoring the introduction of coolie labour was emphatically stated to The Herald last night by Tom Moore, general representative of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, who is in the city acompanied by P. M. Draper, secretary of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada,: A. Bastion, union organizer, of Montreal, and H. J. Halford, of Hamilton, vice-president of the Barbers' Union of America. They had just returned from a thorough investigation of conditions at the mines in Oaipe Breton.
Our answer to Mr. Carvell, said Mr. Moore, is that coolie labour is not needed, and the minute a Chinaman or Coolie enters a mine to work, that moment the miners of Cape Breton down tools and walk out. Continuing, Mr. Moore said, that Hon. Frank Carvell should have informed himself of conditions at the mines before as a public man, condemning the miners as unpatriotic. Mr. Moore said we have personally visited the mines in Cape Breton, and discussed the situation with hundreds of the men-. We found that in the smaller mines of the Dominion Coal Company that the men claim there is sufficient help to work to capacity the present rooms. In the large pit head, known as Dominion No. 2, more mien could be employed. The situation there, however, is thatowing to lack of transportation, the coal at present being produced cannot be handled and taken away, and unless something is done immediately the possibility is that a very large proportion of the present help will have to be laid off during the winter months when there is no water-borne freight.
The labour leader explaining the reason for this serious outlook, said: At the present time there is between 200,000 and 300,000 tons of coal banked at the mines, and considerable fear is entertained by the management that it may become a total loss through spontaneous combustion, and measures are being taken to open up the heap so as to ward off disaster if possible.
What this enormous pile of coal means may be gathered when it is understood that the average production of a miner working at the fgce head is from 7 to 12 tons per day, but when the surface help and other labour is included, the coal produced does not represent more than two tons per day per head of the men employed at the mines.
Therefore, if you take 200,000 tons as the minimum of the pile, and. it certainly is more, that represents 100,000 working days for one man, or 100 working days for 1,000 men. In other words it represents the output of 1,0'00 men for over three months. In the past this pile has always been cleared away in the summer when there was plenty of transportation by rail and water-and then the men were kept on all winter producing coal for another pile, which would be moved in the spring, when navigation was resumed. If the present pile is not removed the outlook is that the mines will have to close down this winter, and instead

of importing coolie labour, Hon. Frank Carvell will have to find employment for the miners of Cape Breton.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we were all interested in the address of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Cal-der), and it was certainly a work of art for fence straddling. Following a course not unskilfully indicated by the Acting -Prime Minister, the Minister of Immigration deprecated party politics. As I understand his attitude, politics is a game which, when the country is progressing favourably and peacefully may be indulged in, but which is out of place in times of stress and strain. It is to be regretted that this minister of the Crown, with such a long experience in public life, has such a low idea of politics. It does little honour to himself and surely less than justice to the political atmosphere in which for a number of years past he has lived and moved and had his being, of which indeed he receives the credit of having been in large measure the mainspring and the real, if not the apparent leader. He does less than justice to that atmosphere, 1 repeat, because during the last few weeks we have seen a minister of the Crown in another province, Mr. Motherwell, leave the responsibilities and emoluments of office and resume the rank of a private member, rather than remain among those from whom he differed on public questions.
No, Mr. Speaker, the old ideas of public life are not dead. Some men will inevitably welcome, and others instinctively shrink from, reform; others by nature love, and others distrust, liberty. The ideals of honesty and sincerity and loyalty are as dear as ever they were in the mind and hearts of the Canadian people-perhaps all the dearer since the ugliness of the lack of these qualities has so recently been so clearly demonstrated.
We are somewhat amused on this side of the House by the assumption of superior political virtue by the Minister of Immigration, and his lofty superiority to the political game. May we, Mr. Speaker, from this side of the House say this to him: He may regard, if he likes, the strife of political parties as a game-if so for many years he has been a player-but that is not the view of those sitting on your left, Sir. We believe that we are here for the purpose of advancing the public interest along principles which we hold in common, principles dear to the heart of Baldwin and Lafontaine, of Howe and Brown, of Mackenzie, Blake and Laurier.
We regret that these principles are poor outworn things to the Minister of Immi-

gration, but we venture to assert that notwithstanding the loss of his adherence thereto, their longevity will not be impaired.
The Minister of Immigration regrets that there has been considerable internal strife. His remedy is that the public men of this country use their heads and hearts for the purpose of putting an end to these conditions. Noble sentiments, certainly ![DOT] But * the minister omitted to place the blame for this internal strife where it really belongs; and that is with a section of the press of Canada for the attitude they have adopted. Was his omission due to the fact that that portion of the press has been largely subsidized and is controlled by the present Government?
After his confession of faith and the reason given by him for the retention of his portfolio, although the war is over, it is quite satisfactory to the gentlemen on this side of the House if it is satisfactory to his Conservative friends of the Union Government. My own view of the matter is that " Ephriam is joined to his idols, let him alone."	-
We on this side of the House, Sir, await with interest the information to be submitted by the Government containing the accounts of last year and the estimates for the next fiscal year, and I can assure you Mr. Speaker, that as far as we are concerned on this side of the House, we will vote any moneys necessary to carry on the business of the country in connection with the soldiers and their dependents with the mobilization and the other necessary services of the Government. Let me, however, say to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell), and the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) that tlie strictest economy must be practised and that owing to the regrettable financial condition of the country at present, we must ask them to go slow. Eternal vigilance should be their watchword, and we will hold them to strict accountability for every dollar spent which is not necessary.
We are living in serious times, and it behooves every member of this House to safeguard the interests of this country, and when we have done this, Sir, we can return to our constituents for the summer recess and they will say to us " Well done, good and faithful servant."
Mr. WILLIAM FOSTER COCKiSHUTT (Brantford): Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address on the very creditable manner in which they have acquitted themselves. I

also desire to concur in all the encomiums that have been passed upon our departed friend, the late leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).
This is an after-the-war assembly, and we are called upon to deal with present-day conditions. We have won the war, and the boys are coming home, and bringing with them problems that will have to be dealt with in a manner which will require the best thought of all political parties and of all members, of this House. We have many causes for rejoicing and thanksgiving when we remember the cloud under which we foregathered a year ago and the auspices under which we now meet. A year ago the horizon was dark and forbidding as a result of the most strenuous campaign of the four years of war. The enemy was not only as strong as ever, but according to report was stronger in man-power than at any previous time during the war. An immense army had been mobilized during the winter, and the Canadian boys along with our Allies were facing a foe ready for all eventualities, it was supposed. It was indeed a time in which our cause, so to speak, hung more or less in the balance. Thanks to the valour of our troops and to the Divine help that we believe was vouchsafed to our armies, things soon began to brighten, but we certainly had to pass through dark days. It is not many months ago that the famous message of Field Marshal Haig rang out to his troops and to every part of the civilized world-"Men, put your backs to the wall. Die at your post rather than retire." That message will be handed down through the ages with the great message of Lord Nelson a hundred years ago at Trafalgar-"England expects that every man this day will do his duty." Both these messages are in the same high rank. The traditions of our forces and those of our Allies certainly justified all the faith we placed in them. They won out. But at what a price! While we mourn the departed statesman to w'hom I referred a moment ago and one or two others whose places are empty in this House, I want to offer a word of sympathy particularly to those members who have had their family circle broken by this terrible war. There is many a vacant seat around many a splendid fireside in the Dominion of Canada to-day as a result of this war. Our young men have died, however, for a noble cause, and had they lived a thousand years it is a question whether they could have died in a greater cause.
They displayed heroism, devotion and selfsacrifice. Those are among the highest
qualities that humanity can display. They are taught in the good iBook, and I can only say to those who mourn the broken family circle, that they have good cause to believe that the great Master who gave His life for others will not forget the sacrifice of the boys of Canada who gave their lives in so great a cause-humanity, civilization and religion. Some people, it is true, have been worried about the final destiny of those who have been called to leave the earthly house of this tabernacle and pass to the great beyond. We know not, but we believe the Judge of all the earth will do right, and I, for one if it is any satisfaction to gentlemen whose family circles have been broken, am prepared to say that, so far as I read the Scriptures and interpret them, the Judge of all the earth will see that those men who have given their lives, who have not hesitated to lay down their lives for others will be found at the right hand, " where loyal hearts and true stand ever in the light, all raptured through and through, in God's most holy sight." I believe that we can leave those heroes in the hand of the Judge of the earth, knowing that he will do right. We know, Mr. Speaker, that this war has only been won as a result of great efforts. It caused a great deal of trouble in this land to raise the army that was raised and keep it up to strength until Tlie finish, but that was accomplished, Mr. Speaker, and it was only accomplished by great sacrifices and denial of one's own inclinations in sending to the front the splendid boys who went there, and keeping them up to strength. That, however, has been done and when the war came to an end, be it known and be it spread abroad to all the earth, that Canada was going just as strong at the finish as she went at the outset. The guns that spoke at Mons commenced the war, and the guns at^ Mons finished the war, because if you take it from Mons to Mons you have the whole history of the war. That is where the British guns first spoke. But they came back to Mons, thanks to the splendid generalship and heroism of men in the providence of God, though 1 driven from Mons and kept out of the battle line there for four years. The Canadians were back in Mons when the last gun was fired. The Canadians were there to fire it, and we have the testimony, not only of laymen but of military men who know whereof they speak, that the one division or the one army corps that Canada had at the front was the strongest fighting unit not only of the British Empire but of all the armies of the Allies, none was equal to the splen-

did fighting Canadian boys that were left at the front the day the last gun was fired at Mons. That is something to be proud of, and that is some reason to rejoice, but I say this has only been accomplished by self-denial not only on the part of the members of this House but of the people of Canada, and of the sons of 'Canada, both those that were at home and those abroad. All this has been accomplished by immense effort. During this debate, Mr. Speaker, we have had remarks addressed front" the other side of the House to our separated brethren. Perhaps, it would not be inappropriate for me to say a few words as a counterpart of that, and address myself more particularly through you, Mr. Speaker, to the united brethren. We have separated brethren and we have united brethren.
Manufacturers.

Yes, manufacturers and farmers all sitting happy and contented over here at the present time. Separated brethren! How you must dislike, that word, hon. gentlemen-"separated." Indifference, lost friendship and all such things come back to you, whilst on this side of the House you see united brethren. You behold them smiling. See how happy and contented they are here, and we are making them welcome. We are giving them a home of which they will take full advantage, and I, for one, trust they are going to stay with us for many a day. It is far better to speak about unity than it is to speak about separation, and I cannot but think that our friends on the other side that invented that term, "separated brethren," will hear the echo ringing down for weeks and months and years, in such a way that they will wish they had not thought of separated brethren, because the separated brethren are united with us, and we are inviting them to stay, and we believe they are going to stay. We have much more to offer them than friends opposite have, and for a very good reason. What was the reason that your separated brethren left the doctrines you preach? It was because your doctrines were not sound.
It was because you were preaching a doctrine that would not save the country and the Empire and that would not win the war. These gentlemen who came from the other side and united with us came over for a reason^ and that reason, Mr. Speaker, was to win the war, and the best answer we can give to you to-day is that the war is won, and that those men had something to do with winning it, and 
if they never do anything great in their lives in the future history will not forget every man jack that came out and became a separated brother for a short time. But he was taken into a far better fold, at any rate, and their names will be handed down as men who sacrificed something in order that the war might be won. The war has been won, and what has been the result of the winning of the war? The winning of the war, Mr. Speaker, is the greatest thing that has ever been done in all the ages since Adam delved and Eve spun down to the present time. Never was there so great a cause. Never was there so much at stake, and never was there more brilliancy won than that which has been won on the battlefields of Europe in the last four years. It was worth while. Humanity has been saved. Christianity has been saved. The right of small nations to live, the right to enjoy justice, freedom and order, not only in the great lands, but also in the small lands, has been achieved, not only among great people, but also among the minor classes. Those are only some of the things that have been won. Why, Mr. Speaker, the prophets and kings have desired .long to see the sight that we see now and have not seen it, and to hear the things that we hear this day, and have not heard them. We have to-day practically a ransomed world as a result of this war, and those gentlemen who came out from the Opposition have given up what we all know is very dear to them, party unity and party ties. I have been a strong party man myself, and I know what that means. I say, all honour to these men, who, in the face of all this, were ready to come over to usj who are ready to sacrifice, it may be, their own outlook and their own advantage in order that the best effort of the Dominion of Canada should be continued and that our troops at the front should be increased. That has all been done and the result justifies the means. In addition to all these things which have been saved to humanity, I may point out a thing that has not often been mentioned in this House, and which is too frequently overlooked in the country, and that is not only has civilization and Christianity been placed in comparative safety as a result of the war, but the great Holy Land which, for a thousand years has called for the best efforts of the nations of Europe, for which many a crusade was undertaken, for which many a spear was sharpened, many a sword ground-the land of Palestine, with its capital, Jerusalem the Golden, the Holy

City, has been wrenched from the hands of the Turk, the infidel, and to-day the British flag floats over Jerusalem, the ancient city of the Jews, about which so many promises have been made and about which cluster so many glorious memories. The Holy Land and Jerusalem have been saved to civilization, and I trust that, after all the blood and treasure that have been expended, never again will these holy places pass into the hands of the Turk and the heretic. That is something that has been accomplished by the war. All honour to the men who came out from the other side and joined us in order that the best that Canada could do should be done in the interests of civilization and humanity.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that mistakes have been made, and, no doubt, have been made by the Government. It is true that some things might have been done that call for criticism. I am not so strong a party man, even a Unionist or a Conservative, that I do not see there are some things that might be different. 1 am not going to spend much time in criticising the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite, but before passing from this particular part of my address, I want to take exception to some remarks which were made by at least two hon. gentlemen opposite, both comparatively new members of the House, and who, I am sorry to see, are not in their seats at the present moment. I am not going to say anything in their absence that I would not say if they were here, and I want it to be understood that any references I make are more to the matter of their speeches than they are personal with regard to the individuals with whom I am called upon to deal. I regret to say that one of these hon. gentlemen, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), made what I conceive to be one of the most damaging statements that was ever made in this House, and that is a good deal to say. I believe that perhaps he did not intend that it should be considered as seriously as I look upon it. But, his reference to the Bolsheviki and his defence of them, in my judgment, was the most serious offence that has ever been committed in this House in my hearing.
I think it is time that this country knew the danger of the Bolsheviki and their doctrines. It is time that they should be put down. It is time that the laws of Canada should be enforced against those who have come over from the old lands, have found sanctuary here and do not appreciate it any more than to preach doctrines so subversive of all law, order and
decency as the Bolsheviki have done in Russia, and as they will do here if permitted. In a free country like Canada no such doctrines as those are justified. In a free country no such company should be introduced, and I regret that the hon. member for Brome found it necessary to enter into a defence of a doctrine that I conceive to be absolutely indefensible.
What is their doctrine?

You have it there in Hansard, and you are a better authority probably on it than I am. I understand that the hon. member for Brome draws his inspiration from the Manchester Guardian. I am a bit of a Lancashire man myself, I know the (Manchester Guardian fairly well and I tell the hon. member for Brome that I consider that he is drawing his inspiration from a very bad and unsafe quarter

Oh, yes-I say a very bad quarter and a very unsafe quarter if he is guided by the Manchester Guardian. It is an unsafe guide for gentlemen opposite to pin their defence of the Bolsheviki too. I am going to take the risk of. saying that I do not believe that this country will ever lie down to such a doctrine as the Bolsheviki preach. What have they done? Did they get elected to power? Not at all. They seized the reins of government. Seized the reins of government, by what?-by the ballot?-no, but by force-absolutely by force, and where do they draw the line? They announce a doctrine which says that you shall shoot down every man who wears a white collar, or a white shirt. They attack women, carry off everything valuable, and disrupt the country. In what way do they convert a man? At the point of the bayonet and at the rifle's mouth. Strong arguments indeed! Yet, we find in this Parliament some hon. gentlemen uttering a defence of that doctrine. The people of Canada will never allow such a doctrine as that to prevail here. You may try to cause a rift between capital and labour, between the so-called classes and the so-called masses, but I tell you that in my

I am just endeavouring to elucidate the doctrine of the Bolsheviki which I understand the hon. gentleman was backing. I say that that doctrine will never prevail in Canada. The women know when they have got a fairly 'good thing and they are not going to let it go until they have got something better. The women are allowed to rule in this country in a way in which they could not rule were the doctrines of the Bolsheviki to prevail and they are going to say: "While we have some evils at home, we had better bear the ills we have than fly to others that we know not of." The member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) may rest assured that his defence of the Bolshevik will not prevail in this country, because that doctrine is one of the most dangerous and seditious that could be formulated here.

I regret that, among other things, some slight reference was not made in the speech from the Throne to labour conditions, the hours of labour, and the wages paid in this country. I am often accused of being a hard-hearted employer, but in my judgment the very best that we can do for labour and for the working man should be done. In order to do that, we must have conditions that justify giving these shorter hours and these high wages. I do not think that either of these things can be brought about in the way the member for Brome suggests. The member for Brome has a tearing down rather than a building up policy. It is easy to criticise. It is easy to pull down the old structure, but it takes a better and a stronger man to put up something better in its place. While we may deplore the difficulties surrounding Canadian trade and Canadian labour conditions, after all, Canada is a fairly happy country for the workingman, and conditions have materially improved during the war. Personally, I trust that we shall not go back to where we were before the war; getting back to pre-war conditions is not my conception of living up to all that we should do. We should stay where we are in so far as we have made advances; we should not make a retrograde step. At any rate, I for one hope that wages will never get back as low as they were. If there ever was a time in the history of Canadian trade when the best judgment should be used, it is now. Many tremendous problems face us which it is going to be very difficult to meet successfully. We must not be pessimists, but optimists. Before I sit down I want to make a brief reference to the Peace Conference. That may be considered a little aside of our functions in this House-
No.

-but as it is a matter of such great moment, I think I would be justified in venturing just a very few remarks upon the Peace Conference and its likely outcome. Sir Robert Borden, the leader of this House, is over there and is, I believe, trying to represent Canada to the best of his ability at one of the greatest gatherings that has ever in the history of the world been assembled. The destinies of nations hang upon it. The map of Europe is being changed. The limits of almost every country in Europe are being defined. Questions of race, creed-everything of that kind are being settled. The whole of Europe is in the melting-pot, as well as a good deal of Asia and some of South Africa. Thank Heaven this continent is free, but the territories of a large portion of the nations of the earth are in the melting-pot, and the maps are being made. We are desirous that all things should be settled on the best and surest foundation, so that peace and happiness, truth and justice, religion and piety may prevail through coming generations. That is the desire of everybody, although it is going to be very hard to reach it. President Wilson of the United States has gone across the water-a thing that has never been' done before by any President of the United States since that confederation became a reality. It has always been considered to be ueyond the prerogative of the President of the United States to leave his country while occupying the presidential chair. President Wilson has broken through that rule on account of this being the most important call that any President of the United States has ever had and he has gone across the ocean. He has taken with him certain ideals. All honour to those who have splendid ideals, and President Wilson has really splendid ideals. I do not desire to belittle all that the United States have done in this war; the heroism with which their boys have acquitted themselves at the front, the splendid speed with which they got them across the water, the way in which they got out the arms and
[Mr. Cockkhutt.[
munition and equipment and furnished an army of almost 2,000,000 men inside of twelve months. All honour to the splendid effort they made, but President Wilson has an ideal and an idea that a league of nations can be formed that will preserve peace in the- world for ever more. Far be it from me to cast any doubts upon the success of this great enterprise. I hope it will be all that is expected. I am free to confess that in my judgment it is too idealistic to meet the spirit of the times yet; that the millennium is not sufficiently near at hand to justify anyone in believing that we shall never have any more wars in the world. I understand that General Pau, who is in the city of Ottawa-I have not yet had the pleasure of hearing him-has made the statement that it is useless and idle for us to believe that all wars are at an end. That was my view before General Pau made his statement and his statement only goes to confirm my opinion in that respect that wars will yet be; that while the world exists wars will not cease. We are told so in the Scriptures. I believe that to be the case and that wars and rumours of wars will continue to the end as long as humanity is as frail as it is, and constructed on so frail a foundation as many of us stand upon. This is not an ideal condition, but I believe it is one that is going to stay with us, and believing that I submit that it would have been wiser for the nations assembled at the Peace Conference to frame a safe and lasting peace treaty and sign that first rather than to endeavour to make a league of nations which may take a few months or longer to work out and which may in the end not prove a success. I submit that only as a criticism of the work that is being done. I simply profess to be a poor, humble layman in that respect and cannot see so far as those men who are assembled there; but my desire is that a lasting peace shall be obtained and that we shall not be robbed by politicians of the work that our men have done in the field. Their heroism has done its share. I have pointed out in the beginning of my speech and I cannot do better than to conclude with the same words, namely, that the boys at the front have brought all honour and glory to this country by their splendid heroism on the field. They were acknowledged to be the spear-head of the armies at the front. They were saved for all the knotty points, for every critical occasion; the Canadian boys were there, and in the final stages they never went after anything that they did

not get. I say that in this re-
5 p.m. spect this House and the country have every reason to rejoice that our boys have displayed all those characteristics that make them physically, morally and mentally the equal of any people in the world. What has been accomplished by Canadians on the battlefield, what has been achieved by heroism, self-denial and devotion to duty on the field can be accomplished in this House and in this country if we are as alive to our duties as the boys overseas have been to theirs. If we are as loyal to our duties as the boys overseas have been to theirs, every one of these mountains in our way that now seem insurmountable will be swept away, and we shall stand a united, contented, and a Christian people that need take a back seat to no other nation in the world.

Since prorogation of Parliament, last May, great and momentous events have happened through the world as well as in Canada. We have witnessed the triumph of Justice and Right-, the crushing of Prussian militarism, Hun barbarism and German autocracy. Under the command of the illustrious Marshal Foch, the Allies have vanquished the Teutonic hordes, broken -through the impr-egnable Hindenberg line, and forced the German armies to beg for mercy; they have brought about the downfall of the haughty and snarling kaiser and obtained, on 'November 11 last, the armistice ending the hostilities and putting a stop to the atrocities of this frightful war which appalled the world for over four years.
While at present holding a conference, the Allies are making use of all the talents and energies of their greatest statesmen, and are calling upon all the resources of diplomacy to lay the foundations of a durable peace, which shall open a new era of progress and civilization and make the renewal of the war an impossibility.
As mentioned in the speech from the Throne, none of the troops who took part in the -struggle proved to be more valiant and daring than the Canadians. Their heroism throughout this war has won for their country undying fame.
I take pride in the bravery and gallantry of our soldiers; our men have behaved like heroes. Let us honour the memory of those who fell on the battlefield. May we respect and protect, without delay or faltering, those who were spared from the shells, shrapnel and gases of the Germans.
However, the glorious events which I have just alluded to have made way, here in Canada, to a very sad and sorrowful occurence, which our hearts and minds are loath to accept as an accomplished fact. The empty seat here before me, the laurel wreath which adorns it, are more eloquent than any panegyric of the undying fame of him who has departed. Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier is no more . . .
As one of the last survivors of the Liberal group elected at the time of Sir Wilfrid's glorious accession to power in 1896, I feel, it soems, more than any one else the immense gap which his death has created in this House. I find, however, satisfaction and consolation in the thought of always having remained true to him, through bright and dark days, in triumph and defeat, in power and opposition, and it is not for me to feel the pang of remorse at having, at the last minute, proved unfaithful to the greatest, most noble and illustrious Canadian in the social, economic and political history of Canada. Aye, great all through his life, he proved still greater in death; always and everywhere his actions and words were noble and generous; and impartial history will reveal his career to future generations as having been illustrious both at home and abroad.
May those who lived in his days and those who will come after him never forget the high ideal towards which were bent-all his energies from the very beginning' of his public life-the establishment of union and harmony between the two great races of this young country.
In his lifetime we loved him, we admired him and we respected him; under his wise direction the ship of state sailed clear of dangerous rocks put in the way by unscrupulous adversaries who were very often blinded by their hatred of all that is French and Catholic. Let us hope that death has disarmed those despicable foes and that the pact of Confederation, that our lamented chief has always safeguarded like the apple of his eye, will be maintained in all its integrity by all Governments to come.
The main idea that runs all through the Governor General's speech that is now before us, is that of the industrial, financial, commercial and economic reconstruction of Canada. In other words, Parliament is invited to solve the entangled problem of the after-war policy of this country. It is a problem the importance, of which the Government failed to grasp if we are to judge by what has been done since the cessation oi hostilities and the signing of the armis-
